translation: Well, what am I, then? — they all do it; they glory in their diseases and in self-conceit, while I perhaps do even more than they. Let’s not argue; my objection is foolish. But still, I am firmly convinced that not only an excess of consciousness, but even any kind of consciousness is a disease. I stand by that. Let’s set that aside for a moment. Tell me this: why did it happen that, as if on purpose, at the very same times, in which I was most capable of perceiving the subtlest nuances of ‘all that is beautiful and noble,’ as we used to say, I would fail to perceive and would do such unseemly deeds, such that… yes, I mean, which, while all do them, would happen to coincide precisely with the times when I was most conscious of how I shouldn’t do them at all? The more I was conscious of the good and of all that was ‘beautiful and noble,’ the deeper I would sink into my mire and the more capable I would be of sinking into it completely. But the main point was that all of this seemed to me as though it was not a coincidence but as though it should be so. As though this was my most normal state, not a disease and a corruption, so that, finally, the will to struggle against this corruption completely left me. It ended with me almost believing (and perhaps I really did believe), that this was perhaps my normal state. But at first, in the beginning, what suffering I endured in this struggle! I didn’t believe that it happened to others, and so I kept this a secret to myself all my life. I was ashamed (and perhaps I am still ashamed); I reached a point where I felt a certain secret, abnormal, underhanded pleasure in returning, on occasion, to my vilest Petersburg night and trying to be conscious that today, once again, I had done a foul deed, that the deed had been done and could not be undone, and to gnaw at myself internally, secretly, with my teeth, to chew and devour myself to such a degree that bitterness turned, finally, into a shameful, cursed sweetness, and finally — into a definite, serious enjoyment! Yes, into enjoyment, into enjoyment! I stand by that. I began to talk because I want to know for sure: do others experience such enjoyments? I will explain: the enjoyment here was due to the bright awareness of my own humiliation; from feeling that I had already reached the last wall; that it was bad but that it could not be otherwise; that I had no way out, that I would never be a different person; that even if there was still time and faith to be transformed into something else, I would not want to change; and even if I did want to, I would not have done anything, because, in fact, there might not be anything to change into. And the main point, the end of the matter, was that all this happens in accordance with the normal and basic laws of intensified consciousness and in inertia that flows from these laws, so that not only can one not change, but there is nothing one can do. For example, as a result of intensified consciousness: right, that he’s a scoundrel, as if that’s a consolation to the scoundrel, because he already feels that he is really a scoundrel. But that’s enough… Ah, what a mess I’ve made, and what have I explained? But I will explain! I will see this through to the end! I picked up my pen for this reason…

Well, what am I, then? – they all do it; they glory in their illnesses, and I, perhaps, even more than all of them. Let’s not argue; my objection is foolish. But still, I am firmly convinced that not only is there too much awareness, but that any awareness is an illness. I stand by that. Let’s leave that aside for a moment. Tell me this: why did it so often happen, as if on purpose, that during those very moments, yes, the very same moments, when I was most capable of grasping all the subtleties of the “beautiful and noble,” as they used to say, I would already fail to grasp, but instead commit such unseemly acts, such that… well, in any case, which everyone, perhaps, does, but which, as if on purpose, would be precisely when I was most aware that they should never be done at all? The more I was aware of goodness and of all this “beautiful and noble,” the deeper I sank into my muck and the more adept I became at being completely mired in it. But the main point was that it all seemed to be not accidental, but as if it should be that way. As if it were my most normal state, and not a disease or corruption, so that, finally, I lost all desire to fight this corruption. It ended in my almost believing (or perhaps I did indeed believe), that this might well be my most normal state. But at first, at the beginning, how much suffering I endured in that struggle! I did not believe that such things happened to others, and so I hid it all away as a secret my whole life. I was ashamed (and perhaps I still am); I would even go so far as to say that I would feel some kind of secret, abnormal, petty pleasure in returning, from time to time, to some vile St. Petersburg night, to a corner of my own, and strenuously be aware that today I had again committed some evil deed, that it could no longer be undone, and to gnaw at myself from the inside, secretly, with my teeth, to scrape and suck at myself until the bitterness turned into a shameful, cursed sweetness and finally into a firm, serious pleasure! Yes, into a pleasure, into a pleasure! I stand by that. I speak because I want to know for sure: do others have such pleasures? I will explain: the pleasure here was exactly from the overly clear awareness of my humiliation; from feeling that I had already gone to the very last wall; that it was indeed terrible, but that it could not be any other way; that there was no escape for me, that I would never be a different person; that if there was still time and faith to become something else, then I would certainly not want to change; and if I wanted to change, then I would not do anything because, in fact, there may not be anything to change into. The main thing, and the end of it all, was that all of this occurred according to the normal and fundamental laws of increased awareness and inertia directly flowing from these laws, so that here one could not only not change, but simply do nothing at all. For instance, as a result of increased awareness: right, that I am a scoundrel, as if this were comfort for a scoundrel who already feels that he is truly a scoundrel. But that’s enough… Ah, what a mess I’ve made, and what did I explain?… What explains this pleasure? But I will explain! I will carry this to its end! I took up my pen for this very reason…

K. waited day by day during the following week for further communication, unable to believe that his waiver of interrogations had been taken literally. When the expected communication did not come until the Saturday evening, he assumed he had been quietly re-invited to the same house for the same period of time. Thus, he went there again on Sunday, going straight up the stairs and through the corridors. Some people who recognized him greeted him at their doors, but he no longer had to ask anyone and soon found the right door. On knocking, it was opened for him immediately, and without bothering to look for the woman who stood by the door, he wanted to go into the adjoining room. "There is no meeting today," said the woman. "Why should there not be a meeting?" he asked, not wanting to believe it. But the woman convinced him by opening the door of the adjoining room. It was indeed empty and looked even more pitiful in its emptiness than the previous Sunday. On the table, which stood unchanged on the platform, lay some books. "Can I look at the books?" asked K., not out of particular curiosity, but only to have not been entirely in vain. "No," said the woman and closed the door again, "that is not allowed. The books belong to the investigating judge."

Ether from under a door crack. I began to pace. It occurred to me that I had been directed here, into this crowd, to this overflowing general consultation. It was, as it were, the first public acknowledgment that I belonged to the discarded; had the doctor discerned it in me? But I had made my visit in a tolerable suit and had sent in my card. Nevertheless, he must have found out somehow, perhaps I had betrayed myself. Now that it was a fact, I did not find it so bad; the people sat still and did not pay attention to me. Some of them suffered and swayed one leg slightly to make the pain easier to bear. Several men had their heads in their flat hands, others slept deeply with heavy, spilled-out faces. A fat man with a red, swollen neck sat bent over, staring at the floor, spitting periodically onto a spot that seemed fitting. A child sobbed in a corner; its long, thin legs it had pulled up onto the bench and now held pressed to its chest, as if bidding them farewell.

As short as possible, please. For the gentlemen had little time. I felt strangely disposed. The young men sat and looked at me with that superior, professional curiosity they had learned. The doctor I knew stroked his black moustache and smiled distractedly. I thought I would burst into tears, but I heard myself say in French: "I had the honour, my lord, to give you all the information I could. If you consider it necessary that these gentlemen be enlightened, you will doubtless be able to do so with a few words after our conversation, while it is very difficult for me." The doctor rose with a polite smile, went to the window with the assistants, and spoke a few words, accompanying them with a horizontal, swaying hand gesture. After three minutes, one of the young men, nearsighted and fidgety, returned to the table and asked, trying to look severe: "Are you sleeping well, my lord?" "No, badly." Then he sprang back to the group. There they argued for a while, then the doctor turned to me and told me they would summon me. I reminded him that I had been ordered at one o'clock. He smiled and made a few quick, springy movements with his small white hands, as if to say he was extremely busy. So I returned to my corridor, where the air had become much more oppressive, and began to pace again, though I was utterly exhausted. Finally, the musty, accumulating stench made me dizzy; I stood by the entrance and opened the door a little. I saw that it was still afternoon and there was a little sunlight outside, and that did me unspeakable good.

After three minutes, one of the young people, short-sighted and fidgety, returned to the table and, trying to look stern, said, "Do you sleep well, my lord?" "No, badly." He smiled and made a few quick, springy gestures with his small white hands, indicating he was extremely busy. I thus returned to my corridor, where the air had become much more oppressive, and began to pace again, even though I felt utterly exhausted. Finally, the damp, accumulated stench made me lightheaded; I stopped by the front door and opened it a little. I saw that it was still afternoon with some sunlight, and that did me incalculable good.

Buddha Shakyamuni extinguished the demon monkey and then summoned Nü and Kasyapa to return to the Western Pure Land. At this time, Tiantong and Tianyu rushed out of the Hall of Supreme Harmony and said, "Please wait a moment, Your Holiness, as our lord is arriving." Buddha Shakyamuni heard this and turned to look. Soon, he saw a procession with eight scenic sedan chairs and nine luminous canopies. There was a chanting of mystic songs and hymns, the recitation of incantations of boundless divine power, the scattering of celestial flowers, and the spraying of true incense, all of which went straight to Buddha Shakyamuni's feet and thanked him, saying, "Thank you for Your Holiness's great virtue in subduing the demon. Please wait for one day and allow us to have a grand banquet to express our gratitude." Buddha Shakyamuni did not dare to defy, so he joined his palms and said, "I was called here by the Great Celestial Ruler. How could I have any magical power? It is the Great Celestial Ruler and the great fortune of all the deities that are laboring to thank me." Buddha Sakyamuni extinguished the demon monkey and then summoned Nü and Kasyapa to return to the Western Pure Land. At this time, Tiantang and Tianyi rushed out of the Golden Imperial Palace and said, "Please wait a moment, your majesty is coming." Upon hearing this, Buddha Sakyamuni turned around and looked back. Soon, he saw the eight-scenery imperial carriage and nine-light umbrella; the sound of the celestial song and exquisite music, reciting countless divine chapters; scattering treasure flowers and emanating genuine fragrance until they reached his throne, where they bowed and thanked him, saying, "We thank your great method for subduing the demon. We wish the Buddha to wait one day and let all the immortals hold a feast to thank you." Buddha Sakyamuni did not dare to contradict, so he clasped his hands and replied, "The old monk came here following the orders of Heavenly Lord. What great power do I have? It is the Heavenly Lord and all the gods' great blessings that have summoned me, so you do not need to thank me." The Jade Emperor conveyed the order, instructing the cloud deities to invite the Three Pure Ones, Four Sovereigns, Five Elders, Six Officials, Seven Origins, Eight Extremes, Nine Planets, Ten Capitals, and all myriad deities to attend the gathering to thank Buddha. He also ordered the Four Great Taoist Immortals and nine celestial fairies to open the Jade Capital, Golden Imperial Palaces, and Cave Yang Precious Pavilion, and to have Buddha sit on the precious and divine tower. He arranged the seats for each class of deities and prepared dragon liver, phoenix brain, jade liquid, and peach of immortality.

Buddha Sakyamuni subdued the demon monkey and then summoned Nü and Kasyapa to return to the Western Paradise. At this time, Tiantong and Tianyou rushed out from the Jade Terrace and said, "Please wait a moment, His Majesty is coming." Hearing this, Buddha Sakyamuni turned around and looked. In a short while, it was indeed seen that eight scenic carriages were arriving, followed by nine bright canopies; music played in the background, chanting divine verses; lotus blossoms and true perfumes were scattered, right up to the Buddha's altar where they said, "We are grateful for your great virtue in subduing the demons and monsters. We hope you will stay for a day and allow us to prepare a banquet to express our gratitude." Buddha Sakyamuni did not wish to offend, and clasped his hands in gratitude, saying, "Your Highness has commanded me to come here, and I have no supernatural power. It is the merit of your Highness and the other gods that has allowed me to do this; how could I be worthy of such honor?" The Jade Emperor ordered the cloud deities to invite the Three Clarity Voids, Four Sovereigns, Five Elders, Six Departments, Seven Principles, Eight Extremes, Nine Planets, and Ten Fiefs, as well as all the myriad true and sacred beings, to attend the gathering and express their thanks for the Buddha's kindness. He also ordered the Four Great Heavenly Masters and the Nine Heavenly Nymphs to open the gates of the Jade Capital, Golden Palace, and Dantang Tranquil Hall to invite the Buddha to sit on the precious and spiritual platform, and to arrange seating and serve dragon liver, phoenix brain, jade dew, and peach of immortality.

Buddha Sakyamuni subdued the demon monkey and then called in Nvrey and Kasyapa to return to the Western Pure Land. At this time, Tiantang and Tiyou rushed out of the Jade Emperor's palace and said, "Please wait a moment, His Majesty is coming." Upon hearing this, the Buddha turned around to look. Soon enough, he saw eight-scene dragon coaches, nine-light ceremonial canopies; celestial music and songs of divine praise; scattering of precious flowers and the perfume of the True Fragrance; and they all approached the Buddha to offer thanks, saying, "Thank you for your grace in subduing the demon. Please wait for one more day; we will prepare a grand banquet to express our gratitude." The Buddha did not wish to refuse and clasped his hands in gratitude, saying, "I am merely following the heavenly emperor's command. What powers do I possess? It is your great fortune, my lord, that has allowed this, and I thank you for your kindness." The Jade Emperor issued orders, commanding the cloud spirits to invite the Three Pure Ones, Four Kings of the Universe, Five Elders, Six Departments, Seven Stars, Eight Extremes, Nine Planets, Ten Cities, and all the thousand true and ten thousand saints to this gathering to thank the Buddha for his benevolence. He also ordered the Four Great Immortal Teachers and the Nine Heavenly Nymphs to open the jade capitals, the palace of supreme mystery, and the palace of the sublimely pure to invite the Buddha to sit in the precious and miraculous platform. They arranged the seating according to rank, serving dragon liver and phoenix brain, and the elixir and peach of immortality.

Buddha Shakyamuni subdued the demon monkey and then called for Nu and Kasyapa to return to the Western Pure Land. At that moment, Tiantang and Tianyi hurriedly emerged from the Golden璘Tower and said, "Please wait a moment, Your Holiness. Our master is coming in state." Upon hearing this, Buddha Shakyamuni turned to look. Soon, he saw an eight-scene dragon coach, a nine-color canopy; the sounds of transcendent songs and wonderful music, and the recitation of countless divine scriptures; scattering of precious flowers, and the fragrance of true incense, all until before the Buddha. They knelt and thanked the Buddha, saying, "We are grateful for Your Holiness's great method in subduing the evil. We humbly ask Your Holiness to wait another day, so that all the immortals may hold a feast to thank you." Buddha Shakyamuni could not defy their request and clasped his palms in gratitude, saying, "I am only obeying the commands of the Heavenly Sovereign and have no great abilities. It is your vast good fortune that allowed me to perform this service, so there is no need for any thank-you." The Jade Emperor then issued orders, instructing the cloud spirits to invite the Three Pure Ones, the Four Kings, the Five Elders, the Six Officials, the Seven Startlosers, the Eight Extremes, the Nine Rays, the Ten Halls, and all the myriad true and immortal beings to this gathering to thank the Buddha. He also ordered the Four Heavenly Teachers and the Nine Celestial Immortal Maidens to open the Jade Capital, the Golden Mansion, the Palace of Great Mystery, and the Pavilion of Subtle Yang, and to invite the Buddha to sit on the precious and divine platform. The seating arrangements and the banquet were then prepared with dragon liver and phoenix marrow, and jades and immortal peaches.

Even as the Jade Emperor fumed in anger, he ordered the Left辅 Minister of State to strip him of his imperial robes, armor, and rank, and to lead him to the execution ground. Fortunately, the Red-Footed Great Heavenly Immortal overrode protocol to intercede on his behalf, beseeching the emperor to spare his life. The emperor decreed that he be banished to the eastern banks of the流沙 river, where he could feast when full and lie down in the mountain when hungry. If he was hungry, he should stir the waves to seek food. Woodcutters who encountered him met their end, and fishermen who saw him suffered the same fate. Many devouring and endlessly harmful, he vowed: "If you dare to commit such deeds at my door, today you will face my wrath. Do not speak of me being too coarse to eat; I will cut you and grind you into fish paste!" Hearing this, the pig demon grew furious and cursed, "You miserable creature, with no sense at all! I, the Old Pig, still exude vitality, and you dare to call me coarse and suggest fish paste! Clearly, you mistake me for the Old Salt. Do not be rude! Taste this!” The monster saw the pike spear coming and dodged it with a Phoenix Head Bow. They fought in the water, breaking through the waves and stepping on the ripples. This battle was unlike the last; observe: the Curtain-lowering Official and the Heavenly General of Pigs, each showing their true power in a truly wondrous way. The monster brandished his Magic Bone Staff over his head, while the Pigsnout wielded his Nine-Toothed Piked Staff with incredible speed. Their movements shook the mountains and surged the waters, the waves darkening the world. The demon was like a stern God of the Wilds, his actions as vile as a Door Opener of the Netherworld. This one, with unwavering loyalty to Tang Sanzang, and that one, mired in crime.

Even when the Jade Emperor fumed with anger, he commanded his Left辅Minister to preside over the administration: remove his hat, unsheathe his sword, and strip of his official rank; then push him onto the battlefield. Thankfully, the Red-Haired Heavenly Messenger overstepped his rank to intercede on his behalf, begging for his release. The emperor decreed a pardon, sparing his life, and instead demoted him to the eastern banks of the流沙River. When full, he would lie dormant in this mountain; when hungry, he would flip the waves in search of sustenance. Woodcutters would meet their end where he stood, and fishermen, upon sighting him, would perish. Many who encountered him were devoured, and his actions spread harm and violence far and wide. If you dare to transgress at my door, you shall face the consequences today. Do not say I am coarse and unfit to eat; I will chop you up and turn you into chili paste! Upon hearing this, Pig Eight-Hears was incensed and rebuked: "You impudent creature, you have no sense! Even I, Old Pig, am still moist and juicy, and yet you dare to say I am coarse and should be turned into chili paste! Clearly, you mistake me for Old Sores. Do not be so impertinent! Feel the wrath of my ancestors with this pike!" Seeing the pike coming, the monster ducked with a Phoenix-Headed Bow to avoid it. The two of them broke through the waves, stepping on the waves, and began a battle that was different from previous ones. Look at this: the Curtain-Opening General and the Heavenly General each showcased their true prowess. The subduing-beast Magic Staff was whirled overhead, while the nine-pronged pike was wielded with great speed. Their movements shook the mountains and stirred the waves, making the world look dark. As ferocious as the Earth Tyrant, it was as sinister as the Star of Disaster. This one, with a pure heart, vowed to protect Tripitaka, while the other, drunk on sin, sought to ravage the waters.

Even when Jade Emperor was enraged, he ordered the Left辅 Minister in Charge of the Court to remove his hat, take off his armor, and strip of his official title, then push him to the killing field. Fortunately, the Red-Haired Great Celestial Immortal stepped out of line to intercede and said he would allow the other to be released. He was spared death and banished to the eastern banks of the流沙River. When he was well-fed, he would take refuge in this mountain; when hungry, he would venture into the waves to seek food. Woodcutters met their end when they encountered him, and fishermen who saw him met their demise. He had devoured many who came and gone, and repeatedly injured countless lives. You dare to commit violence at my door today; today, your belly will find a way out. Don’t say I am coarse and unpalatable! I will grab you, stop you, and chop you into mincemeat and salted pork!” At this, Zhu Bai was enraged and cursed, "You insolent thing, completely without sense! I, Old Pig, am still oozing blood, and you dare to say I am coarse and want to chop me into mincemeat! It seems you take me for Old Chalk! Don’t be impudent! I’ll let my ancestor’s spade take care of you!" The monster saw the spade coming and dodged with a phoenix-head dip. Both fought, breaking through the water and stepping on waves. The newcomer seemed to avoid speaking much about himself; when he did speak, it was in commonplaces with noticeable modesty, and the conversation in such cases took on a somewhat bookish turn. He considered himself a negligible worm in this world, unworthy of much concern, and had experienced much over his lifetime. He had endured much hardship in his service for truth, had many enemies who even attempted to take his life, and now, seeking peace, he wished to finally choose a place to reside. When he arrived in this city, he felt it was his duty to convey his respects to its leading officials. That was all the city learned about this new face, which did not take long to show itself at the governor’s reception. The preparations for the reception took more than two hours, and in this newcomer, there was such a meticulous attention to dress that it was rarely seen elsewhere. After a short afternoon nap, he had himself washed and lathered his cheeks for a very long time, propping them up inside with his tongue. Then, taking a napkin from the inn servant’s shoulder, he thoroughly wiped his entire face, beginning behind his ears and fuming at the inn servant twice in his face. Then, he donned a waistcoat in front of a mirror, plucked two stray hairs from his nose, and immediately thereafter appeared in a fawn-colored frock coat with a spark. Thus attired, he rolled out in his own carriage along the infinitely wide streets, illuminated with slender light from the few distant oceans that flickered here and there. However, the governor’s mansion was brightly lit, even for a ball; a carriage with lanterns, two guards at the door, and the cries of the foresters in the distance—everything was as it should be. Upon entering the ballroom, Mr. Chichikov had to blink for a moment because the brilliance from the candles, lamps, and ladies’ dresses was horrifying. Everything was bathed in light. Black frock coats flitted and swirled apart and in clusters, as flies dart about on a white, glistening confection during a hot July day, when the old housekeeper cuts and slices it before an open window; children all gaped, gathered around, watching intently the jerky movements of her hard hands raising the mallet, while the aerial squadrons of flies, disturbed by the light breeze, confidently swooped in, taking advantage of the old woman’s dim eyesight and the sun that dazzled her, showering the tempting morsels with scattered bites or dense clusters. Rich and lush from the summer, scattering tempting dishes at every step, they flew in not to eat but merely to show themselves, to stroll back and forth across the sugar heap, to rub one leg against the other, to scratch under their wings, or, extending both front legs, to rub them above their heads, to turn around, and to fly away, and then to return with fresh squadrons of harassers. Before Chichikov could even look around, he was already being tugged by the hand by the governor, who immediately introduced him to the governor’s wife. The newcomer did not lower himself there either: he said a suitable compliment, very befitting for a middle-aged man with a rank neither too high nor too low. When the couples who had already taken to dancing pressed everyone against the wall, he, with his hands behind his back, stared attentively at them for two whole minutes. Many ladies were well-dressed and fashionable, while others put on what they had at hand for a provincial city. The men, as everywhere, were of two kinds: the thin ones who fluttered around the ladies; some of them were so thin that it was hard to tell them from the St. Petersburg types, with their very well-groomed or just plausible mustaches combed with care and taste. They leaned to the ladies as carelessly and flirted in French as much as in St. Petersburg. The other kind of men were fat, or just as fat as Chichikov, not too fat, but not too thin either. These avoided the ladies and looked around to see if the governor’s servants had set up a green table for whist. Their faces were round and plump, some even had warts, and some were freckled. They did not wear their hair in traditional styles like topskirts, curls, or the “damn me” style as the French say. Instead, they had hair that was either short-cropped or slicked back, with rounder and stronger features. These were the honored officials in the city. Alas! the fat ones are better at doing business in this world than the thin ones. The thin ones serve mainly on specific assignments or just exist and flit around; their existence is too light, airy, and unreliable. The fat ones never occupy indirect positions but always direct ones, and when they sit down, they do so securely and firmly, so that the place will crack and bend under them rather than they will fall. They do not care about outward splendor; their frock coats are not as finely tailored as those of the thin ones, but in their desk drawers lies the blessing of the Lord. In three years, the thin one will not have a soul left in pawn at the bank, while the fat one, when he suddenly appears at the end of the city, will have a house purchased in his wife’s name, and then in another part of the city, another house, then a village close to the city, and finally a village with all its lands. Finally, after serving God and the state and earning general respect, the fat one leaves service, moves to the countryside, and becomes a glorious Russian landowner, a breadwinner, and lives happily ever after. And his heirs, in the Russian custom, will again bequeath his possessions to his courier messengers. One cannot help but notice that such thoughts occupied Mr. Chichikov while he was observing the company, and the result of this was that he finally joined the fat ones, where he encountered almost all familiar faces: the procurator with very dark, thick eyebrows, who winked his left eye as if to say, "Come, brother, to another room, I’ll tell you something," a serious and taciturn man; the postmaster, a short man but a wit and a philosopher; the chairman of the chamber, a very thoughtful and amiable person, who all welcomed him like an old acquaintance, to which Chichikov bowed slightly to the side, albeit with some pleasure. There he also met the accommodating and courteous landowner, Manilov, and the somewhat awkward Sobakevich, who had stubbed his toe on Chichikov’s foot, saying, "Please forgive me." They also handed him a card for whist, which he took with a courteous bow. They sat down at the green table and did not rise until dinner. All conversation ceased as it always does when one finally takes up something practical. Although the postmaster was a great talker, as soon as he took the cards in his hands, he instantly adopted a thinking expression, covered his lower lip with his upper, and maintained this posture throughout the game. After drawing a figure, he struck the table with a strong hand, saying, "There goes the old hag!" if a queen, and "There goes the Togliatti peasant!" if a king. The chairman said, "I’ll give him a beard! I’ll give her a beard!" Occasionally, during the strike of the cards on the table, exclamations would erupt: "Ah! I’ll take it or leave it, never mind, I’ll take it with the hearts!" or simply, "Hearts! Heartworms! Picnicias! Picnirass! Piccurushuk!" or "Piccurush!"—names they had given the suits in their society. After the game, they argued noisily as usual. Our newcomer also argued but in a manner that seemed so artful that everyone saw he was arguing, yet it was pleasant to do so. He never said, "You made a mistake," but rather, "You decided to play," "I had the honor to cover your double," and the like. To further agree with his opponents on something, he always offered his silver box inlaid with mother-of-pearl, which contained two violets placed inside for fragrance. The newcomer’s attention was especially drawn to Manilov and Sobakevich, of whom he had just inquired. A few questions revealed not only his curiosity but also his thoroughness. First, he asked about the number of serfs each had and the state of their estates, and then he inquired about their names and surnames. In a short time, he had completely charmed them. Manilov, not yet a very old man, with sweet eyes like sugar, which he would squint every time he smiled, was utterly smitten. He held Chichikov’s hand for a long time and earnestly invited him to visit his village, which was only fifteen versts from the city gate. To which Chichikov responded with a courteous bow and a genuine handshake, saying that he was very willing to do so, and that he would visit them with great pleasure.

Although the postmaster was very eloquent, he immediately displayed a thoughtful expression upon taking the cards, covered his lower lip with his upper one, and maintained this position throughout the game. Exiting a card, he struck the table forcefully with his hand, saying if it was a queen, "She went, the old witch!" and if it was a king, "He went, the Tambov peasant!" The chairman said, "I’ll pluck his beard! I’ll pluck her beard!" Occasionally, during the sound of cards hitting the table, exclamations would burst out: "Ah! it’s a risk, no, for a bell!?" Or simply, "Hearts! Heartworms! Pikeniass! Pikendras! Pickurushuk! Pickur!" and even simply, "Pickuh!"—the names they had given to the suits in their company. After the game, they argued quite loudly as usual. Our newcomer also argued but with such skill that everyone saw he was arguing but still enjoyed it. He never said, "You went," but "You chose to go," "I had the honor to cover your double," and the like. To further agree with his opponents, he always held out his silver scented case, with two violets placed at the bottom for fragrance, to each of them. The newcomer's attention was especially occupied by the landowners Manilov and Sobakevich, about whom he had spoken earlier. He immediately inquired about them, calling the chairman and the postmaster over to him. Several questions he asked revealed not only his curiosity but also his depth; first, he inquired about the number of peasants and the condition of their estates, and then he asked about their names and surnames. In a short time, he managed to completely captivate them. Manilov, a man not yet too old, with sweet eyes like sugar who squinted every time he smiled, was in a daze for a long time, praising him and asking to visit his village, which, according to his words, was only fifteen versts from the city gate. To which Chichikov replied with a very courteous bow and a sincere handshake that he was only too glad to fulfill this request.

The newcomer seemed to avoid talking much about himself; if he did speak, it was with some commonplace remarks and a noticeable modesty, and his conversation then took on a somewhat bookish turn: he considered himself a mere worm of this world, unworthy of much concern, and he had endured much in his lifetime, suffering for the truth in his service, having many enemies who even tried to take his life, and now, wishing to settle down, he was looking to find a place to live. Upon his arrival in this city, he deemed it his duty to address the foremost officials with respect. That was all the city knew about this new face, which soon enough did not fail to make itself known at the governor’s ball. The preparation for this ball took more than two hours, and here the newcomer showed such an attention to his attire that such precision was not seen everywhere. After a light nap in the afternoon, he ordered water to be brought to wash, and he lathered his cheeks for a very long time, propping them up with his tongue inside. Then, taking a napkin from the tavern waiter’s shoulder, he wiped his entire face, starting from behind his ears and giving the tavern waiter a couple of snorts in the face. Next, he put on a waistcoat in front of the mirror, plucked two hairs from his nose, and immediately after that found himself in a violet coat with a spark. Thus attired, he rolled out in his own carriage down the infinitely wide streets, lit by meager illumination from the here and there appearing ocean. However, the governor’s house was lit sufficiently, even for a ball; a carriage with lamps in front, two policemen at the entrance, calls from a police officer in the distance—everything was as it should be. Entering the hall, Chichikov had to squint his eyes for a moment because the dazzling light from the candles, lamps, and the ladies’ dresses was terrible. Everything was flooded with light. The black coats flickered and moved apart and together here and there, just like flies on white confectionary in the middle of a hot July day, when the old scullery maid cuts and divides it into glittering shards before an open window; the children gather around, watching the movements of the stiff hands as they raise the hammer, while the airborne squadrons of flies, stirred by the light breeze, boldly march in as if they were the masters of the place, using the grandmother’s weak eyes and the glare from the sun to pepper the delectable chunks with one blow or stack them in dense heaps. Ample of the summer, and having spread luscious dishes all over the place, they arrived not to eat, but just to show themselves, to parade back and forth over the sugar pile, to rub one’s back legs against the other, or to scratch under the wings, or, stretching both front legs, to rub them above the head, to turn around, and then to fly away, only to arrive again with fresh fleets of annoying squadrons. Before Chichikov could take in his surroundings, he was already being held by the hand by the governor, who presented him to the governor’s wife right there. The newcomer did not fall short in this either: he said a rather appropriate compliment for a man of middle age with a not too small or too great rank. When the couples, accustomed to dancing, pressed everyone against the wall, he, crossing his hands behind his back, watched them attentively for two minutes. Many ladies were well dressed and in the latest fashion, others put on what fate had sent them to the provincial town. The men were of two kinds here, as everywhere: the thin ones, who all followed the ladies; some of them were of such a sort that it was hard to distinguish them from their Petersburg counterparts, who had their sideburns carefully combed or a very good-looking, very smoothly shaven oval face, similarly tilting to the ladies, similarly speaking French, and similarly entertaining the ladies as in Petersburg. The other kind of men were the thick ones, or such as Chichikov, that is, neither too thick nor too thin. These looked and backed away from the ladies and only kept an eye out, wondering if the governor’s servant had set up a green table for whist somewhere. Their faces were round and full, some even had warts, some were ruddy, they did not wear hair on their heads as pigtails, curls, or in the way Frenchmen say "accursed be the devil," but their hair was either cut short or combed down, and the features were more rounded and sturdy. These were the honored officials in the city. Alas! the thick ones handle their affairs better in this world than the thin ones. The thin ones serve more for special commissions or only number among the list and swivel here and there; their existence is too light, airy, and utterly unreliable. The thick ones never occupy secondary positions but only direct ones, and if they sit somewhere, they sit securely and firmly, so much so that the place will sooner crack and bend under them than they will fall. They do not love outward shine; their coats are not as well-tailored as those of the thin ones, but they have bliss in their treasure chests. The thin one’s creditors seize his last soul in a pawnshop within three years; the thick one, just look, and there will appear somewhere at the end of the town a house purchased in his wife’s name, then in another end another house, then a village near the town, then a village with all its lands. Finally, after serving God and the state, and earning general respect, the thick one retires, moves, and becomes a prosperous Russian lord, a breadwinner, and lives, and lives well. And then his thin heirs again dispose of the entire paternal estate through couriers as per the Russian custom. It cannot be denied that reflections of such a sort occupied Chichikov at the time when he was observing the gathering, and the result of this was that he finally joined the thick ones, where he met most of the familiar faces: the procurator with very dark, thick eyebrows, and a slight wink of his left eye as if to say, "Come, brother, to another room, there I’ll tell you something," a person serious and taciturn; the postmaster, a short man, but a jester and philosopher; the head of the chamber, a very judicious and kind person, who all welcomed him as an old acquaintance, to which Chichikov slightly bowed, but not without pleasure. He also met the very courteous and polite landowner Manilov and the somewhat clumsy, in the eyes of others, Sобакевич, who, on the first attempt, stepped on his foot and said, "I beg your pardon." They then thrust him a whist card, which he received with the same courteous bow. They sat down at the green table and did not get up until dinner. All conversations completely ceased, as always happens when one finally devotes oneself to a worthy occupation. Although the postmaster was very eloquent, even when he took up the cards, he immediately expressed a thinking visage, covered his lower lip with his upper one, and maintained that position throughout the game. When he went out of the card, he would strike the table with a firm hand, saying, if a queen, "She’s a crank!" and if a king, "He’s a Tamborian!" The head of the chamber would say, "I’ll shake his beard! I’ll shake her beard!" Occasionally, during the strikes of the cards on the table, expressions would escape, such as, "Ah! It was or wasn’t, it was a futility, so with the clubs!" Or simply exclamations, "Hearts! Cardio! Pikencians! Pikendras! Picurushuk! Picur!" and even simply, "Picuk!" — the names by which they had baptized the suits in their society. After the game, they quarreled, as usual, quite loudly. Our newcomer also argued, but in a surprisingly skillful manner, so that everyone saw that he was arguing, yet he argued pleasantly. He never said, "You made a mistake," but, "You had the courtesy to make the move," "I had the honor to cover your two," and so on. To further conciliate his opponents, he offered them his silver tobacco box with mother-of-pearl inlay, with two violets placed inside for fragrance. The newcomer’s attention was especially drawn to the landowners Manilov and Sобакевич, whom he had mentioned above. He immediately inquired about them, calling over the head of the chamber and the postmaster right away. A few questions he asked revealed in the guest not only curiosity but also thoroughness; first, he asked how many serfs each of them had and in what position their estates were, and then inquired about their first and last names. In a short time, he completely captivated them. The landowner Manilov, still not very old, with sweet eyes like sugar, which he squinted whenever he laughed, was utterly spellbound by him. He hugged his hand for a long time and earnestly invited him to come to his village, to which he claimed was only fifteen versts from the town’s boundary. To which Chichikov, with a very courteous nod and an honest handshake, replied that he was more than willing to comply with such a request.

The stranger seemed to avoid talking much about himself; if he did speak, it was in some generalities, with marked modesty, and the conversation took on a somewhat bookish turn. He said he was a negligible worm in the world, unworthy of much concern, that he had experienced much in his lifetime, had endured many hardships on service for the truth, had many enemies who had even tried to take his life, and that now, wishing to rest, he was seeking to find a place to live, and that having arrived in this city, he felt it was his duty to greet the city’s first dignitaries. This was all that the city learned about this new face, which did not fail to show itself at the governor’s soirée. The preparation for this soirée took more than two hours, and in the stranger there was such attention to grooming that it was not seen everywhere. After a short post-luncheon nap, he ordered to be washed and spent an extremely long time scrubbing both cheeks with lather, propping them up with his tongue inside; then, taking a handkerchief from the inn servant’s shoulder, he wiped his whole face from all sides, starting from behind his ears and even burping twice at the inn servant’s face. Then he donned a frock coat in front of a mirror, plucked two stray hairs from his nose, and shortly afterward appeared in a dark cherry evening coat with a spark. In this way dressed, he rolled off in his own carriage along the infinitely wide streets, lit by meager lighting from now and then visible oceans. However, the governor’s house was illuminated even for a ball; a carriage with lanterns, two mounted guards at the entrance, and far-off calls of the outriders—everything was as it should be. Upon entering the hall, Chichikov had to blink for a moment because the light from the candles, lamps, and the ladies’ gowns was frightful. Everything was bathed in light. Black frock coats flashed and darted in bunches and alone, as flies dart and buzz about a polished cake in the scorching July, when the old housekeeper chops and divides it into sparkling fragments at an open window, with children all around, watching with interest the movements of her stiff hands raising the axe, while the aerial squadrons of flies, lifted by the light air, enter boldly, like full masters, and, taking advantage of the old woman’s bad eyesight and the sun’s glare, bespatter the luscious pieces everywhere, in lumps or in thick heaps. Sated with summer’s riches, and already placing luscious dishes all along the way, they did not enter to eat, but to show themselves, to stroll back and forth over the sugar mound, to rub their back legs or their front ones, or to scratch under their wings, or, stretching out both front legs, to rub them over their heads, to turn around, and to take off, and then to return with fresh squadrons of annoying bugs. Chichikov had not even had time to observe the crowd when he was already seized by the governor, who introduced him on the spot to the governor’s wife. The stranger did not lower himself here either; he made a compliment, rather appropriate for a man of middle age with a not too large or too small rank. When the established couples pressed everyone against the wall, he, crossing his hands behind his back, stared at them attentively for two minutes. Some ladies were well-dressed and fashionable, while others wore whatever came to hand in the provincial town. Men, as everywhere, were of two kinds: some were thin, fluttering about the ladies; some of them were so thin that it was hard to distinguish them from the Petersburgians, they had very thoughtfully and tastefully combed moustaches or just decent, very smooth-shaved oval faces, they sidled up to the ladies just as the Petersburgians did, and they spoke French just as they did, and amused the ladies just as they did in Petersburg. The other kind were thick or just like Chichikov, that is, not too thick, but not too thin either. These, on the contrary, avoided the ladies and only looked around, checking if the governor’s servant had placed a green table for whist. Their faces were round and full, on some even were warts, some were freckled, they did not have hair on their heads in the style of queues, curls, or “damn me,” as the French say—on the contrary, their hair was either short or combed, and their faces more rounded and strong. These were the city’s honorable officials. Alas! the thick do better in this world to get things done than the thin. The thin serve mostly on special orders or just register and move from place to place; their existence is too easy, ethereal, and totally unreliable. The thick, on the contrary, never occupy indirect positions but all direct ones, and if they sit anywhere, they do so firmly and strongly, so that it is more likely for the place to crack and bend under them than for them to fall. They do not love a superficial glitter; their frock coats do not fit as neatly as those of the thin, but there is grace in their money boxes. In three years the thin leave not a soul behind when they go to pawn, while the thick, look, and there appears somewhere at the end of the city a house bought in the wife’s name, then another house in another end, then a village near the city, then a village with all its lands. Finally, after serving God and the state, and earning general respect, the thick leave the service, move, and become a wealthy Russian landowner, a breadwinner, and live happily. And after them, the successors, following the Russian custom, ride off with couriers to inherit all their father’s property. One cannot but admit that such reflections occupied Chichikov while he was observing society, and as a result, he finally joined the thick, where he met almost all familiar faces: the prosecutor with very dark and thick eyebrows and a slightly winking left eye, as if to say: “Come, brother, into another room, there I’ll tell you something,” a person serious and taciturn; the postmaster, a short person, but a wit and a philosopher; the chairman of the chamber, a very reasonable and agreeable person—everyone welcomed him as an old acquaintance, to which Chichikov nodded slightly askew, though with pleasure. There he met the very courteous and polite landowner Manilov and the somewhat awkward Sopotkevich, who at first step on his foot, saying: “Excuse me.” There they gave him a card for whist, which he received with the same polite bow. They sat down at the green table and did not stand up until dinner. All conversations ceased completely, as always happens when someone finally devotes themselves to something useful. Although the postmaster was very talkative, the moment he took the cards into his hands, he immediately showed a thoughtful expression, covered his lower lip with his upper one, and maintained that position throughout the game. At the end of a trick, he struck the table firmly with his hand, saying, “Off you go, old hag!” if it was a queen, or, “Off you go, Volhynian farmer!” if it was a king. The chairman would say: “I’ll grab his beard! I’ll grab her beard!” Occasionally, in striking the cards against the table, out came the expressions: “Ah! If only it had been, it was, it was nothing, so to the spades!” or simply exclaims: “spades! spiky trunk! picnetanka! picnegendras! picnerushuk! picnerus!” and even simply: “picniuk!”—the names under which they had consecrated the suits in their society. At the end of the game, they debated, as usual, quite loudly. Our guest also debated, but in a way that was incredibly skillful, so that everyone saw that he was debating, but at the same time, in a pleasant way. He never said, “You went,” but “You elected to go,” “I had the honor to cover your double,” and so on. To further agree with his opponents in something, he always offered them his silver cased snuffbox, in the bottom of which two violets had been placed for fragrance. The stranger’s attention was especially captured by the landowners Manilov and Sopotkevich, about whom he was asked a few moments earlier. A few questions asked of them showed that the guest was not only curious but also serious, for he first asked how many peasants he had and in what state they were, and only then asked about their first and last names. In a short while, he completely won their hearts. The not particularly old landowner Manilov, with sweet eyes like sugar, which he squinted whenever he smiled, was completely under his spell. He held his hand for a long time and insisted with great persuasion on his visit to a village, which was only fifteen versts from the town gate, according to his words. To which Chichikov, with a very polite nod of the head and sincere handshake, answered that he was not only willing but eager to fulfill.

— To be honest, we do not know what specific terms he was writing about, but he wrote every day, every hour, letter after letter! He was terribly anxious. One night, alone, I rushed to him with tears (oh, I loved him!): "Ask for forgiveness from Emperor Alexander!" — I shouted. That is, I should have said: "Make peace with Emperor Alexander," but, as a child, I naively expressed my whole thought. "My child!" — he replied, — he was pacing up and down the room, — my child! — he seemed not to notice at that time that I was ten years old, and even enjoyed talking to me, — my child, I am ready to kiss the feet of Emperor Alexander, but to the Prussian king, to the Austrian emperor, oh, there is eternal hatred toward them, and... finally... you know nothing of politics! "He seemed to suddenly remember who he was speaking to and fell silent, but his eyes continued to flash for a long time. Well, if I were to describe all these facts — I was a witness to the greatest of them — and publish them now, and all these critics, all this literary vanity, all these jealousies, factions and... no, your obedient servant!

– Murderer of your father! – the old man shouted to the four corners of the world, but he managed to shout only that; suddenly, he fell as if struck by lightning. Mitya jumped back into the garden and bent over the fallen man. In Mitya’s hand was a copper pestle, which he absentmindedly threw to the grass. The pestle fell two steps from Grigory, but not into the grass, but onto the path, in the most visible spot. For a few seconds, he looked at the man lying before him. The old man’s head was covered in blood; Mitya reached out and began to feel it. He remembered later with clarity that at that moment he was extremely anxious to make sure that he had “really proven” whether he had cracked the old man’s skull with the pestle or just “stunned” him on the head. But blood was pouring, terrifyingly, and instantly drenched his trembling fingers in a warm stream. He remembered that he had pulled out of his pocket his clean, white handkerchief, which he had packed for the trip to Khokhlova’s, and applied it to the old man’s head, vainly trying to wipe the blood from his forehead and face. But the handkerchief, too, was instantly soaked with blood. “Lord, what am I doing? – Mitya suddenly awoke, – if I cracked the skull, how will I know now… And does it really matter now! – he added hopelessly, – I killed him, so I killed him… The old man is down and will just lie there! ” he shouted out loud and suddenly dashed to the fence, leaped the alley, and began to run. The handkerchief soaked with blood was clenched in his right hand, and as he ran, he stuffed it into the back pocket of his coat. He ran headlong, and a few rare passersby, whom he met in the darkness on the city streets, remembered the night later as the night they saw an inexplicably running man. He flew back to Morozova’s house. Earlier, Fena, upon his departure, had rushed to the senior gardener, Nazar Ivanovich, and “by Christ and God” begged him not to let Captain in, “neither today nor tomorrow.” Nazar Ivanovich, after listening, agreed, but on his misfortune, he left for the house, where he was suddenly summoned, and on his way, meeting his nephew, a boy of twenty, recently arrived from the village, he ordered him to stay on the grounds but forgot to mention the captain. Reaching the gates, Mitya knocked. The boy instantly recognized him: Mitya had already given him tips several times. The boy opened the gate immediately, let him in, and with a happy smile, warned him, “Well, Aграфeny Alexandrovna is not here at all, you see.”

– I must confess, – Smerdyakov drawled with pedantic calm, – that there is a secret between me and Fyodor Pavlovich. K. was interrupted by a scream from the rear of the hall. He shaded his eyes to see, as the dull daylight turned the mist white and blinded him. It was the laundress, whom K. had recognized as a significant disturbance upon her entry. Whether she was guilty or not could not be determined. K. only saw that a man had pulled her into a corner near the door and was pressing her against the wall. But it was not she who screamed, but the man, who had opened his mouth wide and was looking up at the ceiling. A small circle had gathered around them, and the gallery spectators nearby seemed to relish the disruption to the solemnity that K. had brought to the assembly. K. was about to rush over at first, thinking that everyone would be eager to restore order and at least drive the couple out of the hall. But the first rows in front of him remained fixed in their places; no one moved, and no one let K. through. On the contrary, he was hindered; elderly men held their arms out, and an unseen hand—K. did not have time to turn around—gripped his collar. K. no longer thought of the couple but felt his freedom being restricted, as if the arrest were being taken seriously, and he jumped down from the podium without consideration. Now he was face to face with the crowd. Had he misjudged the people? Had he attributed too much impact to his speech? Had they feigned their reactions while he was speaking and now, when he was concluding, had they had enough of the pretense? What faces surrounded him! Small, black eyes darted about, cheeks hung down as if in drunkenness, long beards were stiff and sparse, and if you reached in, it felt like you were touching claws, not beards. But beneath the beards—K.’s real discovery—shimmered badges of various sizes and colors at the collar. Everyone seemed to have these badges, as far as he could see. Everyone belonged together, those on the right and left who appeared to be factions, and when he suddenly turned around, he saw the same badges on the collar of the examining judge, who sat quietly with his hands in his lap. "So," K. cried, flinging his arms up, the sudden insight demanding space, "you are all officials, as I see, you are the corrupt band I spoke against, you crowded in as spectators and snoops, formed factions, and one faction clapped to test me, you wanted to learn how to seduce the innocent! Well, you were not in vain here, I hope, either you discussed that someone was expected to defend the innocence, or—let me go or I’ll punch you," K. shouted at an elderly man who had moved particularly close to him. "Or, you really did learn something." With that, K. wished them good fortune in their profession. He quickly grabbed his hat, which had fallen at the edge of the table, and forced his way through the general silence, or rather, the most complete surprise. The examining judge, however, seemed to have been even quicker, for he was already waiting for K. at the door. "One moment," he said. K. stopped but did not look at the examining judge, but at the door, which he had already grasped the handle of. "I just wanted to point out to you," the examining judge said, "that you deprived yourself today—this may not have occurred to you yet—of the advantage that a questioning brings to the person who is detained in every case." K. laughed at the door. "You scum," he cried, "I’ll give you all the interrogations." He opened the door and hurried down the stairs. Behind him, the commotion of the revived assembly arose, which probably began to discuss the events like students.

And so it was that the Great Sage had reached the banks of the River Flood, transformed himself into the form of Second Son of the Fairy, and descended from the clouds straight into the temple. The demon wardens could not recognize him, each of them bowing in greeting. He took his seat in the middle, tallying the offerings: Li Hu’s sacrifice of livestock, Zhang Long’s pledge for protection, Zhao Jia’s petition for a son, and Qian Bing’s prayer for recovery from illness. Just as he was inspecting them, someone reported, "Another grandmaster has arrived." The demon wardens hurriedly looked on, all stunned. The True Monarch asked, "Is there any such thing as a Great Sage Equal to Heaven who has come here just now?" The demon wardens replied, "We have not seen any Great Sage; only one grandmaster was inspecting the offerings." The True Monarch entered the temple. And that young, small man with glasses… Mitya had forgotten his last name but knew him, had seen him: this was the investigator, a legal investigator, "from Law," who had arrived not long ago. And this one over there—Station Master Mavriky Mavrikyich, he knew him, a familiar face. And as for these with the badges, what were they for? And two more men, peasants… And there, by the door, Kalganov and Boris Triphonovich…

Mitya stepped out from behind the curtain and stood motionless. The room was full of people, but not the same ones from the day before; they were all new. A shiver ran down his spine, and he shuddered. He recognized all these people at once. There was that tall and stout old man in a coat and a cocked hat—this was the local administrator, Mikhail Makarch. And that dapper tubercular fop, always in such neatly polished boots, was the deputy prosecutor. "He has a chronometer worth four hundred rubles, he showed it off." And there was that young, small man with glasses… Mitya had forgotten his last name, but he knew him; he had seen him: this was the investigator, a judicial investigator, "from the School of Law," who had just arrived. And that one over there—Mikhail Mikhaylovich, the policeman—he knew him, they were acquainted. As for those with badges, what were they for? And there were two other men, farmers… And there was Kalganov and Triphon Borisovich standing in the doorway…

Seeing the master weeping, the monkey could no longer contain his irritation and shouted, "Master, do not be such a quitter! Sit here and wait! Let me go find that creature and make him return our horse!" The master held him back, saying, "Disciple, where do you intend to look for him?"

"I am the son of the caretaker, sir," the lad replied, taking the pipe from his mouth and stepping aside. "The son of the caretaker?" K. asked, tapping the ground impatiently with his cane. "Does His Honor wish for anything? Should I fetch the father?" "No, no," K. said, his voice carrying a hint of forgiveness as if the lad had done something wrong but K. had forgiven him. Then he said, "It's all right," and continued on, but before he climbed the stairs, he turned around once more.

She hurried up onto his lap, her knees spreading wide. K. looked almost startled at her, now that she was so close, and a bitter, teasing scent, like pepper, wafted from her. She took his head in her hands, leaned over him, and bit and kissed his neck, even nipped at his hair. "You traded me in!" she cried from time to time. "Look, now you've traded me in!" With a little shriek, her knee slipped, and she nearly fell onto the carpet. K. caught her to keep her from falling and was pulled down with her. "Now you belong to me," she said.

"Let her then be your mistress now," said Leni, "but you wouldn’t miss her much if you lost her or traded her for someone else, like for me, for instance." "Certainly," said K. with a smile, "that would be possible, but she has a great advantage over you: she knows nothing of my lawsuit, and even if she were to find out, she wouldn’t think about it. She wouldn’t try to persuade me to be more lenient." "That’s no advantage," said Leni. "If she has no other advantages, I won’t lose heart. Does she have any physical flaw?" "A physical flaw?" asked K. "Yes," said Leni, "for instance, I have this small defect. Look." She stretched out the middle and ring fingers of her right hand so that the skin between them almost reached the knuckle of her little finger. In the dark, K. did not immediately understand what she wanted to show him, so he took her hand and let her guide him until he could feel it. "What a natural curiosity," said K., and when he had a better look, he added, "What a pretty claw!" In the course of the first day, the father laid out all the family's financial circumstances and prospects for both the mother and the sister. Occasionally, he got up from the table and fetched some document or a memorandum from his small safe at Wertheim's, which he had saved from the collapse of his business five years ago. One could hear him unlocking the complicated lock and then relocking it after taking out what he needed. These were the first pleasing explanations Gregor had heard since his imprisonment. He had believed that the father had nothing left from that business venture, at least he had never said anything to the contrary, and Gregor hadn't asked about it. Gregor's concern at the time had been to help the family forget the business disaster that had left everyone in complete hopelessness as quickly as possible. And so, with great zeal, he had started working, transforming himself from a junior clerk into a traveling salesman almost overnight, who had many more opportunities to earn money and who saw his earnings immediately transformed into cash, which he willingly deposited at home for the astonished and delighted family. It had been good times, and they had never recurred in that luster, even though Gregor later earned so much money that he was able to cover the entire family's expenses and did so. One had gotten used to it, both the family and Gregor, and they gratefully accepted the money, and he gladly handed it over, but the warmth was gone. Only the sister had stayed close to Gregor, and it was his secret plan to send her, who loved music very much and played the violin with moving tenderness, to the conservatory next year, without regard for the large expenses that would be incurred, which would have to be managed in other ways. Often during Gregor's brief stays in the city, the conservatory was mentioned in conversations with the sister, but only as a beautiful dream whose realization was out of the question. The parents even did not like to hear these innocent mentions; but Gregor thought about it very seriously and planned to announce it solemnly on Christmas Eve.

His appearance at the ball produced an extraordinary effect. Everything and everyone turned to meet him. Let me embrace you, Pavel Ivanovich! Come here, Pavel Ivanovich, I'll kiss you more closely, my dear Pavel Ivanovich!" Chichikov suddenly found himself in several embraces at once. The police major handed him over to the medical inspector, who then passed him on to the tax farmer, who passed him on to the architect… The governor, who at the time was standing by the ladies, holding a confectionery ticket in one hand and a dalmatian in the other, dropped both the ticket and the dalmatian when he saw him; only his little dog barked; in any case, he spread extraordinary joy and merriment. There was no face that didn't reflect pleasure or, at the very least, an echo of general pleasure. Such is the way it happens with officials during an inspection by a superior: after the initial fear has passed, they see that a great deal pleases him and that he has even chosen to jest, i.e., to utter a few pleasant words with a cheerful smile. Long gloves were not drawn all the way to the wrists, but rather left the excitable parts of the hands above the elbows bare, which in many cases shone with enviable plumpness; in some cases, even the sable gloves burst, compelled to move farther down - in short, it seemed as if everywhere was written: no, this is not a province, this is a capital, this is Paris itself! But occasionally, some unheard-of hat or even a peacock feather, contrary to all the fashions, appeared out of place according to personal taste. But without this, it wouldn't do; such is the nature of a provincial city: somewhere it would necessarily be cut off. Standing before them, Chichikov thought, "Which, however, is the author of the letter?" and was about to stick out his nose; but a whole row of sleeves, cuffs, the ends of ribbons, fragrant nightgowns, and dresses tugged at his nose. The gallop was at full gallop: the postmistress, the captain of the judicial police, the lady with the blue feather, the lady with the white feather, the Georgian prince Chipchailidishev, a St. Petersburg official, a Moscow official, the Frenchman Cukuk, Perkhunovskii, Berabinovskii - all rose and galloped.

His appearance at the ball produced extraordinary effects. Everything, whatever it was, turned towards him, some with cards in their hands, others interrupting the most interesting parts of conversations to exclaim: "The district court replies... " and then immediately forgot what the district court had replied and hurried to greet the hero of the evening. "Pavel Ivanovich! Oh my God, Pavel Ivanovich! Dear Pavel Ivanovich! Most honorable Pavel Ivanovich! My soul, Pavel Ivanovich! There you are, Pavel Ivanovich! There he is, our Pavel Ivanovich! Allow me to embrace you, Pavel Ivanovich! Bring him over here, and let me kiss him tightly, my beloved Pavel Ivanovich!" Chimikov felt himself embraced in a moment. Before he could extricate himself from the arms of the chairman, he was already in the arms of the police chief; the police chief passed him on to the medical inspector, who passed him on to the land tax collector, who passed him on to the architect... The governor, who was standing by the ladies, holding a confectionery ticket in one hand and a terrier in the other, on seeing him, dropped the ticket and the dog; only the little dog barked; in short, he spread unusual joy and merriment. There was no face that did not express delight or, at the very least, the reflection of general delight. This is what happens on the faces of officials during an inspection by the arriving head of their department: after the initial fear subsided, they saw that much of what he liked, and that he had even taken it upon himself to joke, that is, to say a few words with a pleasant smile. Those around him laughed twice as much in response; those who, however, only half-heard the words he spoke also laughed from the heart, and finally, a policeman standing at the door near the exit, who had never laughed in his entire life and had just before shown the crowd a fist, expressed some kind of smile on his face, though it looked more like someone preparing to sneeze after a strong dose of tobacco. The hero replied to everyone and felt an extraordinary dexterity: he bowed to the right and to the left, as usual slightly off-center, but with complete freedom, which charmed everyone. The ladies surrounded him with a glowing garland and took along with them clouds of various scents: one smelled of roses, another of spring and violets, and the third was entirely filled with rue; Chimikov lifted only his nose and sniffed. Their taste in attire was lost: silks, velvets, gauzes were of such pale, fashionable colors that it was impossible to give them names (to such a degree had their taste become subtle). Ribboned bows and floral bouquets flitted haphazardly about the dresses in the most picturesque disorder, though some head had struggled with this disorder. A light hat hung only on the ears, and it seemed to say, "Hey, I'll fly away, but I'm sorry, I won't take the beauty with me!" Their waists were laced up and had the most firm and pleasing forms for the eye (it should be noted that all the ladies of the city N were somewhat plump, but were laced up so skillfully and had such pleasant manners that one could not notice their plumpness). It required incredible caution to live with this blood. The Duke was confined within himself, and at times he would cower and grow dark when it circled around him. This nimble, half-portuguese blood, which he scarcely knew, could be horrendously alien to him. Often he was terrified that it might strike him in his sleep and rend him. He pretended to subdue it, but he always stood in his fear. He never dared to love a woman lest it become jealous, and so relentless was it that wine never crossed his lips; instead, he calmed it with rosewater. Yet, once he did drink, in the camp before Lausanne, when Granson had been lost; then he was sick and isolated and drank much pure wine. But at that time, his blood slept. In his senseless final years, it sometimes fell into this deep, animal sleep. Then it showed how much it was in control; for when it slept, he was nothing. No one from his surroundings was allowed in; he did not understand what they said. The foreign envoys he could not show himself to, forlorn as he was. Then he sat and waited for it to awaken.

If the author had only looked deeper into his soul, stirred the depths that are hidden from the light, revealed the most secret thoughts that a person confides only to no one else, and had shown him as he appeared to the entire city, to Malinnikov and the other people, everyone would have been delighted and welcomed him as an interesting man. It does not matter if his face and the whole image did not flit about like a living entity before the eyes; instead, the soul would not be agitated after reading, and one could return to the card table, which amuses all of Russia. Yes, my dear readers, you would not have wanted to see the exposed human poverty. Why, you ask, do we need this? Do we not already know that life is full of contemptible and stupid things? We often see things that are by no means reassuring. It is better to show us the beautiful, the captivating. Let us forget!
