But little joy could Dunya and her husband derive from these tidings, especially at first. Sonia reported incessantly that he remained perpetually gloomy, uncommunicative, and, indeed, seemed to show almost no interest in the news she conveyed from the letters she received; that he sometimes asked about his mother; and when, seeing that he already anticipated the truth, she finally informed him of her death, it surprised her that even the news of his mother’s passing did not, at least outwardly, affect him greatly. She also reported that, despite appearing so immersed in himself and seemingly locked away from everyone, he embraced his new life very straightforwardly and simply. He clearly understood his position, did not expect anything better soon, had no frivolous hopes (which were so characteristic of his position), and did not marvel at much of his new surroundings, which bore no resemblance to anything familiar. Sonia said that his health was satisfactory. He went to work, never shirking or begging for work. He showed almost no interest in food, but the poor quality of his meals, except on Sundays and holidays, finally prompted him to accept a little money from her, Sonia, to set up a daily tea at his place. About everything else, he asked her not to trouble herself, insisting that all these concerns over him only annoyed him. Furthermore, Sonia wrote that his quarters in prison were communal, and she did not see the interiors of the barracks but concluded that they were cramped, squalid, and unhealthy; that he slept on benches, covering himself with felt, and did not want anything else. But that he lived so simply and poorly was not due to any premeditated plan or design, but rather out of negligence and external indifference to his fate. Sonia plainly wrote that, especially at first, he did not care about her visits, even begrudging them, was uncommunicative, and sometimes even rough with her, but that by the end, these meetings had become a habit for him and almost a necessity, so that he was quite distressed when she was ill for a few days and could not visit. She would see him on holidays by the prison gates or in the guardhouse, where he was called out to meet her for a few minutes; on weekdays, she would visit him at his workplace, or in the workshops, or at the brick kilns, or in the stables along the Irtysh River. Sonia herself noted that she had managed to gain some acquaintances and patronage in town; she engaged in sewing and, since there was no modiste in town, she became indispensable in many households; she did not mention, however, that through her, Razumikhin also received a patronage from his superiors, whose workloads were eased, among other things. Finally, she wrote (Dunya even noticed a certain unusual agitation and anxiety in her recent letters) that he avoided everyone, that the prisoners in the camp did not like him; that he remained silent for whole days and became very pale. In her last letter, Sonia wrote that he had fallen seriously ill and was lying in the hospital, in the cell for prisoners.

But Dounia and her husband could derive little comfort from these tidings, especially at first. Sonia continuously reported that he remained perpetually gloomy, uncommunicative, and almost completely uninterested in the news she relayed to him from her letters; that he occasionally inquired about his mother; and when she, seeing that he already anticipated the truth, finally told him about her death, to her surprise, the news of his mother’s passing did not seem to greatly affect him, at least so it appeared from his demeanor. She mentioned that, despite the fact that he seemed so deeply engrossed in himself and seemingly cut off from everyone else, he approached his new life very straightforwardly and simply, clearly understanding his position, expecting nothing better in the near future, having no flippant hopes (which are so typical of his situation), and not being astonished by much of his new surroundings, which bore so little resemblance to anything familiar. She reported that his health was satisfactory. He went to work, not shirking from or begging for the tasks assigned to him. He was almost indifferent to food, but that this food, except on Sundays and holidays, was so poor that, eventually, he was happy to accept a few coins from her, Sonia, to set up a daily tea service; regarding everything else, he asked her not to worry, asserting that all these concerns only irritated him. Sonia further wrote that his cell in the fortress was communal with others; she had not seen the interior of the barracks but concluded that it was cramped, squalid, and unhealthy; that he slept on a straw bed, placing felt underneath himself, and refused to make any other arrangements. But that he lived so rudely and in such poverty not because of any predetermined plan or intention, but simply due to a lack of attention and superficial indifference to his fate. Sonia directly wrote that, at first, he did not only show no interest in her visits but almost resented her, was uncommunicative, and even rude to her, but that by the end, these meetings had become a habit for him and even a necessity, so that he was quite distressed when she was sick for a few days and could not visit him. She saw him on holidays outside the fortress gates or in the guardhouse, where he was summoned to see her for a few minutes; on weekdays, she would go to him at the work sites, or in workshops, or at brickworks, or in the sheds along the Irtysh River. Sonia herself noted to herself that she had even made some acquaintances and gained some patronage in the city; she sewed, and since there was no modiste in the town, she became indispensable in many homes; she did not mention, however, that through her, Raskolnikov had received patronage from his superiors, that his tasks were made easier, and so on. Finally, word came (Dounia even noticed a certain unusual agitation and anxiety in her recent letters) that he shunned everyone, that the convicts in the fortress did not love him; that he was silent for entire days and became very pale. Suddenly, in her last letter, Sonia wrote that he had fallen seriously ill and was lying in the hospital in the cell of an arrested prisoner…

But little cheer was derived by Dounia and her husband from these tidings, especially at first. Sonya constantly informed them that he was perpetually moody, speechless, and even seemingly hardly interested in the news she imparted from the letters she received, which she read to him; that he sometimes inquired about his mother; and when she, seeing that he already suspected the truth, finally told him about her death, she was astonished to observe that even the news of his mother’s death did not, at least according to her outward appearance, have much effect on him. She reported that, despite his apparent immersion in himself and his withdrawal from everyone, he approached his new life very straightforwardly and simply, clearly understanding his situation, not expecting anything better nearby, and having no idle hopes (which would be so characteristic for his position), and he was almost not surprised by anything in his new surroundings, so little did they resemble anything from the past. She noted that his health was satisfactory. He went to work, neither shirking from it nor seeking to obtain it. He was almost indifferent to food, but that this food, except on Sundays and holidays, was so bad that he finally willingly accepted from Sonya a few coins to start a daily tea service for himself; for the rest, he asked her not to trouble herself, assuring her that all these worries for him only annoyed him. Sonya went on to report that his cell was communal with all the others, she had not seen the interiors of the barracks, but surmised that it was cramped, squalid, and unhealthy; that he slept on bunks, covering himself with felt, and did not want anything else. But the fact that he lived so coarsely and in poverty was not due to any deliberate plan or purpose, but simply because of his inattention and outer indifference to his fate. Sonya bluntly wrote that, especially at first, he did not only not care about her visits but even seemed annoyed by them, was speechless and even rough with her, but that toward the end these meetings turned into a habit with him and even a kind of necessity, so that he was very pained when she was sick for a few days and could not visit him. She saw him on holidays outside the prison walls or in the guardhouse, where he was summoned to her for a few minutes; on weekdays, at the works, where she would go to see him, or in the workshops, or on the brickworks, or in the stables on the Irtysh riverbank. Sonya wrote to herself that she had managed to acquire in town some acquaintances and patronage; that she engaged in sewing, and since there was almost no modiste in town, she became indispensable in many households; she did not mention, however, that through her, and because of her, Rakitin had received patronage from his superiors, and his workload was made easier, and so on. Finally, she wrote that he shunned everyone, that the convicts in the prison had not taken to him; that he was silent for entire days and grew very pale. In her last letter, Sonya suddenly wrote that he was seriously ill and lying in the hospital in the prisoner’s ward.

This was the third time Ivan Fyodorovich had spoken to Smerdyakov since his return from Moscow. The first time he had met him after the disaster, on the very first day of his return, and they had talked immediately. Then he visited him again two weeks later. But after that second encounter, he stopped seeing him, so it was now more than a month since he had last seen him, and he had heard very little about him. Ivan Fyodorovich returned from Moscow only on the fifth day after his father's death and did not even see the coffin: the funeral had taken place just the day before his arrival. The reason for Ivan Fyodorovich's delay lay in the fact that Alyosha, not knowing his exact Moscow address precisely, had turned to Katerina Ivanovna for a telegram, and she, also in ignorance of his actual address, had sent a message to her sister and aunt, hoping that Ivan Fyodorovich would immediately visit them in Moscow upon his arrival. But he only visited them on the fourth day after his return and, after reading the telegram, immediately rushed to us. I was the one to greet Alyosha, but upon talking with him, I was very surprised that he did not even suspect Mitya, but rather pointed directly to Smerdyakov as the murderer, which was contrary to all other opinions in our town. After then seeing the district attorney and the prosecutor, and learning the details of the accusation and arrest, I was even more astonished by Alyosha and attributed his opinion solely to the extreme brotherly feeling and compassion he felt for Mitya, whom Alyosha, as Ivan knew, loved very much. By the way, let us say only a few words forever about Ivan's feelings toward his brother, Dmitry Fyodorovich: he did not love him at all and sometimes felt compassion for him, but this was mixed with great contempt, verging on disgust. Mitya was completely distasteful to him, even in his very appearance. Ivan looked on with anger at the love for Mitya that Katerina Ivanovna had for him. However, he did see Mitya on the very first day of his arrival and this encounter did not lessen his conviction of Mitya's guilt, but rather strengthened it. He found Mitya then in great anxiety, in a state of acute mental distress. Mitya spoke much, but was distracted and incoherent, and spoke very sharply, accusing Smerdyakov and getting hopelessly tangled up. He spoke most of all about the three thousand rubles that "the dead man" had "stolen" from him. "They were my money," Mitya kept repeating, "even if I had stolen them, I would have been right." He hardly disputed any of the evidence against him and when he did discuss facts in his favor, he did so in a most incoherent and absurd manner – as if he did not want to justify himself at all before Ivan or anyone else, but rather took offense, arrogantly disregarded the accusations, scolded, and became indignant. He laughed mockingly at Gregory's testimony about the door being open and insisted that it was "the devil who had opened it." But he could not offer any coherent explanation for this fact. He even managed to offend Ivan Fyodorovich during this first meeting, sharply telling him not to suspect and question those who themselves claim that "everything is permissible." In general, on this occasion, he was very unfriendly toward Ivan. Immediately after this meeting with Mitya, Ivan Fyodorovich went straight to Smerdyakov.

For a long time he sat there, not knowing what exactly was worrying him, only occasionally glancing nervously over his shoulder towards the door of the ante-room, where he had mistakenly thought he had heard a sound. But as no one came, he grew calmer, went to the washbasin, washed his face with cold water, and returned to his window seat with a clearer head. The decision to take his own defense proved more formidable than he had originally assumed. While he had been largely untouched by the trial as long as he had entrusted his defense to his lawyer, he had observed it from a distance and had been scarcely affected by it, he could have checked how his case was going whenever he wanted, and he could also have withdrawn his head whenever he wanted. There was virtually nothing to do. I wandered through the city and noted that it had changed. It was pleasant to step out of the hotel where I had checked out and see that it was now a city for adults, embracing me, almost as if I were a stranger. Everything seemed a bit smaller, and I promenaded down Langlinie all the way to the lighthouse and back. When I reached the Amaliengade district, something might well emerge from somewhere, something that had been acknowledged for years and was once more attempting to exert its power. There were certain corners or archways or lanterns where one knew much and threatened. I looked them in the eye and let them know that I lived at the 'Phoenix' hotel and was ready to set off again at any moment. But my conscience was not at peace. The suspicion arose within me that none of these influences and connections had truly been overcome. They had been secretly abandoned one day, unfinished as they were. Childhood too, therefore, would have to be borne with, if one did not want to give it up forever. And as I realized how I was losing it, I simultaneously felt that I would never have anything else to rely on.

Just as they were debating, the True Monarch arrived and asked, "Brothers, why did he suddenly disappear?" The deities replied, "We just surrounded him, and he disappeared." Two-Feathers broadened his phoenix eyes and surveyed. Seeing that the Monkey King had transformed into a sparrow, nailed to the tree, he retracted his magical form, discarded his divine spear, and took off his slingshot. Shifting shape, he turned into a falcon and fluttered his wings, flying to pounce. Seeing this, the Monkey King took flight with a swoop, transforming into a large cormorant and soaring into the sky. Two-Feathers swiftly fluffed his feathers and morphed into a great heron, diving into the clouds to seize him. The Monkey King immediately sank lower into the stream, turning into a fish and darting into the water. Two-Feathers arrived at the stream and found no trace. Thinking to himself, "This monkey must have gone into the water; he'll surely turn into a fish or some kind of shrimp. I'll transform again to catch him," he did indeed transform into a fish eagle, gliding on the surface of the lower rapids. After a moment, the Monkey King, transformed into a fish, swam downstream. Suddenly, he spotted a bird that looked like a kite, but the feathers were not blue; it seemed like a heron, but there was no crest; it appeared like an old stork, but the legs were not red. He thought, "This must be Two-Feathers waiting for me..." He abruptly turned and fled. Two-Feathers saw this and exclaimed, "The fish is fleeing, looking like a carp, but its tail is not red; like a perch, but the scales are not patterned; like a blackfish, but there is no star on its head; like a crucian, but there are no needle-like fins on its cheeks. Why did he turn around and flee when he saw me? He must be that monkey!" He pursued and pecked the fish. The Monkey King leaped from the water and transformed into a water snake, swimming toward the shore and burrowing into the grass. Two-Feathers, having missed his target, noticed a snake darting out of the water and recognized the Monkey King. He immediately turned back and transformed into a red-crested gray heron, stretching a long beak like a pair of iron tongs, and approached to consume the snake. The snake leaped, transforming into a houby, a very lowly and lustful bird, and stood on the reed islet. Two-Feathers, seeing that the houby was so humble, decided not to approach. Returning to his original form, he took his slingshot, drew it back, and fired, striking the houby on the foot.

In the midst of their shouting, the True Immortal arrived and asked, "Brothers, where did he disappear to when we surrounded him?" The gods replied, "Just here, he was surrounded, and then he disappeared." Golden-Eyed Second Lord flared his eyes to observe, seeing Sun Wukong transformed into a sparrow nailed to a tree. He then reined in his spiritual carriage, cast aside his divine spear, and let down his bow and arrows. Changing himself into a falcon, he spread his wings and flew forward to attack. Seeing this, Sun Wukong unfolded a wing and soared skyward, transforming into a great cormorant, and flew upward. Second Lord, seeing this, immediately shook his feathers and transformed into a great sea gull, soaring into the clouds to seize him. Sun Wukong, pressing himself down, dove into the ravine and transformed into a fish, plunging into the water. Second Lord, catching up to the ravine's edge, saw no trace of him. Inwardly pondering, he thought, "That monkey must have dived into the water. He must have transformed into a fish or some other aquatic creature. I will transform again and catch him." He accordingly changed into a fish eagle, floating on the rapids' surface. After a while, Sun Wukong, transformed into a fish, swam downstream, and suddenly, he spotted a bird resembling a sparrowhawk, but its feathers were not black; it resembled a white crane, but it lacked a plume on its head; it resembled an old stork, but its legs were not red: "This must be Second Lord transforming to catch me..." He abruptly turned, shooting off. Second Lord saw this and said, "This fish turning back, it resembles a carp, but its tail is not red; it resembles a mandarin fish, but its scales do not stand out; it resembles a black fish, but it lacks a star on its head; it resembles a river bream, but its cheekbones do not have a needle. Why did he turn back when he saw me? He must have transformed into a monkey!" He pursued and pecked at its beak. Sun Wukong leaped out of the water, transforming into a water snake, swimming toward the shore, and burrowed into the grass. Second Lord, having failed to catch him, saw a water snake spring from the water, recognizing it as Sun Wukong, and immediately changed into a crimson-crowned heron, stretching its long beak like a pair of pincers, to devour the water snake. The water snake leaped, transforming into a night heron, standing woodenly on a reed bed. Second Lord, seeing it had transformed into a lowly creature—night herons are the most debased and lustful birds, even mingling with parrots and crows—did not pursue it and instead showed his true form, rushing forward with his bow drawn full, and in one shot, he hit it squarely in the foot.

I do not understand how what followed could have unfolded in approximately five seconds. As much as one tries to recount it, it takes much longer. I had injured myself in the rush against him; I was small, it seemed to me that not crying was already a lot, and I expected him, without realizing it, to comfort me. Since he did not do so, I thought him awkward; I suspected that the right joke did not come to him, to unravel this situation. Already pleased enough to help him, it was necessary to see his face. I had said that he was tall. Now, he had not, as would have been natural, bent down over me, so that he would be at a height that I was not prepared for. There was still nothing but the smell and the peculiar hardness of his suit that I had felt before me. Suddenly, his face came. How it was, I do not know, I do not wish to know. It was the face of an enemy. And beside this face, close by, at the height of his terrible eyes, stood, like a second head, his fist. Before I even had time to lower my face, I ran; I sidestepped to the left around him and ran straight down a desolate, terrible alley, an alley of a foreign city, a city where nothing is forgiven.

I was already satisfied enough to assist him, but for that, I needed to see his face. I said he was tall. But he had not, as would have been natural, bent over me, so that he stood at a height that I was not prepared for. Still, there was nothing but the smell and the peculiar hardness of his suit, which I had felt. Suddenly, his face came into view. How it was, I do not know, and I do not want to know. It was the face of an enemy. And beside this face, close by, at the level of his terrifying eyes, stood, as a second head, his fist. Before I even had time to drop my face, I ran; I veered left around him and raced down a deserted, terrifying alley, the alley of a foreign town, a town that gives nothing.

"I do not want public success as a speaker," K. said, coming to this conclusion. "It is probably not within my reach anyway. The Judge in Charge of Investigation likely speaks much better; after all, it is part of his profession. What I want is merely the public discussion of a public malpractice. Listen: I was arrested about ten days ago. I laugh at the fact of my arrest myself, but that does not belong here. I was attacked in bed early in the night. Perhaps, as the Judge in Charge of Investigation said, such a command was not impossible, but someone else was chosen instead of a harmless painter. The room next to mine was occupied by two rough guards. If I had been a dangerous criminal, one could hardly have done better. These guards were demoralized scum; they bombarded me with talk, they wanted to be bribed, they wanted to persuade me to give them my clothes under false pretenses, they wanted money to bring me a breakfast which they shamelessly ate in front of my eyes. That was not all. I was led to another room to see the superintendent. It was a lady's room, which I greatly respect, and I had to watch how this room, without my fault, was desecrated by the presence of the guards and the superintendent. It was not easy to keep my composure. But I managed to do so and, in a completely calm voice—something this superintendent, whom I now see sitting on the chair of the aforementioned lady in a disgusting display of obtuse arrogance, would have to confirm—I asked him why I was arrested. What did this superintendent, whom I can see now, answer, seated in the chair of the aforementioned lady, displaying the grossest arrogance? Gentlemen, he really did not answer much, perhaps he did not know anything at all. He had me arrested and was content with that. Moreover, he had brought three low-level employees from my bank into the lady's room, who were occupied with examining and disarranging her property. The presence of these employees had another purpose: they, just like my landlord and her maid, spread the news of my arrest, damaged my public reputation, and, in particular, shook my position at the bank. Nothing of this succeeded, not even in the slightest. Even my simple landlord—let me mention her name in honor here; her name is Frau Grubach—realized that such an arrest meant no more than an attempt carried out by an unsupervised boy on the street. I repeat, the whole thing only caused me inconvenience and temporary annoyance, but could it not have had much worse consequences?"

Raskolnikov felt that the clerk had become more negligent and contemptuous towards him after his confession, but strangely, he suddenly felt utterly indifferent about any opinion, no matter whose it might be, and this change happened in a single moment. If he had reflected on it for a moment, he would certainly have been surprised at how he could have spoken to them just a moment ago, and even have thrust his feelings upon them? And where did these feelings come from? On the contrary, now, if the room were suddenly filled with his first-rate friends instead of quarter-masters, he would probably have not a single human word for them, his heart was so empty. A dark sensation of endless isolation and estrangement suddenly became conscious in his soul. It was not the baseness of his heart’s revelations to Ilya Petrovich, nor the superiority of the captain’s triumph over him that had overturned his heart all at once. Oh, what does it matter to him now about his own meanness, about all these ambitions, the captain, the German women, the reprimands, the office, and the like! If they were to sentence him to be burned at this very moment, he would hardly pay attention to the sentence, let alone stir a finger. Xuanzang wept as he returned to the temple and told his master. He then immediately bid farewell and proceeded directly to Hongzhou. Upon arriving at Flower Shop Village, he asked Liu Xia'er, the owner, "Last year, Mr. Chen from Jiangzhou stayed at your inn with his mother. Is she well?" Liu Xia'er replied, "She used to stay here, but later she lost her sight. She hasn't paid me any rent in three or four years. She is now in a dilapidated earthen kiln by the South Gate, begging on the streets for a living. That guest has been gone for a long time, and there has been no news of him." Xuanzang, upon hearing this, immediately went to the dilapidated earthen kiln by the South Gate to find the grandmother. The grandmother said, "Your voice sounds like my son, Chen Guangrui." Xuanzang said, "I am not Chen Guangrui, but I am his son. Wen娇 Miss is my mother." The grandmother said, "Why aren't your parents here?" Xuanzang said, "My father was murdered by bandits, and my mother was forced to marry one of them." The grandmother asked, "How do you know you should look for me?" Xuanzang replied, "My mother sent me to find you. She has a letter and a ring of incense with her." The grandmother accepted the letter and ring and cried aloud, "My son came seeking his fortune, and I thought he had forgotten his duties and obligations, but I never knew he was murdered by others! Fortunately, heaven has taken pity on me and not left my son without descendants. Today, my grandson has come to find me." Xuanzang asked, "Why are your eyes all cloudy?" The grandmother replied, "I grieved for your father day and night, but he never returned, and as a result, my eyes became cloudy." Xuanzang then knelt towards the sky and prayed, "O Xuanzang, at eighteen, could not avenge my parents' deaths. Today, I come to find you as per my mother's command. May heaven have mercy on my sincerity and restore my grandmother's sight!" After the prayer, he touched the tip of his tongue to his grandmother's eyes. In a short while, her eyes were cleared and she regained her vision. The grandmother then looked at the young monk.

One day, inside the cave, the Monkey King ordered his four chief lieutenants to prepare a feast and invited the Six Kings to join in the drinking, slaughtering cattle and horses, and sacrificing to heaven and earth. He instructed all the monsters to dance and sing in celebration. They all became so tipsy they were utterly drunk. After seeing the Six Kings off, he rewarded the senior and junior leaders and leaned against the iron plank bridge under the shade of the pines, falling asleep. The four chief lieutenants surrounded him, keeping quiet. Suddenly, he saw two people entering in his dream, holding a document with 'Sun Wukong' written on it. They approached him without hesitation, tied him up, and spirited his spirit away. The Monkey King stumbled and staggered, being dragged all the way to the city gates. As he gradually sobered up, he looked up and saw a sign on the city wall that read 'Yōumíng Jìe' (The Realm of the Dead). The Monkey King suddenly woke up and exclaimed, "The Realm of the Dead is where King Yama resides. How could I be here?" The two people said, "Your life on earth is now over. We are here to summon you." Hearing this, the Monkey King retorted, "I, the Old Sun, have transcended the Three Realms and am not bound by the Five Elements. Why would I be under their control? How dare you come to fetch me?" The two grim reapers pulled and tugged at him, insisting on dragging him in. The Monkey King, angered, pulled out a treasure from his ear, shook it, and it grew to bowl-sized. He raised his hand and smashed the two grim reapers into a pulp. He then broke free and brandished his staff, charging into the city. The Bull-Faced Demon ghostly wardens scurried east and west, and the Horse-Face Demon ghostly wardens fled north and south. The ghostly attendants ran up to the Great Hall of the Ksitigarbha and reported, "O Great King! Trouble! Trouble! A bearded and grinning Thunder God is coming in!"

One day, in the cave, he instructed the four chief officers to arrange a feast, inviting the Six Kings to drink. They slaughtered cattle and horses, sacrificing to the heavens and earth, and had the various fiends dance and sing. They all drank until they were thoroughly drunk. After sending the Six Kings off, he then rewarded the big and small leaders. Leaning against the iron plank bridge under the shade of the pines, he soon fell asleep. The four chief officers surrounded and protected him, daring not to speak loudly. Suddenly, he saw in his dream two people carrying a decree with the three characters “Sun Wukong” on it. Approaching him, they did not allow him to speak, put a rope around him, and dragged his spirit away. He stumbled and staggered, being led straight to the edge of a city. As the monkey king gradually regained his senses, he suddenly looked up, and saw a metal sign on the city wall with the three characters “Yōumíng Jie” [幽冥界]. The monkey king suddenly awoke, saying, "Yōumíng Jie is where the King Yama resides. Why have I come here?" The two people said, "Your lifespan on earth is now at an end. We bring you this decree to summon you." The monkey king heard this and said, "I, Sun Wukong, am beyond the three realms and not among the five elements, and am not subject to his jurisdiction. How dare you blur the line and come to drag me away?" The two soul-catchers continued to tug at him, insisting on dragging him inside. The monkey king, infuriated, pulled out a treasure from his ear and swung it, making it as thick as a bowl. Raising his hand, he smashed the two soul-catchers into pulp. He then untied the rope, threw down his cudgel, and smashed into the city. This terrified the Bull Demon King, who scurried around, and the Horse-faced Demon King, who ran in all directions. The other fiends ran up to the Hall of the Underworld, reporting, "Great King! Trouble! Trouble! A monkey-faced thunder god is coming in!"

I am informing you, my dear, that a sorrowful incident has occurred in our apartment, truly deserving of pity! This morning, at five o'clock, little Korchkov breathed his last. I do not know the cause, perhaps scarlet fever, God knows! I paid a visit to the Korchkovs. Well, they are in a sorry state! What disorder! And no wonder: the entire family lives in one room, separated only by screens for propriety. There stands a simple, but quite nice coffin – they bought it ready-made, for a boy who was about nine years old; they say he showed promise. But to look at them, Varenka! The mother doesn't cry, but she is so sad, poor thing. Perhaps it is easier for them, now one burden is lifted; but they still have two left – a baby and a little girl, who is about six. What a pleasant sight it is to see a child suffering, and one’s own child at that, and yet there is nothing one can do to help! The father sits in an old, greasy frock coat on a broken chair. Tears are flowing from his eyes, though perhaps not out of sorrow, just from habit, for his eyes are watering. He is such a strange fellow! He turns red when you talk to him, fidgets, and doesn’t know what to say. The little girl, his daughter, stands next to the coffin, leaning against it – such a poor little thing, so sullen and thoughtful! And I, Varenka, do not like when a child is lost in thought; it is unpleasant to look at! A rag doll lies beside her on the floor – she doesn't play with it; she holds a finger to her lips and stands there, motionless. The mistress gave her a candy; she took it but didn't eat it. It is sad, Varenka – isn't it?

He glanced at the alarm clock ticking on the stand. "Heavenly Father!" he thought. It was a quarter to seven, and the hands moved steadily forward; in fact, it was already past the half. Should the alarm not have sounded? From the bed, it was clear that it was set to four o’clock; surely, it had rung. Yes, but was it possible to sleep through such a booming alarm? Well, he hadn’t slept soundly, but probably the deeper. What should he do now? The next train left at seven o’clock; to catch it, he would have had to hurry nonsensically, and the collection was still not packed away, and he himself did not feel particularly fresh and agile. And even if he caught the train, a thunderstorm from the boss was inevitable, for the secretary had waited for the five o’clock train and had reported his absence long ago. It was a creature of the boss, spineless and without common sense. What if he called in sick? That would be very embarrassing and suspicious, for Gregor had never been sick during his five years of service. Certainly, the boss would come with the health insurance doctor, would blame his parents for a lazy son, and would cut off all objections with the reference to the health insurance doctor, for whom there are only very healthy but lazy people. And had he been completely wrong in this case? Gregor felt actually, apart from a really unnecessary sleepiness after the long nap, quite well and even had a particularly strong appetite.

Fear was the beginning, fear and pleasure and a horrified curiosity about what was to come. Night reigned, and his senses listened; for afar approached a din, a mixture of sound: clashing, drumming, and deep thunder, shrill whooping, and a specific howl drawn out in a rounded U sound, all overlaid and sweetly tainted by a deep, insidious flute playing, which charmed his entrails in a shamelessly pressing manner. But he knew a word, dark yet naming what came: "The strange god!" Gassy glows flared up: then he recognized mountainous land, similar to that around his summer cottage. And in shredded light, from wooded heights, between trunks and mossy stone fragments, it rolled and tumbled down: men, animals, a swarm, a raging pack, and flooded the meadow with bodies, flames, tumult, and staggering round dances. Women, staggering over their too-long pelts hanging from their belts, shook bell drums over their moaning, flung-back heads, swung sputtering torches and naked daggers, held writhing serpents in their middles, or carried their breasts screaming in their hands. Men, horns on their foreheads, in fur garments and shaggy hides, bowed their necks and raised their arms and legs, clashed iron cauldrons and beat wildly on drums, while smooth boys with leaf-veiled rods prodded the goats, gripping their horns and eloping in leaps of joy. And the elated ones howled the cry with soft middle vowels and drawn-out U sounds at the end, sweet and wild at once, never before heard: here it resounded into the air, resounding like from deer, and there it was given back in raucous triumph, driving each other to dance and flinging limbs, and never letting it cease. But the deep, alluring flute tone pervaded and dominated everything. Did it not also lure him, the reluctant experiencer, shamelessly persistently to the feast and excess of the ultimate sacrifice? Great was his revulsion, great his fear, honest his will to protect his own against the stranger, the enemy of the resolved and worthy mind. But the din, the howling, amplified by echoing mountain walls, grew, took the upper hand, swelled into raving madness. Fumes assailed the senses, the reeking scent of goats, the breathing of panting bodies, and a whiff like from putrid waters, to which another, familiar one was added: wounds and encircling sickness. With the drumbeats, his heart thundered, his brain whirled, rage seized him, delusion, stupefying lust, and his soul longed to join the god's dance. The obscene symbol, enormous and made of wood, was unveiled and exalted: then they unleashed their wild password. Froth at their lips, they raged, enticing each other with lascivious gestures and supplicating hands, laughing and groaning—thrusting the studded poles into each other's flesh and lapping at the blood from the limbs. But with them, in them, the dreamer was now and now belonged to the strange god. Yes, they were himself as they tore and murdered the animals and devoured steaming flesh pieces, as boundless mixing began, to offer to the god. And his soul savored the debauchery and madness of the decline.

Another crack was heard, and the second gate opened. The Monkey King flew in, whimpering. Inside, the old demon ordered the guards to be vigilant and began to prepare weapons: "I fear that storm of yesterday did not kill Sun Wukong. He will surely come back today. When he does, I will make sure his life ends." Hearing this, the Monkey King flew past the hall and headed to the rear. There, he found a locked, secure door. He squirmed through a crack in the door and found himself in a large, empty courtyard. There, tied to a wind-stilling stake, was Tang僧. The master wept, only thinking of Wukong and Wenheng, not knowing where they were. The Monkey King perched, tapping on his bald head and calling, "Master." The master recognized his voice and said, "Wukong, I almost died! You called for me?" The Monkey King replied, "Master, I'm on your head. Don't be so anxious and don't worry. We'll catch the demon and save your life." Tang僧 said, "When will we catch the demon?" The Monkey King said, "The tiger demon that captured you has been killed by Pig, but the old demon's wind is very powerful. I expect to catch him today. Don't worry, don't cry. I'll be right back."

The Monkey King flew in and found the old demon instructing his guards to be vigilant and preparing weapons: "That Monkey King may not have been blown away by the storm yesterday. "It's a long story, Madame Avdotya Romanovna. There's, as you might say, a kind of theory involved. The same case where I find, for example, that a single act of wrongdoing is permissible if the main goal is good. One evil and a hundred good deeds! It's undoubtedly painful for a young man with virtues and an inflated sense of self to know that if there had been just three thousand fewer, his entire career, all his future, would have taken a different shape. Yet there were no such three thousand. Add to this the irritation from hunger, from a cramped apartment, from tattered clothes, from a vivid awareness of the beauty of his social standing, and that of his sister and mother. Above all, his vanity, his pride, and his vanity again, though, of course, who knows, perhaps with good inclinations... I blame him not, please don't think that; it's not my affair. There was also a personal theory here, you see, a theory such as it was, according to which people are divided into material and special individuals, that is, into those for whom, by their high position, the law is not written, while they, on the contrary, make laws for other people, the material, the dross. Such a theory, of course; one theory is as good as another.[88] Napoleon utterly captivated him, in fact, captivated him with the notion that many geniuses overlook a single evil and proceed straight through it, without thinking. It seems he imagined himself a genius, for a while, at any rate. He suffered greatly, and still does, from the thought that he could formulate the theory but cannot leap over it, without thinking, and so is not a genius. Well, that's humiliating for a young man with a high sense of self, especially in our time."

Add to this the irritation from hunger, a cramped apartment, tattered clothes, and a vivid awareness of the social superiority of his own position, along with that of his sister and mother. But more than anything, pride and vanity, vanity and pride, though, who knows, perhaps it could be different with better inclinations… Please don’t think I blame him; it’s not my affair. There was also my own theory, – a theory, you know, – according to which people are divided, you see, into raw material and special people, that is, people for whom, by their elevated status, the law is unwritten, while, on the contrary, they themselves make laws for the raw material, the raw stuff. Nothing much, just a theory; une théorie c’est une théorie. Napoleon greatly inspired him, I mean, really inspired him, with the idea that many brilliant people did not look askance at a single act of evil but simply stepped over it without a second thought. He seemed to imagine himself a brilliant person – that he had felt so for a certain period. He suffered and still suffers greatly from the thought that while he could devise the theory, he cannot cross over without thinking, and therefore is not a brilliant person. Well, for a young man with such self-respect, it’s humiliating, especially in our times…

When Emperor Taizong heard this in the Treasure Hall, he was very delighted, and then asked, "That monk, what are the benefits of the nine-tusked staff?" The Bodhisattva replied, "My metal staff is made of copper and iron, encased in nine rings of immortal vine that keep one young forever. It is in people's hands to look on as it repels the green bones and sickly flesh, and it carries light clouds as it descends the mountains. Mahayana's Five Elders traveled through the heavenly realm, and the horned radish sought its mother and broke through the ground barrier. It is untainted by the slightest bit of the worldly mire, and it delights in accompanying the divine monk up to the Jade Mountain." Upon hearing this, Emperor Taizong immediately ordered the unfurling of the monk's robes to examine them closely from top to bottom, and indeed, they were fine articles. He said, "Elder Dharma, I dare not hide it from you. I am currently promoting virtue, expanding my merit, and gathering many monks in the Palyzed Birth Temple to preach the scriptures. Among them is a man of great virtue, named Tripitaka. I have purchased these two treasures to bestow upon him. How much are you asking for them?" The Bodhisattva, with Ksitigarbha, bowed and took refuge, sounded a Buddhist mantra, and stepped forward to say, "If he has great virtue, I, a poor monk, am willing to give him these treasures, and I will not take any money." Having said this, he turned and left. Emperor Taizong, being eager to show his courtesy, grabbed Prince Xiao Yu to hold him back, and then stood by the dais and asked, "You said the robes were worth five thousand taels and the staff was worth two thousand. You said you would not take any money when I wanted to buy them, but it seems you think I am relying on my position to force you to give them to me. That is not the case. I will offer you the exact price you asked for, so do not refuse." The Bodhisattva said, "I made a vow before, saying that if there were respect for the Three Treasures, and you were to practice the virtues and take refuge in my Buddha, I would not take any money and would give them away. Seeing your wisdom and goodness, your respect for our Buddhist teachings, and the high virtue and practice of this great monk who preaches the great law, I ought to offer them freely. I will not take any money. I leave these treasures as a token of my departure." Emperor Taizong was very pleased with his earnestness, and then ordered a grand vegetarian banquet to be laid out to thank the Bodhisattva, who firmly refused and departed happily, still hiding at the local temple without further mention.

It is delightful to hold and the bones are seen to be green, and when leaving the mountain, the staff is light and brings back a bit of cloud. The Fifth Patriarch Mahākāśyapa roamed the celestial palaces, searching for his mother beneath the earth with a ram. It does not stain itself with the slightest bit of the mundane, and loves to accompany the divine monk to the Jade Mountain." King Tang, hearing this, immediately ordered the robe to be spread out and examined carefully. It was indeed a good thing. He said, "Senior Dharma Priest, I cannot hide it from you, I now open up the virtuous teachings widely, planting fields of good karma, gathering many monks in the Sutras in the Birth-and-Transformation Temple. The Bodhisattva, upon hearing this, clasped his hands in reverence and bowed, saying a Buddha name, and stepped forward to say, "If he has virtue, I, the poor priest, am willing to give it to him, and will not take money." Finished speaking, he turned to leave. King Tang, eager, caught hold of Xiao Yu and, bowing, stood on the throne and asked, "You originally said that the robe is five thousand taels of silver, and the staff is two thousand taels of silver. Seeing me wishing to buy, you now say that you will not take money, are you saying that I rely on the position of my kingship to forcibly take your thing? There’s no way such a thing could be. The Bodhisattva, raising his hands, said, "The poor priest has made a vow in advance, saying that if there is respect for the three treasures, appreciation for virtue, and an act of faith in my Buddha, the item will not be bought and given without charge. So evening came. It began to rustle more strongly in the old pines, and a mighty wind swept through, swishing and howling through the dense boughs. This sounded so beautifully to Heidi that it was filled with joy, leaping and bounding under the pines, as if it had experienced an unprecedented joy. The grandfather stood under the eaves and watched the child. Now a shrill whistle sounded. Heidi stopped in his jumps, the grandfather stepped out. It leaped down, goat by goat, like a hunt, with Peter in the middle. With a shout of joy, Heidi leaped into the midst of the pack and greeted each of his morning friends one by one. At the hut, everything stood still, and two beautiful, slender goats, a white one and a brown one, came from the herd and lapped at the grandfather's hands, for he held a bit of salt in them, as he did every evening to welcome his two little creatures. Peter vanished with his flock. Heidi caressed the one and then the other of the goats tenderly, and leaped around them, caressing them from the other side as well, and was all joy and happiness over the little creatures. "Are they ours, grandfather? Are they both ours? Will they come to the stable? Will they stay with us always?" Heidi asked one after the other in his delight, and the grandfather could barely get his constant "Yes, yes!" in between the one and the other question. When the goats had licked up their salt, the old man said, "Go and get your bowl and the bread."

Grandfather stood under the roof porch and watched the child. Now a shrill whistle sounded. Heidi paused in her leaps, and Grandfather stepped out. Perhaps some of the readers might think that my young man was a sensitive, ecstatic, poorly developed nature, a pale dreamer, a gaunt and jaded little man. On the contrary, Alyosha was, at the time, a tall, ruddy-cheeked lad with a bright look, healthy, a nineteen-year-old youth. He was, in fact, quite handsome, well-built, of medium height, dark-haired, with a well-defined, though slightly elongated, oval face, and with bright, dark-gray eyes, widely spaced, very thoughtful and seemingly very serene. It may be said, perhaps, that red cheeks do not hinder fanatical zeal or mysticism; but I think that Alyosha was even more of a realist than anyone else. Oh, certainly, at the monastery he believed in miracles as firmly as anyone else, but in my opinion, a realist's faith is never shaken by miracles. It is not miracles that lead a realist to faith. The true realist, if he is not a believer, always finds within himself the strength and the ability not to believe in miracles. If a miracle appears before him as an irresistible fact, he will rather doubt his feelings than admit the fact. And if he does admit it, he will admit it as a natural fact, until then only unknown to him. Faith in a realist is not born from a miracle, but a miracle is born from faith. If a realist once believes, then by virtue of his realism he must necessarily admit a miracle. The Apostle Thomas declared that he would not believe until he saw, but when he saw, he said, “My Lord and my God!” Did the miracle cause his faith? It is more likely that it did not; he believed only because he wished to believe, and perhaps he was already fully believing in his heart even when he said, “I will not believe until I see.”

Do not wrong the people," Qing Feng said. "You may have not eaten yourself, but your attendants still might try to steal some."

Tripitaka said, "You are right. Do not fuss for now. Let me ask them. If they did indeed steal, I will make them compensate you."

Ming Yue said, "Compensate? Where would they get the money to buy more?"

Tripitaka said, "Even if there is money, where could they buy it? The saying goes, kindness and righteousness are worth more than gold. Make them apologize instead, and that would be enough. We still do not know if it was them or not."

Ming Yue said, "How could it not be them? Did they not argue over the distribution?"

Tripitaka called out, "Come, disciples."

Sand Monks heard and said, "Trouble! We're in trouble! The teacher is calling us, and the boys are yelling at us. This isn't the wind getting in our sails, is it?"

Monkey said, "Awkward! This is just about food. If we admit it, it would look like we are stealing. Let's not claim responsibility."

Pig said, "Yes, yes, let's not admit it."

The three of them left the kitchen and walked onto the main hall. How they would argue their case and escape blame? To be continued.

Once it was almost dark over this story, I was on the verge of telling Maman about the 'Hand': at that moment, I would have done it. I was about to start, but then I remembered how well I had understood the servant, that he could not have come to look at their faces. And I was afraid of Maman's face, even in the darkness, if it had seen what I had seen. I drew another quick breath to make it seem as though I had not wanted to do anything else. A few years later, after the strange night at the Gallery in Urnekloster, I went around telling little Erik about it for days. But after our nighttime conversation, he had closed himself off from me again, avoiding me; I believe he despised me. And that was precisely why I wanted to tell him about the 'Hand'. I imagined that I would win his opinion (and I desperately wished it for some reason) if I could make him understand that I had really experienced it. But Erik was so adept at sidestepping that it didn't come to that. And then we did leave right away. So it is, rather strange, that it is the first time I (and, finally, only to myself) am telling a story that occurred far back in my childhood.

One day, the Master and his disciples were playing before the Three Stars Cave. The Master said, "Wukong, have you finished your task?" Wukong replied, "Thanks to your great kindness, my discipleship is complete, and I have mastered the technique of rising on clouds and soaring through the skies." The Master said, "Try rising on clouds for me." Wukong showed off his skill, leaped up, and performed somersaults, jumping several dozen feet into the air. He rode the clouds for about the time it takes to eat a meal, but returned without traveling more than a few miles. Landing, he said to the Master, "This is the rising on clouds and soaring through the skies, Master." The Master laughed and said, "This doesn't count as soaring through the skies. It's just cloud-climbing. It has been said since ancient times, 'A sage visits the Northern Sea in the morning and the Southern Mountain at dusk.' With you, in half a day you haven't traveled more than a few miles; that doesn't count as cloud-soaring at all!" Wukong asked, "What do you mean by 'visits the Northern Sea in the morning and the Southern Mountain at dusk'?" The Master said, "Those who ride the clouds rise in the morning from the Northern Sea, fly over the Eastern Sea, Western Sea, and Southern Sea, and return to the Southern Mountain by dusk. The Southern Mountain is the phrase for the Northern Sea city of Lingling. All the seas and lands should be traversed in a day. Only then can it be said that one soars through the clouds." Wukong said, "This is difficult! This is difficult!" The Master said, "There is no difficult thing in the world, as long as you have the heart to do it." Wukong, hearing this, bowed and said, "Master, one must strive for perfection. Please, with great compassion, teach me this cloud-soaring technique as well, so I will never forget your kindness." The Master said, "All sages who soar on clouds take off with a stamp of the foot. You aren't like that. I saw you jump up a few dozen feet and then tumble. I will teach you the 'somersault cloud' based on your movement." Wukong bowed again and begged, and the Master gave him a诀, saying, "When you use this cloud, hold this gesture, chant the true words, clench your fist tightly, and shake your body. You will travel ten-wan eight-thousand li with one somersault!" Everyone heard this and laughed, "Wukong's good luck! If you learn this technique, you can work as a delivery boy or a document courier; you can find a job everywhere!" The master and disciples returned to their respective caves as the day grew dark. That night, Wukong practiced and mastered the somersault cloud. Every day, he could travel freely, with no bounds and no restrictions, enjoying the bliss of eternal life.

One day, the master and the disciples played in the courtyard of the Three Stars Cave. The master said, "Wukong, have you accomplished it?" Wukong replied, "Thanks to Master's great kindness, my discipleship is complete, and I can already soar and ascend." The master said, "Try to soar and ascend for me." Wukong showed his skill, leaping several somersaults, rising six or seven zhang from the ground, and riding the clouds for about the time it takes to eat a meal, traveling not more than three li before returning. He then landed and crossed his hands, saying, "Master, this is soaring and ascending on clouds." The master laughed and said, "This doesn't count as soaring and ascending; it's merely crawling on clouds. As the saying goes, 'A immortal travels north to the Northern Ocean in the morning and south to Mount Heng at night.' With you, you haven't even traveled three li in a half-day. You haven't even crawled on clouds!" Wukong asked, "What does 'traveling north to the Northern Ocean in the morning and south to Mount Heng at night' mean?" The master replied, "When one soars, one begins in the morning at the Northern Ocean, passes through the East, South, and West Seas, and returns to Mount Heng by night. Mount Heng is simply a play on words for the Northern Ocean's Lingling. In one day, one travels around the entire perimeter of the four seas, then one may be said to be soaring." Wukong said, "This is difficult! Very difficult!" The master said, "There is no difficult thing in the world, only those who fear it." Wukong heard this and knelt to pay respects, saying, "Master, 'a man should strive to be thorough.' Let me receive a great compassion and give me this technique of soaring and ascending, and I will never forget your kindness." The master said, "When all the immortals soar, they jump up by stomping their feet, but you do it differently. I saw you jumping and tumbling. I will teach you 'somersault cloud' based on this." Wukong then knelt to beg again, and the master taught a mnemonic, saying, "This cloud, make a hand gesture, recite the true words, clench your fist, shake your body, and jump up; a somersault can carry you ten myriads and eight thousand li!" The disciples all laughed and said, "Wukong is lucky! If you learn this technique, you can be a messenger, deliver documents, or carry dispatches; you can find work anywhere!" The master and disciple each returned to their caves as dusk fell. That night, Wukong practiced and mastered the somersault cloud. From then on, he was carefree and self-assured, enjoying the beauty of eternal life.

But all my verses came into being differently, thus they are not verses. And when I wrote my drama, how misguided I was. Was I a follower and fool, needing a third to tell the tale of two people who make life hard for each other? How easily I fell into the trap. And yet I should have known that this third, who roams through all lives and literatures, this ghost of a third who never was, has no meaning and must be denied. He belongs to the natural excuses, which are always eager to divert human attention from its deepest secrets. He is the curtain behind which a drama plays out. He is the noise at the entrance to the hushed silence of an actual conflict. One would think that it had been too difficult for them to speak of the two who matter; the third, precisely because he is so unreal, is the easiest burden to bear; they could all manage him. Even at the very beginning of their dramas, one senses their impatience with the third, they could hardly wait for him. As soon as he appears, everything is fine. But how boring if he is late, nothing can happen without him, everything stalls, waits. Yes, and what if this waiting and anticipation continued? How then, O dramatist, and you, the audience that knows life, what if he were gone, this popular rogue or this presumptuous young man who locks himself into marriage like a key? What if, for example, the devil had fetched him? Let us assume it.

"Mother, Mother," Gregor whispered and looked up at her. For a moment, the procurator had slipped his mind; but he could not resist trying to catch the flowing coffee in the air with his jaws. Over this, the mother screamed anew, fled from the table, and fell into her rushing father's arms. But Gregor now had no time for his parents; the procurator was already on the stairs; his chin resting on the banister, he glanced back for the last time. Gregor made an effort to catch up with him as safely as possible; the procurator must have sensed this, for he leaped over several steps and disappeared; but he still shouted, "Huh!" and his voice resounded through the whole stairwell. Unfortunately, this flight of the procurator now seemed to thoroughly confuse the father, who until now had been relatively calm; instead of chasing the procurator himself or at least not hindering Gregor in his pursuit, he seized the procurator's stick, which the procurator had left behind on a chair together with his hat and overcoat, with his right hand, and with his left hand picked up a large newspaper from the table. He then began to push Gregor back into his room with stamping feet, swinging the stick and the newspaper. No pleading from Gregor helped; no pleading was understood either, no matter how humbly he turned his head. The father merely stamped his feet harder. Over there, despite the cool weather, the mother had opened a window, and leaning out, she pressed her face far outside the window into her hands. A strong draft arose between the alley and the stairwell; the curtains at the window fluttered, the newspapers on the table rustled, and individual sheets of paper were blown across the floor. Unyieldingly, the father urged ahead and, like a wild beast, hissed. But Gregor had no practice at all in backward walking; it really was very slow. If only Gregor could have turned around, he would have been in his room immediately, but he was afraid that the father would become impatient at the time-consuming turn-around and, at any moment, could strike him fatally with the stick in his hand on the back or on the head. Finally, however, Gregor had no other choice, for he realized with horror that he did not even know how to maintain the right direction in backward walking; and so he began to turn around very quickly but actually rather slowly, making continuous nervous glances back at the father. Perhaps the father noticed his good intentions, for he did not disturb him but directed the turning movement from a distance with the tip of his stick. Only that damned hissing of the father! Gregor lost his head completely over it. He was already almost completely turned around when, always listening to this hissing, he even turned back a little more. When he finally reached the door frame with his head, he realized that his body was too wide to pass through without further ado. Of course, it did not even occur to the father in his present condition to open the other door, in order to provide Gregor with sufficient passage. His fixated idea was simply that Gregor had to get back into his room as quickly as possible. He would never have allowed the elaborate preparations Gregor needed to get up and perhaps thereby pass through the door. Perhaps he now urged Gregor forward with an even greater noise as if there were no obstacle; it no longer sounded behind Gregor like the voice of a single father; now there was really no fun left, and Gregor pushed himself – come what may – into the door. One side of his body lifted up; he lay skewed in the door frame, one side of his body was very rubbed raw, leaving ugly stains on the white door; soon he got stuck and could no longer move on his own, the legs on one side hung trembling in the air, the ones on the other side were painfully pressed to the ground – then the father gave him a really relieving hard push from behind, and he flew, bleeding heavily, far into his room. The door was still closed with the stick, then it was finally quiet.

"Mother, Mother," Gregor whispered and looked up at her. The notary had momentarily slipped his mind; yet, he could not resist attempting to seize the flowing coffee again and again with his jaws. Over this, the mother would scream anew, dart away from the table, and rush into her father's arms as he came towards her. Oh, morality! I'm not a boy anymore, I know that myself, — Ganya fiercely interjected, — and I started this conversation with you, my prince, for that very reason. I wouldn't have taken this step for profit, for I would surely have erred, given my inexperience and inchoate character. I am venturing into this darkness out of passion and impulse, because I have a solid goal. You think I'm going to get seventy-five thousand and immediately buy a carriage. No, I would wear an old, third-hand coat and break off all my social connections. We have few principled people here, even though everyone is a usurer, and I want to be one of them. The main thing is to see it through to the end — that is the task! Pytorin slept on the street as a seventeen-year-old, selling pocketknives, and started with a kopeck; now he has sixty thousand, but after what kind of a struggle! I will cut straight to the goal and start from a capital position. In fifteen years, people will say: "There is Ivolygin, the Jewish king." When you tell me I'm not an original, you wound me deeply as a man of my time and race. You didn't even consider me a good scoundrel, and you know, I wanted to eat you just now for that! You have outraged me more than Epanchin, who considers me (without any enticements, in the simplest way, notice this) capable of selling his wife! Oh, Father, this has been annoying me for a long time, and I want money. By earning money, I will become a person of the utmost originality. Money is the most despicable and hateful thing, even giving talents, which they will continue to give until the end of time. You'll say that this is all childlike or, perhaps, poetic, but the better for me, because the matter will still get done. I will see it through and endure. He who laughs last laughs best!1 Why is Epanchin so insulting? Out of spite, perhaps? Never. Simply because I am insignificant. Well, then... However, enough, it's time to leave. Kolya has already called you to dinner twice. I'll go from the yard. I'll sometimes drop by. You will be very well off here; now you will be taken in by the family. Just don't give it away. I think we will either be friends or enemies. What do you think, prince, if yesterday I had kissed your hand (as I was sincerely willing to do), would I have become your enemy for that?

After thus dispelling her misgivings about him, he found the quiet tête-à-tête by the window too long; he tapped the lectern with his knuckles and then with his fist. The student glanced briefly over the woman’s shoulder at K, but was not disturbed, and even pressed closer to her and clasped her. She lowered her head deeply, as if listening attentively; he kissed her as she bent down, loudly on the neck, without interrupting his speech much. K saw his tyranny confirmed, as the student had exercised it after the woman’s complaints about him, and rose, pacing back and forth in the room. He considered how to get rid of the student as quickly as possible, and was not displeased when the student, apparently annoyed by K’s walking around, which had become almost a trampling, remarked: “If you are impatient, you can leave. You could have left earlier, no one would have missed you. Yes, you should have left immediately, and quickly.” This remark might have expressed all kinds of anger, but it also carried the arrogance of a future court official speaking to an unpleasant defendant. K stood very close to him and said smilingly: “I am impatient, that’s true, but this impatience will be easiest to overcome if you leave us. If, however, perhaps you came here to study – I heard that you are a student –, I would gladly make room for you and go away with the woman. You will have to study much more before you become a judge, however. I know your court system only slightly, but I assume that it is not enough to do it merely with rough talk, which you know to deliver quite unseemly well.” “He shouldn’t have been allowed to walk around so freely,” the student said, as if he wanted to explain K’s offensive remark to the woman, “it was a miscalculation. I told the investigating judge. At least during the hearings, he should have been kept in his room. The investigating judge can be incomprehensible at times.” “Useless talk,” said K, stretching out his hand to the woman, “come on.” “Oh, so,” said the student, “no, no, you won’t get her,” and with a force not to be expected of him, he lifted her onto one arm and ran with a bent back, looking lovingly up at her, to the door. A certain fear of K was not to be concealed here, although he dared still to provoke him by caressing and pressing her arm with his free hand. K ran a few steps alongside him, ready to seize him and strangle him if necessary, when the woman said: “It won’t help, the investigating judge will have me, I can’t go with you, this little devil,” she ran her hand over the student’s face, “this little devil won’t let me.” “And you don’t want to be released!” K shouted and placed his hand on the student’s shoulder, who snapped at him with his teeth. “No!” the woman cried and pushed K away with both hands, “no, no, not that, what are you thinking of! That would be my ruin. Let him go, please, let him go. He’s only carrying me to him as the investigating judge orders.” “Then he may go and I’ll never see you again,” K said furiously, pushed the student in the back, and he stumbled, only to spring higher with his burden in sheer joy at not having fallen. K walked after them slowly, realizing that this was the first clear defeat he had experienced from these people. Of course, there was no reason to be scared about that; he only received this defeat because he sought out the fight. If he stayed at home and led his usual life, he would be ten times superior to every one of these people and could easily sweep each one aside with a kick. And he imagined the most ridiculous scene, for example, this pitiful student, this puffed-up child, this hunchbacked bearded man, kneeling before Elsa’s bed and begging for mercy with folded hands. K liked this image so much that he decided to take the student with him to Elsa as soon as he got the chance.

His sleep was fleeting; the deliciously monotonous days were separated by brief nights full of joyful unrest. Though he retired early, for at nine o'clock, when Tadzio vanished from the scene, the day seemed to him concluded. But at the first dawn, he was awakened by a delicate tremor of alarm, his heart remembering the adventure, no longer suffering in the pillows. He rose, and, lightly wrapped against the morning showers, he sat at the open window, waiting for the sun to rise. This wonderful event filled his sleep-imbued soul with reverence. Still, heaven, earth, and sea lay in ghostly glassy twilight; still, a fleeting star swam in the insubstantial. But a stir came, a buoyant message from unreachable dwellings, that Eos would rise from her husband's side, and that the first, sweet blush of the farthest heavens and seashores took place, through which the sensuousness of creation made itself known. The goddess approached, the young man-stealer, who carried off Kleitos, Kephalos, and, defying the jealousy of all the Olympians, enjoyed the love of beautiful Orion. A scattering of roses began at the edge of the world, an inconceivably holy gleaming and blooming, childlike clouds, transfigured, penetrating, floating like serving Amor cups in the rosy, blueish fragrance. Purple fell upon the sea, which seemed to advance and carry him forward in waves, golden spears twitched from the bottom to the height of the heavens, the brilliance became a blaze, silently, with divine overwhelming force, heat and yearning and roaring flames rolled up, and with rearing hooves, the brother's sacred steeds ascended the earth. Radiant with the god's splendor, he sat in solitary watch, closing his eyes and letting his eyelids be kissed by the glory. Former feelings, early, sweet pangs of the heart, which had perished in the strict service of his life and now returned so strangely—recognizing them with a bewildered, amazed smile, he mused, dreamed, slowly forming a name with his lips, and still smiling, with his face turned upward, hands clasped in his lap, he dozed off again in his chair.

K. paused and looked down at the floor. For now, he was still free; he could continue walking and through one of the three small, dark wooden doors not far from him, he could make his escape. It would simply mean that he hadn’t understood, or that he had understood but didn’t care to. If, however, he turned around, he would be held, for then he would have confessed that he had understood, that he was indeed the one summoned and that he wanted to follow. If the priest had called again, K. would certainly have left, but since everything remained silent while K. waited, he turned his head slightly, wanting to see what the priest was doing now. The priest stood calmly on the pulpit as before, but it was clear that he had noticed K.’s turn of head. It would have been a child’s game of hide-and-seek if K. had not turned completely around. He did, and the priest beckoned him closer with a flick of his finger. Now that everything could happen in the open, K. ran—out of curiosity and to shorten the matter—to the pulpit in long, flying strides. When he stopped at the first pews, the priest seemed to think the distance was still too great; he reached out and pointed his sharply lowered finger at a spot just in front of the pulpit. K. obeyed; he had to bend his head back far to see the priest. "You are Josef K.," the priest said, raising his hand on the railing in an indeterminate gesture. "Yes," said K., thinking of how freely he had once stated his name, how now it was a burden to him, even to people he met for the first time. "You are on trial," the priest said softly. "Yes," said K., "I was informed." "Then you are the one I am looking for," said the priest. "I am the prison chaplain." "Ah, so," said K. "I called you here to talk to you." "I did not know that," said K. "I came here to show an Italian the cathedral." "Let us leave that aside," said the priest. "What are you holding in your hand? Is it a prayer book?" "No," replied K., "it is an album of the city’s sights." "Put it down," said the priest. K. threw it away so hard that it opened and the pages, crushed, dragged across the floor. "Do you know that your case is not going well?" the priest asked. "It seems that way to me too," said K. "I have done everything I can, but so far without success. I have not yet finished filing the case." "What do you think the outcome will be?" the priest asked. "I used to think it would end well," said K., "but I doubt it now. I don’t know how it will end. Do you know?" "No," said the priest, "but I fear it will end badly. They think you are guilty. Your case might not even reach a court of higher authority. They think, at least for now, that you are guilty." "But I am not guilty," said K., "it is a mistake. How can anyone be guilty. We are all human, one like another." "That is true," said the priest, "but the guilty often speak like that." "Do you have a prejudice against me?" asked K. "I have no prejudice against you," said the priest. "Thank you," said K., "but the others involved in the case do. They instill it in the uninvolved as well. My situation is becoming increasingly difficult." "You misunderstand the facts," said the priest, "the judgment does not come all at once, the case gradually leads to the judgment." "So it is," said K. and lowered his head. "What will you do next in your case?" the priest asked. "I will seek help," said K. and raised his head to see how the priest would judge this. "There are still certain possibilities I have not utilized." "You are seeking too much help from others," said the priest disapprovingly, "especially from women. Do you not see that it is not true help?" "Sometimes, and even often, I might agree with you," said K., "but not always. Women have great power. Now, since the Tripitaka monk saw that the Monk Who Walks on the Winds did not arrive in a hurry, he was very puzzled, not knowing whether the Bodhisattva had not been summoned or whether the Monk Who Walks on the Winds had made a pretext to escape. Just as he was guessing and speculating wildly, he saw a colorful mist shimmering in mid-air, and the Monk Who Walks on the Winds suddenly fell to the steps, calling out, "Teacher, the robe has arrived." The Tripitaka monk was greatly pleased, and all the monks were likewise delighted, saying, "There! There! Our lives are finally saved today." The Tripitaka monk took the robe and said, "Wukong, you went early this morning, originally agreeing to return at noon after the meal, how are you returning so late in the day?" The Monk Who Walks on the Winds recounted all the matters of summoning the Bodhisattva and causing transformations to subdue demons. The Tripitaka monk heard and then set up a sacrificial altar and bowed southward. He said, "Disciple, since we have the Buddha's robe, you should quickly pack your belongings and go." The Monk Who Walks on the Winds said, "Not so quick, not so quick. It's late today, not a good time to travel, let's wait until tomorrow morning." All the monks then fell to their knees together.
