Mrs. Margarete Brigge had always, so far as I can remember, been a tall, inaccessible old woman. I cannot imagine her being any younger than the chamberlain. She lived among us, her life completely to herself, without considering anyone else. She relied on no one and had always had a companion, an aging Countess Oxe, whom she had bound to herself through some act of generosity. This must have been an exception, for she was not generally a charitable person. She did not love children, and animals were not allowed near her. I do not know if she loved anything else. It was said that when she was young, she had been engaged to the handsome Prince Felix Lichnowski, who then died so cruelly in Frankfurt. Indeed, a portrait of the Prince was there after her death, which, if I am not mistaken, had been returned to the family. Perhaps, I think now, she had missed out on a different, more glittering life: her natural one. It is difficult to say if she mourned for it. Perhaps she despised it for not having happened, for having missed the opportunity to live with skill and talent. She had absorbed all of this within herself and enveloped it in many, brittle, somewhat metallic gleaming shells, whose uppermost layer was always new and cool. Yet, occasionally, she betrayed herself through a naive impatience at not being sufficiently attended to; at my time, she could suddenly choke on something at the table, in some visible and complicated way that secured everyone's attention and made her, for a moment at least, so sensational and exciting as she might have been in the grander scheme. However, I suspect that my father was the only one who took these far too frequent accidents seriously. He leaned politely forward and watched her, one could see how he offered her his own, proper air passage in his thoughts and placed himself entirely at her disposal. The chamberlain, of course, had stopped eating as well; he took a small sip of wine and refrained from any opinion.

Mrs. Margarete Brigge had always, as far as I can remember, been a tall, aloof old hag. I can only imagine that she must have been much older than the Chamberlain. She lived among us, her life, without considering anyone else. She was dependent on none of us and had always had a kind of companion, an elderly Countess Oxe, whom she had somehow obligated to herself through some act of benevolence. This, I suppose, must have been an exception, for charity was not her way. She did not love children, and animals were not allowed in her proximity. I do not know if she loved anything else. It was said that she had been engaged to the handsome Felix Lichnowski when she was young, who then died a cruel death in Frankfurt. Indeed, after her death, a portrait of the Prince was there, which, if I remember correctly, was returned to the family. Perhaps, I think now, she missed having remained enclosed in this rural life, which, year by year, had become more characteristic of Ulsgaard, and had missed out on another, more brilliant one: her natural one. It is hard to say if she regretted this. Perhaps she despised it because it had not come to be, because it had missed the opportunity to be lived with skill and talent. She had taken all of this in, and wrapped it in many, brittle, somewhat metallic gleaming shells, of which the uppermost was always new and cool. Occasionally, however, she betrayed herself through a naive eagerness not to be overlooked; in my time, she could suddenly choke at the dinner table in some clear and complicated way, securing everyone’s attention and, for a moment at least, making her so sensational and exciting as she might have been in a grander context. Nevertheless, I suspect that my father was the only one who took these much too frequent coincidences seriously. He saw her, politely leaning forward, and one could see how he offered her, in his thoughts, his own orderly airway, entirely at her disposal. The Chamberlain, of course, had also stopped eating; he took a small sip of wine and said nothing.

"I saw," the townsman began, "that the janitors wouldn't come, because they said it was too late, and perhaps they'd get angry that I hadn't sent them sooner. It made me upset, and I decided to go to sleep. I started asking around. Yesterday and today, I was inquiring. I was the first to come, but he wasn't there. He came after an hour, and they didn't let him in, but in the third attempt, they admitted him. I began to tell him everything, as it had happened, and he started pacing the room, hitting his chest with his fist: 'What are you, robbers, doing to me? If I had known about this matter, I would have requested a guard for it!' Then he rushed out, called someone, and began talking to them in a corner. Afterward, he came back to me, asking and berating me. He reproached me many times, and I told him everything I knew and said that, based on my words from yesterday, they hadn't dared to reply to me at all and hadn't recognized me. He started running around again, hitting his chest, fuming, and running. When you were reported, he said, 'Climb over the partition, sit there and don't move, no matter what you hear, bring me a chair, and lock me in; maybe I'll ask you something.' And when Nikolai was brought in, he led me out after you and said, 'I'll still need you and will still ask you questions...'"

-"I saw," began the townsman, "that the janitors wouldn't come, saying it was too late already, and he might be even more angry that they hadn't come while he was still there. It made me upset, and I decided to sleep on it and investigate further. Yesterday and today, I went around asking around. I was there for the first time, and he wasn't there. He arrived a little later and refused to let me in, but on the third attempt, he finally let me in. I told him everything that happened, and he began to pace back and forth, pounding his chest with his fist, shouting, 'What are you, robbers, doing to me? If I had known about such a case, I would have demanded it with an escort!' And after Nikolai was brought in, he led me out after you, saying, 'I'll still demand you and ask more questions...'"

Fathers and teachers, I think: "What is hell?" I reason: "It is the suffering of not being able to love any longer." Once, in an infinite being, unmeasurable by time or space, a spiritual creature was given the ability to say to itself: "I am, and I love." Once, only once, was that creature given the moment of active love, of living love, and for that was earthly life given, with its times and durations. But, what happened? That blessed creature rejected the invaluable gift, did not appreciate it, did not love it, looked at it with derision, and remained insensitive. This one, who has already left the earth, sees Abraham’s bosom and speaks with Abraham, as the parable of the rich man and Lazarus shows us, and he sees paradise, and may ascend to the Lord, but precisely by that fact he suffers, because he will ascend to the Lord, having not loved, having come into contact with those who have loved, having neglected love. For he clearly sees and says to himself: "Now I have knowledge and although I long to love, there will be no effort in my love, no sacrifice, for the earthly life has ended, and Lazarus will not come again, alive in a drop of water (that is, not a new earthly life, but a previous and active one) to cool the flame of spiritual love which now burns within me, having neglected it on earth; there is no longer life, and no more time! Although I might have been willing to give my life for others, but it is no longer possible, for that life which could have been offered as a sacrifice for love has passed, and now there is a void between that life and this being." They speak of the hellish flame: I do not investigate this mystery and am afraid, but I think that if there were a material flame, they would indeed be glad of it, for I dream thus that in the suffering of the material, for a moment, the most terrible spiritual suffering would be forgotten. But to take away from them this spiritual suffering is impossible, for this suffering is not external, but within them. If it were possible to take it away, I think, they would become even more wretched. For although the righteous in paradise might forgive them by looking upon their suffering and call them to themselves, loving infinitely, thereby they would only increase their suffering, for they would kindle in them an even stronger flame of the longing for a return, an active and grateful love, which is now impossible. With the timidity of my heart, I think, however, that the very awareness of this impossibility would serve them finally to some alleviation, for by accepting the love of the righteous and the impossibility of repaying it, in the humility of this and the action of this humility, they will finally find some semblance of that active love which they neglected on earth, and some action resembling it... I regret, brothers and friends, that I cannot express this more clearly. But woe to those who have destroyed themselves on earth, woe to the suicides! I think that no one is more unfortunate than they. God tells us that we should not pray to Him for them, and the church outwardly rejects them, but I think in the depths of my soul that we could pray for them. For Christ did not harden His heart over love. For such I have prayed inwardly all my life, confessing to you, fathers and teachers, and continue to pray each day.

Zhang Shao said, "Li Ding, we can truly coexist and enjoy each other's company with just a light recitation, without the need for a board and goblets. But since we have no need to display our prowess with verse, why don't we each compose a couplet and see how our words fare in conversation?" Li Ding replied, "Brother Zhang, you speak most wisely. Please go first." "Our boats rest in the green waters amid smoke and mist, and our homes are nestled in the deep mountains, far from the world. We especially love the spring floods in the stream bridges, and the early morning clouds shrouding the rock peaks. Fresh carp from the Dragon Gate are often cooked, while worm-eaten firewood is burnt daily. We have various fishing nets for our old age, and two farming tools to sustain us. Lying on a small boat to watch flying geese, we walk a winding path to listen to the cries of cranes. In the verbal arena, I have no part, and in the sea of strife, I seldom tread. By the stream, we hang and dry our silk like brocade, and grind our axes on stones like blades. I often fish alone under the autumn moon, and no one meets me in the silent spring mountains. With extra fish, we share wine with our wives, and with leftover firewood, we share drinks with our sons."

Zhāng Sháo said, "Li Dìng, we are truly comrades in verse, needing no board or golden goblet. Our talent for composing poems is not rare, let us each compose a few lines and see how our conversation as fishermen and woodcutters fares?" Li Dìng replied, "Brother Zhāng, your words are most delightful. Please go first."

"On green waters and misty waves, my boat moors at home in the depths of the mountains. I love the spring tide in the stream, and the morning mist clinging to the rocks. Fresh carp from the Dragon Gate are cooked and consumed, while chipped logs roast all day. My fishing nets and tools are sufficient for a peaceful old age, and my donkey is suited for my daily pursuits. Lying in my small boat watching flying geese, I lean on a grass path listening to the honking of cranes. In the arena of words, I have no part, and in the sea of strife, I leave no trace. On the streamside, my dyed cloth hangs like a fine tapestry, and my axe, polished on the rock, gleams like a blade. I often fish alone by the autumn moon, and rarely meet anyone in the silent spring mountains. I trade fish for wine with my wife, and share my remaining firewood with my sons in a cluster of mugs."

Zhāng Shāo said, "Li Dìng, we truly can share our little verses without the need for boards or golden goblets. We can just recite poems and verses, and let's each compose a couplet and see how our boatman's chat fares?"

Li Dìng said, "Brother Zhang speaks most aptly. Please compose first."

"In waters of the green stream, my boat moors; I dwell deep in the mountain's vast embrace.
I delight in the spring flood at the stream bridge; I love the mist-wrapped dawn at the rocky cliffs.
Fresh carp from the Dragon Gate are often cooked; I burn worm-eaten wood for daily heat.
Net and line, these means suffice for my old age; basket and staff, these tools can see me through.
Lying in my boat, I watch the flying geese; stepping on the grass path, I hear the honking cranes.
In the arena of words, I hold no stake; in the sea of strife, I leave no trace.
I hang and dry my nets like brocade near the stream; I sharpen my axes on the stone again and again.
Fishing alone by the autumn moon, I find no one; in the silent spring hills, I roam unmet.
I trade fish for wine with my wife; with leftover wood, I toast with my son."

Zhang Shao said, "Li Ding, we are truly friends who can indulge in delicate poetry, without the need for the clapping of boards or golden goblets. Though our words on literature may not be rare, let us exchange lines and see how our conversation as fishermen and woodcutters fares?"

Li Ding said, "Brother Zhang, your suggestion is perfect. Please begin."

"On tranquil waters, the greenboat ties,  
In deep mountains, my home lies wide.
I love the spring water's rise at the stream bridge,  
Admiring the morn's cloud on rock's side.
Fresh carp from Dragon Gate I cook each day,  
Burnt wood I tend to, day by day.
My fishing nets to old age can provide,  
With my yoke and pole, I'll make a ride.
Lying on a small boat, gazing at flying geese,  
On a grass path, leaning, listening to wild goose's cries.
In the fray of words, no part I play,  
In the sea of strife, scarce my way.
Clothesline by the stream, my cloths are hung like brocade so bright,  
Stone slab by the rock, my axe's edge sharpened, keen and fit.
常独钓于秋月之辉辉，  
寂无人逢春山寂。
换酒与妻共饮鱼多时，  
柴剩沽壶同子丛。"

Zhāng Shāo said, "Li Dìng, we truly share the pleasure of subtle and resonant poetry, without the need for boards or golden goblets. While it's not rare to spread our verses, let us each couplet a few lines and see how our fisher's chatter fares?" Li Dìng replied, "Brother Zhāng, your words are most fitting. May I have the honor of going first?"

"On green waters, my boat rests in misty waves,  
In deep mountains, my home is far from the town's noise.  
I especially love the spring floods on stream bridges,  
Most fond of the early mists veiling rocky peaks.  
Fresh carp from the Dragon Gate are often cooked,  
Burnt wood, worm-eaten, is used daily to cook.  
My fishing nets are varied, suited for my old age,  
And my cart ropes serve my life's journey well.  
Lying in my small boat, gazing at flying geese,  
Walking on a slanted path, listening to cranes cry.  
In the arena of words, I have no part,  
In the sea of disputes, I leave few traces.  
By the stream, I hang and dry my colorful cloths,  
On the stone, I sharpen my sharp axes.  
Under the autumn moon, I fish alone,  
In the silent spring mountains, I seldom meet others.  
I trade my fish for wine with my wife,  
I share my leftover firewood with my children."

The Master said, "Among the Thirty-Six Taoist Schools under the Way, each has its own fruit of attainment. I wonder which school you wish to learn from?" Monkey said, "I will follow my master's will. I will give my full attention." The Master said, "I will teach you the path of the 'Jue' School. How do you find that?" Monkey said, "What is the path of the Jue School?" The Master said, "The Jue School teaches fortune-telling and divination, the summoning of spirits and mediums, to discern auspiciousness and avoid inauspiciousness." Monkey said, "Can such knowledge lead to eternal life?" The Master said, "No! No!" Monkey said, "I will not learn! I will not learn!"

The Master said, "There are three hundred and sixty side schools within the Way, and all these side schools can attain the true fruit. I do not know which school you wish to learn." Sun Wukong replied, "I will follow the Master's wishes. My disciple will listen and obey." The Master said, "Teach you the path of the 'Skill' school, how does that sound?" Sun Wukong asked, "How is the path of the Skill school?" The Master said, "The Skill school is about summoning spirits, spirit writing, divination, and predicting fortune or misfortune." Sun Wukong said, "Can this lead to immortality?" The Master said, "No! No!" Sun Wukong said, "Not learning! Not learning!"

The First Teacher said, "Among the 'Way' sect there are three hundred and sixty offshoots, each with its own fruit of enlightenment. Do not know which sect you wish to study?" Monkey said, "Dependent on Master's will. Disciple listens with all heart." The First Teacher said, "I shall teach you the Way of the 'Technique' sect, how say you?" Monkey said, "How is the Way of the Technique sect?" The First Teacher said, "The Technique sect involves summoning spirits and spirits riding on phoenixes, divination and manipulation of yarrow stalks, and the ability to know how to seek good fortune and avoid misfortune." Monkey said, "Can this lead to eternal life?" The First Teacher said, "No! No!" Monkey said, "Not to learn! Not to learn!"

The Senior Master said, "The Door of Dao contains 360 offshoot doors, each with its own true fruit. I wonder which door you wish to study?" Buddha said, "I follow your esteemed teacher's guidance. The disciple listens intently and complies." The Senior Master said, "I will teach you the path of the ‘J technic’ Door, how about that?" Buddha said, "What does the J technic path entail?" The Senior Master said, "The J technic path involves inviting immortals, performing spirit writing, divination, and the use of yarrow stalks, all to understand how to seek good fortune and avoid misfortune." Buddha said, "Can this lead to eternal life?" The Senior Master said, "No! No!" Buddha said, "No! No!"

The First Ancestor said, "In the sect of the Dao, there are three hundred and sixty minor sects, each with its own ultimate achievement. I do not know which sect you wish to learn from." Monkey said, "I will follow whatever Master sees fit. I will listen with all my heart." The First Ancestor said, "I will teach you the path of the 'Jue' sect. What do you think of that?" Monkey said, "How does the Jue sect's path go?" The First Ancestor said, "In the Jue sect, there is seance and spirit communication, divination, and divining with yarrow stalks, all to understand how to seek good fortune and avoid disaster." Monkey said, "Can this lead to immortality?" The First Ancestor said, "No! No!" Monkey said, "No! No!"

Aschenbach was tempted to warn him with a finger. “But I advise you, Kritobulos,” he thought, smiling, “go on a journey for a year! For that much time you will need at least to recover.” And then he ate large, fully ripe strawberries, which he bought from a vendor. It had become very warm, even though the sun could not penetrate the layer of mist in the sky. Laziness held the mind captive, while the senses enjoyed the endless and stupefying conversation of the still sea. To guess and explore what name it was, roughly called “Adgio,” seemed to the serious man a fitting and completely fulfilling task and occupation. And with the help of some Polish memories, he realized that “Tadzio” must be the name, an abbreviation of “Tadeusz” and pronounced “Tadziu” in calling. Tadzio was swimming. Aschenbach, who had lost sight of him, spotted his head and arm, with which he was paddling far out in the sea; for the sea seemed flat to the horizon. But already there was concern for him, and women's voices from the huts called out to him, uttering again that name that dominated the shore like a watchword, with its soft consonants and the drawn-out u-sound at the end, something sweet and wild: “Tadziu, Tadziu!” He obeyed and ran back through the waves, water-washed head and limbs. To see the living figure, at once noble and heroic, emerging from the depths of sky and sea, dripping with wet locks and beautiful as a delicate god, as it emerged from the elements: this sight inspired mythological conceptions, it was like poetical knowledge from the earliest times, the origin of form and the birth of the gods. Aschenbach listened with closed eyes to this singing within him; and once more he thought that here was good, and that he wanted to stay.

Being a rightful monk, one must endure hardships and toil to be a proper disciple," the Buddha said. "Brother, how heavy is this burden?" Zhu Bajie asked. "Brother, since you and Sand Monk joined, I haven't been carrying it; how could I know how heavy it is?" Zhu Bajie said, "Brother, look and count: four pieces of yellow bamboo, eight strips of rope. To guard against rain, there are three or four layers of felt. The flat pole is slippery, so nails are hammered in on both ends. A copper-hilted iron club with nine rings, bound with bamboo and woven with vines for a large cloak. With such a heavy load, it's hard for old pig like me to carry it day in and day out, yet you get to follow the Master as his disciple, while I have to be his hired hand!" The Monkey King laughed and said, "Dumbass, who are you talking to?" Zhu Bajie said, "Brother, I'm talking to you." The Monkey King said, "You're speaking to the wrong one. I look out only for the Master's well-being. You and Sand Monk are responsible for the luggage and horses. If either of you slack off, you'll get a good whack with a stout stick first!"

Since you are a disciple of the right path, you must endure hardships to become one. So, Brother, how heavy is this load?” said Zhu Bajie. “Brother, have you not noticed how heavy it is?” said the Monkey King. “Brother, please count: four yellow rattan strips, eight pieces of string. We must also prepare for rain; we need three or four layers of felt. We are afraid of the flat baskets sliding, so let’s nail them down. A nine-ringed cane with iron hoops, covered with a large cloak woven from rattan and twigs. With all this luggage, it’s difficult for Brother Pig to carry it every day. But you, Brother, are fortunate enough to follow the master as his disciple, while I’m just a long-term laborer!” The Monkey King laughed and said, “Oaf, who are you talking to?” “Brother, I am talking to you,” said Zhu Bajie. “You’ve said the wrong thing, Brother. I care only for the master’s welfare. You and Sand Monk are in charge of the luggage and horses. If you are negligent even a little, I’ll give you a good beating first with a rough stick!”

Later, Nikolai Kushtich always assured everyone that although he was naturally in a rather downcast mood that Sunday evening, he had not drunk anything. He was therefore completely sober when the following happened, if one can actually say anything did happen. Perhaps, he dozed off for a bit in his corner; one might well imagine that. This small nap brought him an initial sense of relief. I have been dealing with these numbers, he told himself. Well, I don’t understand numbers. But it is clear that they should not be given too much importance; they are, after all, just a state institution, for the sake of order. Nobody had ever seen numbers elsewhere, on a wall or in real life. For example, a seven or twenty-five would never appear at a party; there simply weren’t such numbers. And then there had been this little mix-up, purely out of carelessness: time and money, as if one couldn’t distinguish between them. Nikolai Kushtich almost laughed. It was good to come to such realizations, and in time, that was the important thing, in time. It was time for a change. Time, yes, that was a delicate matter. But did it concern him alone? Did it not affect others, as he had discovered, in a matter of seconds, even if they did not know it?

Upon hearing this, the Great Sage chuckled to himself, saying, "This Buddha is very foolish! I, Old孙, can travel ten-thousand eight-thousand miles in a single somersault. His palm does not even span a square foot, how could I not jump out?" He quickly said, "If so, can you make a guarantee on this?" The Buddha replied, "I can! I can!" and stretched out his right hand, which seemed as large as a lotus leaf. The Great Sage then folded his divine will and, with a single bound, stood in the Buddha's palm, saying, "I go now!" You see, he vanished into a trail of cloud light, invisible and formless. The Buddha's wise eye observed, seeing the monkey king like a whirlwind, unceasingly advancing. As the Great Sage walked, he suddenly saw five red pillars, supporting a strand of green air. He thought, "This is the end of the road. This time, with the Buddha as witness, the Jade Emperor's Palace will surely be mine." Then he thought, "Hold on! Let me leave a mark so we can talk about this." He plucked a hair, blew on it with divine breath, and said, "Change!" It transformed into a fine, double-tipped brush, with which he wrote a single large character on the middle pillar, reading: "The Great Sage, Ever-Victorious, has been here." Done with the hair, he, not being respectful, urinated a bit of monkey urine by the first pillar. He then turned his somersault cloud and returned straight to his place, standing in the Buddha's palm. "I've gone, and now I'm back. You tell the Jade Emperor to give me the Heavenly Palace."

That Monkey King, upon hearing this, sneered to himself, "This Buddha is truly foolhardy! I, Old孙, can travel ten thousand eight thousand li in a single somersault. His palm, no bigger than a square foot, how could I not jump out?" He swiftly said, "Since it is thus, can you make good on your claim?" The Buddha replied, "Certainly! Certainly!" He stretched out his right hand, which appeared no larger than a lotus leaf. The Monkey King, stowing his magic staff, exerted his divine power, leaped, and stood in the palm of the Buddha, saying, "I am leaving now!" You see him vanish in a trail of cloud, formless and invisible. The Buddha's divine vision watched, seeing the monkey king continue to travel like a spinning wheel, pressing on. As the Monkey King walked, he suddenly noticed five red pillars, supporting a patch of green air. He thought, "This must be the end of the path. This time, when I return, the Buddha will bear witness, and the Heavenly Capital will surely be mine to sit in." Then he pondered, "Wait! I must leave a mark so I can speak with the Buddha." He plucked a hair, blew a breath of spiritual air, and said, "Transform!" It transformed into a fine, double-tipped brush, which he used to write a single line of characters on the pillar, saying, "Visiting Scholar of Heaven, was here." Finished, he tucked away the hair. Yet, he did not behave with due reverence, and instead urinated on the base of the first pillar. The son-in-law, following his mother’s instructions, also summoned a few servants, each carrying hunting equipment, and they headed down the main road. The scenery of the forest and the views from the mountain tops were enchanting. After half a day, they reached a mountain in the distance that truly touched the clouds, towering and steep. Tripitaka reached the foot of the mountain in a short time. The son-in-law climbed the mountain easily as if it were flat ground. When they reached the halfway point, Bochen turned around and stood by the roadside, saying, "Master, you continue on your way. I must return now." Hearing this, Tripitaka dismounted and said, "Please, Your Excellency, do not hesitate to accompany me a little further!" Bochen replied, "Master, you are unaware that this mountain is called the Boundary Mountain. The eastern half belongs to our Tang Empire, while the western half is Tartar territory. The wolves and tigers there do not submit to my rule, so I cannot cross the border. You may continue on your way." Tripitaka was frightened, and as he held Bochen’s robe, tears streamed down his face. Just as they were saying their farewells, a voice from below the mountain cried out like thunder, "My master is here! My master is here!" This caused Tripitaka to go blank with fear, and Bochen struggled. It was unknown who was calling out. The story continues in the next chapter.

Once, I had to carry some Bohemian dishes, the edges were smooth and slippery—may they fall to hell! A fine and ancient position, really: just sit there looking important, cross your legs, and sway them, but don’t answer right away when anyone comes in, first roar, and then, if you feel like it, let them in or shove them out of the door; but to the good guests, of course, right in the chest with a pin! — Zakharchuk waved his hand right in the chest. — It’s grand to talk about it! But what an unpleasant lady! Good riddance! Once she glanced into my room, saw a louse, went mad, and started screaming as if I had invented lice! What do you expect without lice in the house! Another time, she passed by me, thought I smelled of wine… such a thing can happen! And she refused.

You see, the King of Monkeys split the waterway and returned to the iron plate bridgehead, darting up onto it. There, the four older monkeys led by the others were waiting by the bridge. Suddenly, Monkey King leaped out from the waves, completely dry and glistening, and strolled onto the bridge. This frightened the other monkeys, who all kneeled down and cried, "Your Majesty, how splendid! How splendid!" Monkey King smiled, his face beaming, as he mounted the throne and stood the rod upright in the center. The other monkeys, ignorant of the rod's worth, came to take the treasure, but it was as if dragonflies were trying to shake a cypress tree; not even a bit could they move it. Each one bit their fingers and stuck out their tongues, saying, "Grandfather, it’s so heavy! How did you manage to bring it?" Monkey King advanced and, with an open palm, seized the rod and said with a smile, "Every item has its owner. This treasure was sealed in the sea for thousands of years. It suddenly shone last year. The Dragon King thought it was just a piece of black iron and called it the Godly Treasure at the Bottom of the Celestial River. Nobody could budge it, so they asked me to fetch it myself. At that time, the rod was over two dozen feet long, as thick as a ladle, but after I grabbed it, I thought it was too big, so it shrank. I made it smaller and it became even smaller, and then even smaller; only then, when I looked at it under the light of the heavens, did I see a line of characters, '如意金箍棒, 一万三千五百斤' (Widu Jinkubang, 13500 jin). Step back, I’ll show you how it can change size." He took the rod in his hand and shouted, "Smaller! Smaller! Smaller!" It instantly shrank to the size of a sewing needle, fitting inside his ear. The monkeys were alarmed and called, "Your Majesty, take it out and play with it again!" Monkey King indeed took it out of his ear and held it in his palm, shouting, "Bigger! Bigger! Bigger!" and the rod grew into a ladle-sized thickness and two dozen feet long. Delighted by his demonstration, Monkey King leaped onto the bridge, walked out to the cave entrance, gripped the rod in his hand, and employed his power to alter the heavens and earth. He bent his waist and shouted, "Grow!" and he grew to be ten thousand feet tall, his head like a mountain, waist like a steep ridge, eyes like lightning, mouth like a blood basin, and teeth like swords. In his hand, the rod reached the thirty-third heaven above and the eighteen layers of hell below, terrorizing the tigers, leopards, wolves, and insects, the mountain’s bandits, and the seventy-two cave demon kings. They all knelt and paid homage, trembling and their souls fleeing. In an instant, he retracted his form and changed the rod back to the size of a sewing needle, hiding it in his ear, returning to his lair. The various cave demon kings were so startled that they rushed to congratulate him.

First of all, where did the possibility of such suspicion arise? – Il'ya Kirillovich began with this question. – The first to shout that Smerdyakov had killed was the defendant himself at the moment of his arrest, and yet, from the moment of his outburst until this very trial, he did not present a single fact in support of his accusation – neither a fact, nor even any hint, however reasonable, of a fact. Then, only three people confirmed the accusation: the defendant's two brothers and Madam Svetlova. But the older brother of the defendant only declared his suspicion today, in a fit of illness, delirium, and fever, and until the last two months, as we know for certain, he shared the belief in his brother's guilt, even without attempting to dispute the idea. But we will deal with this more specifically later. Then, the younger brother of the defendant himself declared recently that there are no facts to support his belief in Smerdyakov's guilt, not even the slightest ones, and he concludes thus only on the word of the defendant and "by the expression of his face" – yes, this colossal piece of evidence was stated twice recently by his brother. Madam Svetlova went even further, perhaps: "Believe what the defendant says to you, for such a man would not lie." These are all the factual evidence presented by these three interested parties in the defendant's fate. And yet, the accusation against Smerdyakov persisted and still does – can we believe in this, can we imagine it?

For several years now, the Indian Cholera had shown a heightened tendency to spread and wander. Originating from the warm mud flats of the Ganges Delta, rising with the mephitic odour of that lush, inhospitable wilderness, avoided by men and full of bamboo thickets where tigers crouched, the disease had ravaged Hindustan persistently and unusually fiercely, had overreached into China to the east, Afghanistan and Persia to the west, and, following the main caravan routes, had spread its terror as far as Astrachan, and even to Moscow. But while Europe shuddered in fear, as if the spectre might enter through land from there, it was almost simultaneously, carried across the sea by Syrian merchants, that it appeared in several ports of the Mediterranean, raised its head in Toulon and Malaga, and showed its face in Palermo and Naples, and seemed unwilling to leave Calabria and Apulia. The northern part of the peninsula had been spared. However, in mid-May of this year, one and the same day, the dreadful Vibrios were found in the emaciated, blackish corpses of a ship's boy and a vegetable vendor in Venice. The cases were concealed. But after a week, there were ten, then twenty, thirty, and these appeared in different quarters. A man from an Austrian province, who had stayed in Venice for pleasure for a few days and had returned home, died under unmistakable signs of illness, and so news of the plague's visitation to the lagoon city reached German daily papers. The authorities of Venice replied that the city's health conditions had never been better and took the necessary measures to combat the disease. But probably the food had been infected. Vegetables, meat, or milk, for it was denied and covered up, death ate in the narrow lanes, and the premature summer heat, which heated the water of the canals into a hissing, was especially favourable for the spread. Indeed, it seemed that the disease had renewed its strength, that the tenacity and fertility of its germs had doubled. Cases of recovery were very rare; eighty percent of those infected died in a horrifying manner, for the evil appeared with extreme ferocity and often took the most dangerous form, known as 'dry'. Here, the body was unable to get rid of the mass of water that was exuded from the blood vessels. Within a few hours, the patient withered away and suffocated in the thick, coagulated blood, convulsed by fits and hoarse screams. Well he was if, as sometimes happened, the attack came after a slight illness in the form of a deep faint, from which he did not or hardly ever awakened. In the beginning of June, the quarantine barracks of the civic Ospedale were filled in silence, the two orphanages began to lack space, and a horrifying rush reigned between the dock of the new foundations and San Michele, the cemetery island. But the fear of general damage, the consideration for the recently opened painting exhibition in the public gardens, the great losses that threatened the hotels, the shops, the whole diverse foreign trade in case of panic and slander, proved more powerful in the city than truthfulness and respect for international agreements; they enabled the authorities to maintain their policy of concealment and denial obstinately. The chief medical officer of Venice, a deserving man, had resigned from his post in protest and was replaced by a more compliant personality in secret. The people knew this; and the corruption of the superiors, together with the prevailing uncertainty, the state of emergency into which the sudden death cast the city, brought about a certain demoralization of the lower classes, an encouragement of light-hearted and antisocial impulses, which manifested themselves in excess, wantonness, and growing criminality. Against the rules, one noticed many drunkards in the evenings; it was said that dangerous ruffians made the streets unsafe at night; robberies and even murders were repeated, for it had already been proven twice that people supposedly killed by the disease had been poisoned by their own relatives; and the mercenary laxity assumed the intrusive and flagrant forms that were unknown here and only customary in the south of the country and in the Orient.

Against the grain, many were seen drunk in the evenings; it was said that after dark, dangerous elements made the streets unsafe; robberies and even murder were repeated, for it had already been proven twice that persons who had supposedly fallen victim to the plague had, in fact, been done away with by their own relatives using poison; and the venality had taken increasingly intrusive and unrestrained forms that were otherwise unknown here and had only been found in the south of the country and in the Orient.

For a few hours each day, I spent time in Dronningens Tværgade, in the narrow rooms that seemed offended, like all the rented apartments where someone had died. I walked between the desk and the large white tiled stove, burning the Jägermeister’s papers. I had started to throw the bundles of letters into the fire as they were, but the small packages were tightly tied and only charred at the edges. It took great resolve to loosen them. Most had a strong, persuasive scent that penetrated me as if it sought to arouse memories. I had none. Sometimes photographs would slip out, heavier than the rest; these photographs burned excruciatingly slowly. I do not know how it came to pass, but suddenly I thought it could be Ingeborg’s picture. But whenever I looked, they were full, magnificent, clearly beautiful women, which distracted me. It turned out that I was not entirely without memories. Exactly those eyes were the ones in which I would sometimes find myself when, at the time I was growing up, I walked down the street with my father. Then they would encircle me from within a car, from which it was almost impossible to escape. Now I knew that he had compared me to them and the comparison did not favor me. Indeed, the Jägermeister had nothing to fear in terms of comparisons.

On Place St-Michel, many vehicles were about and people hurried by; we were often caught between two cars, and then he would catch his breath and ease up a little, as if to rest, and a bit he bounced and nodded a bit. Perhaps this was the trick with which the captive illness sought to overcome him. His will was broken at two points, and the yielding had left in the possessed muscles a gentle, tempting lure and the compelling second beat. But the cane was still in its place, and his hands looked fierce and angry; so we crossed the bridge, and we went. We went. Now uncertainty entered his gait; now he took two steps, and now he stood. Stood. The left hand gently detached itself from the cane and rose so slowly that I could see it tremble in the air; he pushed his hat back slightly and combed his forehead. He turned his head a little, and his gaze swayed over sky, buildings, and water without anchoring, and then he gave in. The cane was gone; he stretched out his arms as if to take flight, and something burst forth from him like a natural force, bending him forward and pulling him back, making him nod and lean, and flinging out dancing power among the crowd. For already many people surrounded him, and I could no longer see him.

The head monk said, "Only twenty li away, and the mountain peak is already in sight from here." The Monkey smiled and said, "Master, be at ease; no need to say any more. Someone must have slandered Josef K., for although he had done nothing wrong, he was arrested one morning. Frau Grubach’s cook, who brought his breakfast every morning at eight, did not come this time. This had never happened before. K. waited for a while, watching the old woman who lived opposite and who was observing him with an unusual interest. Then, simultaneously surprised and hungry, he rang the bell. Immediately, there was a knock, and a man entered whom K. had never seen in this apartment before. He was slim but solidly built, dressed in a close-fitting black coat with various pleats, pockets, clasps, buttons, and a belt, which, similar to a travel suit, made it seem particularly practical, but without it being clear for what. “Who are you?” asked K. and sat up halfway in bed. The man, however, skirted the question, as if he expected to be accepted, and simply said, “You rang?” “Anna should bring me breakfast,” said K. and tried, at first silently, to determine, by means of attention and thought, who the man really was. But this man did not endure K.’s scrutiny for long, and he turned to the door, which he opened slightly, to say to someone who stood behind it, “He wants Anna to bring him breakfast.” A small laugh followed from the next room, and though it was not certain whether it came from more than one person, K. did not suspect that the stranger could learn anything he did not already know. Nevertheless, he now said to K. in a report-like tone, “That’s impossible.” “That’s new,” said K. and jumped out of bed, quickly pulling on his trousers. “I want to see who’s in the next room and how Frau Grubach will explain this disturbance to me.” Although he thought he had no need to voice his intention and in doing so had granted the stranger some kind of oversight, it seemed to him not to matter. The stranger, however, took it that way, for he said, “Don’t you want to stay here?” “I don’t want to stay here, nor will I be addressed by you until you introduce yourself,” said K. “It was well intended,” the stranger said and now opened the door voluntarily. The next room, into which K. slowly entered as he wanted, appeared on first glance almost exactly the same as it had the evening before. It was Frau Grubach’s living room, and perhaps, in this filled with furniture, curtains, porcelain, and photographs, there was today a bit more space than usual, but this could not be seen immediately, not to mention the main change, which was the presence of a man who sat by the open window reading a book and who now looked up. “You should have stayed in your room! Didn’t Franz tell you?” “Yes, what do you want?” said K., looking from the newcomer to the one called Franz, who had stopped in the doorway, and then back again. Through the open window, one again saw the old woman, who had approached the opposite window with a truly greyhound-like curiosity to see everything. “I want to speak to Frau Grubach—” said K., made a move as if to free himself from the two men, who were far away from him, and wanted to continue. “No,” said the man at the window, threw the book onto a little table, and stood up. “You must not leave, you are under arrest.” “It seems so,” said K. “And why is that?” he then asked. “We are not here to tell you that. Go back to your room and wait. The process has already been initiated, and you will learn everything in due time. If I were to exceed my instructions by addressing you so kindly, I would be doing so for the sake of Franz, and he is, of course, himself kind to you against all regulations. If you continue to have as much luck with your guards as you did with your assignation, then you can be optimistic. But you must sit down,” said the stranger, and K. noticed that there were no seats in the room except the chair by the window. “You will soon see how true all of this is,” said Franz and then walked toward K. together with the other man. Especially the latter was much taller and patted K. on the shoulder several times. Both examined K.’s nightgown and said that he would now have to wear a much worse shirt, but they would keep his nightgown and, if his case were to be resolved in his favor, would return it to him. “It is better if you hand the clothes over to us,” they said, “because the depot is often rife with crooks, and furthermore, they sell all the items after a certain time, regardless of whether the process has concluded. And how long do such processes last, especially nowadays! You would finally receive the proceeds from the depot, but these proceeds would of course be pitiful, since the amount received does not depend on the offer but on the bribe, and the proceeds decrease with each change of hands and with each passing year.” K. paid little attention to this speech, for he did not highly value the right to dispose of his belongings, but what mattered to him was to gain clarity about his situation. However, in front of these people, he could not even think, for the belly of the second guard—surely only a guard—often hit him in a friendly manner. When K. looked up, he saw a face that did not match the thick body—dry, bony, with a strong, sideways-tilted nose—which communicated with the other guard. Who were these people? What did they talk about? Which authority did they belong to? K. lived in a state where the law prevailed, where peace reigned, and where all laws were upheld. Who dared to storm into his apartment? He always tended to minimize everything and not take the worst scenario seriously until it actually happened, not to worry about the future, even when everything threatened him. But here, he felt that was not the right approach. He could still see this as a joke, as a rather rough joke that his colleagues at the bank had played on him for an unknown reason, perhaps because today was his thirtieth birthday. Of course, it was possible, and perhaps he only had to laugh in the face of the guards, and they would join in, or they were just doormen from the corner of the street, who looked alike—nevertheless, since the first sight of the guard Franz, he was determined not to let go of any advantage he might have over these men. In the possibility that they would later say he had not understood the joke, K. saw a minor danger, but he remembered, without this being his usual way of learning from experience, some minor cases where he, unlike his friends, had behaved thoughtlessly and recklessly, without the slightest awareness of the possible consequences, and had been punished for it. It would not happen again, at least not this time; if it was a comedy, he wanted to be part of it.

But the man ignored the question and only said, “You rang?” “Anna should bring me my breakfast,” said K., trying to deduce, through silence and careful observation, the identity of the man. But this man did not stay long, turning to the door, which he opened a bit to tell someone standing just behind it, “He wants Anna to bring his breakfast.” A small laugh followed from the adjoining room; it was not clear whether there were several people involved. Even though the stranger might have known nothing more than what he already did, he now said to K. in a tone of official announcement, “That is impossible.” “That would be new,” said K., and he jumped out of bed, hastily pulling on his trousers. “I want to see the people in that adjoining room and how Frau Grubach will explain this to me.” Though he realized he did not have to voice this aloud, he felt that he was acknowledging a kind of surveillance by the stranger, but it seemed to matter little to him now. The stranger, however, took his words as an indication, for he said, “Don’t you want to stay here?” “I want neither to stay here nor to be addressed by you until you introduce yourself,” said K. “It was well meant,” said the stranger and now opened the door of his own accord. In the adjoining room, into which K. slowly entered as he had wanted, it appeared on first glance almost exactly as it had the night before. It was Frau Grubach’s living room, perhaps with a bit more space today, given the crowded furniture, curtains, porcelain, and photographs, but the main difference was a man who sat at an open window with a book, looking up from his reading. “You should have stayed in your room! Didn’t Franz tell you?” “Yes, what do you want?” said K., looking at his new acquaintance and then back at the one called Franz, who was standing in the doorway. Through the open window, he could see the old woman, who, with truly senile curiosity, had moved to the window opposite to continue watching. “I want to see Frau Grubach—” said K., and he made a movement as if to break free from the two men, who were still some distance away, and wanted to continue. “No,” said the man at the window, putting down his book and standing up. “You cannot leave; you are arrested.” “It looks that way,” said K. “And why?” he then asked. “We are not supposed to tell you that.” “Go back to your room and wait,” said the man. “The process is now initiated, and you will be told everything in due time. I am overstepping my duties by addressing you so kindly. But I hope no one else will hear it, especially not Franz, who is already being friendly with you against all regulations. If you continue to have as much luck in choosing your guards as you did with them, you can be hopeful. ” K. wanted to sit down, but he noticed that there was no seating available in the entire room except the chair by the window. “You will see that it is all true,” said Franz and moved toward K. with the other man. The latter, who stood well above K., patted him on the shoulder several times. Both men examined K.’s nightgown and said that he would now have to wear a much worse shirt, that they would keep his nightgown and his other clothes and return them if the case was favorable. “It is better to hand these things to us,” they said, “since the depot often gets counterfeit goods and everything is sold there after a certain period, without considering whether the process is finished. And how long do such processes last, especially nowadays? You would finally get the proceeds from the depot, but such proceeds are generally already small, because when goods are sold, it is not the highest bid that matters, but the highest bribe, and such proceeds decrease over time, when they are passed from hand to hand and from year to year.” K. barely paid attention to these words. He did not much care about the rights he might have over his possessions; what mattered to him was clarity about his situation. But with these men present, he could not think at all; the bloated belly of one of the guards – he could only be a guard – kept jostling him in a friendly manner, and when K. looked up, he saw a strangely fitting, dry, knotty face with a strongly turned nose, engaged in some sort of discussion with the other guard. Who were these people? What were they talking about? Which authority did they belong to? K. lived in a legal state; everywhere, peace prevailed, all laws were respected. Who would dare to attack him in his home? He tended to take things lightly, to believe the worst only when it was already upon him, to make no plans for the future, even when everything seemed to threaten him. Here, however, it seemed to him that this was not the case. One could view the entire matter as a practical joke, a rather coarse one, perhaps even in celebration of his thirtieth birthday. His bank colleagues could have done it for an unknown reason. Of course, it was possible that K. could simply laugh at the guards, and they would laugh with him, or that they were just a couple of guards from the corner of the street, who looked similar. Nevertheless, K. was now determined, ever since the first sight of the guard named Franz, to not give up the smallest advantage he might have over these men. He saw very little danger in being called stupid, but he recalled – without this being his usual practice of learning from experience – a few minor cases where he, unlike his friends, had deliberately acted carelessly and without considering the consequences, only to be punished for it. He would not let it happen again, at least not this time; if it were a farce, he wanted to participate.

Someone must have slandered Josef K., for without having done anything evil, he was arrested one morning. The cook of Frau Grubach, his landlady, who brought him his breakfast every morning at eight o'clock, did not come this time. This had never happened before. K. waited for a while, observing the old woman who lived opposite him and who, with an unusually keen interest, watched him. Feeling both puzzled and hungry, he rang the bell. Immediately, there was a knock, and a man, whom he had never seen in this apartment, entered. He was slender yet well-built, dressed in an adhering black outfit similar to a travel suit, with various folds, pockets, latches, buttons, and a belt, which, despite its complexity, seemed particularly practical in some ways. "Who are you?" K. asked, sitting up in bed halfway. But the man ignored the question, as if his appearance had to be accepted, and merely said, "You rang?" "Anna is to bring me my breakfast," said K., trying to deduce, through silent observation and thought, who the man was. However, the stranger did not remain long under K.'s gaze and turned towards the door, opening it slightly to say to someone who, apparently, was standing right behind it, "He wants Anna to bring him his breakfast." A small laugh followed in the neighboring room, its source uncertain; it was unclear whether several people were involved. Although the stranger, through this, might not have learned anything he did not already know, he now said to K. in a reporting tone, "It's impossible." "That's new," said K., leaped out of bed, and quickly put on his trousers. "I want to see who's in the neighboring room and how Frau Grubach will account for this disturbance to me." Although it occurred to him that he need not have said that and that, by doing so, he had somewhat acknowledged the stranger's right to supervise him, he now thought it unimportant. Nonetheless, the stranger interpreted it this way and said, "Why don't you stay here?" "I will neither stay here nor be addressed by you until you introduce yourself to me," said K. "It was well-intentioned," the stranger said and now opened the door voluntarily. In the neighboring room, which K. entered more slowly than he wanted, it appeared at first glance almost exactly as it had the previous evening. It was the sitting room of Frau Grubach; perhaps there was a bit more space in this room, filled with furniture, blankets, porcelain, and photographs, than usual, but one could not tell at once, let alone when the main change was the presence of a man sitting at an open window and reading a book, which he now laid down and stood up. "You should have stayed in your room!" said, "Haven't Franz told you so?" "Yes, what do you want?" said K., looking from the new acquaintance to the man called Franz, who had stopped in the doorway, and then back again. Through the open window, one again saw the old woman, who, with truly elderly curiosity, had stepped towards the window facing him, to continue watching everything. "I want to see Frau Grubach," said K., made a gesture as if he wanted to free himself from the two men, who were far from him, and wanted to continue on his way. "No," said the man at the window, threw the book on a little table, and stood up. "You cannot leave; you are arrested." "It seems so," said K. "Why?" he then asked. "We are not instructed to tell you. Go back to your room and wait. The procedure has been initiated, and you will learn everything in due time. I go beyond my duty by speaking to you so friendly. But I hope that nobody else, especially not Franz, will hear it, and he, at least, is friendly to you, like the rest of your guards. If you continue to have as much luck with your guards as you did with their assignment, you may be confident. "K. wanted to sit down, but now he noticed that there was no place to sit in the whole room, except for the chair at the window. "You will see how true all this is," said Franz and, at the same time, the other man approached him. The latter, especially, towered over K. and often patted him on the shoulder. Both examined K.'s nightshirt and said that he would now have to wear a much worse shirt and that they would keep his clothes, and if the case turned out well, they would return them to him. "It is better if you hand them over to us as deposited goods," they said, "because in the depot, there are often fakes, and all goods are sold after a certain period, regardless of whether the proceedings are still in process. And how long do such cases take, especially recently! You would, of course, get the proceeds from the depot, but such proceeds are, in any case, low, for the sale is not decided by the bid but by the size of the bribe, and, according to experience, such proceeds decrease from hand to hand and from year to year." K. paid little attention to their words; the right to dispose of his clothes, which he might still have, was not highly valued by him. What mattered more to him was to gain some clarity about his situation; but in front of these people, he could not think. Again and again, the second guard’s—surely a guard—protruding belly hit him in a friendly manner. When he looked up, he saw a face that did not fit this thick body: dry, bony, with a strong, obliquely positioned nose, which communicated with the other guard. What kind of people were these? What did they talk about? Which department did they belong to? K. lived in a state governed by the rule of law; everywhere, peace prevailed, and all laws stood firm. Who would dare to attack him in his home? He always tended to take things lightly, to believe the worst only at the worst moment, to make no preparations for the future, even when everything threatened to. Here, however, it seemed to him that this was not right. One could view the entire situation as a joke, a crude one, that his colleagues in the bank had pulled on him for unknown reasons, perhaps because it was his thirtieth birthday; it was certainly possible, he might just laugh in the face of the guards, and they would join in. Perhaps they were simply street urchins who looked alike. – Nevertheless, he was determined, ever since his first glimpse of the guard Franz, to not give up the slightest advantage he might have over these people. He saw in the allegation that he had not understood the joke only a very small danger. However, recalling—without his usual inclination to learn from experience—some insignificant cases in which he, unlike his friends, had acted without the slightest awareness of the possible consequences and had been punished, he did not want this to happen again, at least not this time; it was a comedy, and he wanted to play it.

At the beginning of the trial, Rakhat’ko’s mother fell ill. Dunya and Razumikhin judged it best to take her out of Petersburg for the duration of the trial. Razumikhin chose a town on the railway, close to Petersburg, so that he could regularly follow the proceedings and also meet as often as possible with Avdotya Romanovna. Pulkheriya Alexandrovna’s illness was somehow strange and nervous, accompanied by something akin to madness, if not complete, at least in part. When Dunya returned from her last meeting with her brother, she found her mother very ill, burning up with fever and delirious. That same evening, she had arranged with Razumikhin how to respond to her mother’s questions about her brother and even invented a story together for her mother, about Rakhat’ko’s departure for some distant place, to the border of Russia, on a personal commission, which would finally give him money and fame. But it struck them that Pulkheriya Alexandrovna neither then nor later inquired about any of this. On the contrary, she herself had a whole story about her son’s sudden departure; she wept as she related how he had come to say goodbye to her; she alluded to the fact that only she knew many important and mysterious details and that Rodia had many very powerful enemies, so that he even had to hide. As for his future career, it seemed to her certain and brilliant, once certain hostile circumstances were overcome; she assured Razumikhin that her son would become a man of state one day, which she saw as a proof of his talent and his brilliant literary gift. She read this article endlessly, sometimes even aloud, never parted from it, but still hardly ever asked where Rodia was, despite the fact that she was obviously avoided when it came to talking about this—this already aroused her suspicion. They eventually began to fear this strange silence of Pulkheriya Alexandrovna concerning certain points. For example, she did not complain that she was receiving no letters from him, even though, when living in her little town, she had only lived in hope and expectation of receiving a letter from her beloved Rodia as soon as possible. This last detail was too inexplicable and greatly disturbed Dunya; she began to think that perhaps her mother sensed some terrible fate in store for her son and feared to inquire so as not to discover something even more terrible. In any case, Dunya clearly saw that Pulkheriya Alexandrovna was not in her right mind.

They interrogated the Poles as well. Though they had tried to sleep in their room, they did not manage to do so all night, and as soon as the authorities arrived, they quickly got dressed and tidied up, well aware that they would certainly be summoned. They appeared with dignity, albeit not entirely without fear. The main one, the little squire, turned out to be a retired official of the twelfth class who had served as a veterinarian in Siberia, and his surname was Pan Muszowski. Pan Wrublevsky, on the other hand, was an unlicensed dentist, or as they would say in Russian, a dentist. Upon entering the room, both of them immediately, despite the questions of Nikolai Parfenovich, started to respond to Michael Makarovitch, standing aside, whom they, due to their ignorance, considered the main official and the one in charge here, calling him “pan pulkovnik” with every word. It was only after several repetitions and Michael Makarovitch’s own instructions that they realized they should only address their answers to Nikolai Parfenovich. It turned out that they could speak Russian quite correctly, except for the pronunciation of certain words. Pan Muszowski began to speak warmly and proudly about his relations with Grushenka, past and present, so that Mitya lost his temper at once and shouted that he would not allow a “scoundrel” to talk like that in his presence. Pan Muszowski immediately noticed the word “scoundrel” and asked to have it entered in the protocol. Mitya erupted in rage.

Radiant with the eight mountain nodes,  
In the four seasons' lake, my heart freely roves.  
Gathering firewood, I find the joy of immortals,  
Fishing, free from the mundane.  
Outside the door, wild flowers scent the air,  
On the boat, green water waves softly.  
Peaceful in my bones, I need not speak of the Three High Officials' posts,  
My mind at ease, more potent than a ten-li city's fortifications.  
A ten-li city high to guard military orders,  
The Three High Officials' illustrious positions to hear imperial commands.  
Pleasing in mountains, pleasing in waters—how rare,  
I thank heaven, thank earth, thank the gods.  

Hearing these words, the two men exchanged verses,  
At the parting, they bowed.  
Zhang Shao said, "Brother Li, travel with care!  
Be cautious of tigers on the mountain.  
Should anything go wrong,  
Tomorrow's street will have fewer old friends!"  
Li Dì, hearing this, was greatly angered,  
"You lazy fellow! Even in life and death, good friends would help each other,  
Why curse me?  
If I meet a tiger and am harmed,  
You will surely meet the waves and be swept away by the river!"  
Zhang Shao said, "I will never be swept away by the river."  
Li Dì said, "There are unforeseen changes in heaven,  
And sudden misfortunes in life.  
How can you guarantee that nothing will happen?"  
Zhang Shao said, "Brother Li, you may say this,  
But you have yet to grasp the full extent of your own affairs;  
Unlike my livelihood, which is predictable,  
I will surely not meet such misfortune."  
Li Dì said, "Your occupation on the water is extremely perilous,  
Always shrouded in uncertainty,  
What measure of certainty do you have?"  
Zhang Shao said, "You do not understand.  
In Chang'an City, at the West Gate Street,  
There is a diviner who sells fortunes.  
I send him a golden carp every day,  
And he secretly transmits the divination to me,  
Depending on the direction, I always succeed.  
Today, I went to buy fortune,  
He advised me to set a net at the eastern bend of the Jinghe River,  
And cast a line on the western bank.  
I will surely return with a full catch of fish and shrimp.  
Tomorrow, I will sell the catch in town,  
Buy wine, and meet old brother again."  
The two parted ways from there.

In the Eight-Trigram Mountain, seek no fixed rhythm;  
In the Four-Season Lake, let passions freely arise.  
Felling wood brings joy to the immortal's heart;  
Fishing reveals no trace of worldly art.  
Flowers outside the gate scent the air;  
Green waters on the boat, waves gently laid.  
Saying I am not third in rank,  
Steadiness ranks beyond ten li of wall.  
Ten li of wall guards the commander's will,  
Third rank hears the lord's call.  
Who truly loves the mountain, the stream,  
More so than I, than I, than I?  
Pray to the heavens, the earth, the deities,  
For their grace.  

He said to Li, "Brother Li, take care on the road!  
Be wary of tigers when climbing the mountain.  
Should fate deal you a blow,  
Tomorrow's city square will have fewer acquaintances!"  

Li, hearing this, was greatly angered.  
"You scoundrel, unworthy!  
A true friend can share life and death,  
How can you curse me?  
Should a tiger meet and harm you,  
You'll drown in the river!"  

"Never will I drown," replied Zhang.  
"Alas, the sky is unpredictable,  
Man's fortunes wax and wane.  
How can you guarantee me safety?"  

"Li Brother, though you speak thus,  
You have not considered.  
My livelihood has some assurance;  
It will surely not meet such a fate."  

"Your water-related trade is exceedingly perilous,  
Secret and obscure, what assurance is there?"  

"You do not know.  
In the west gate street of Chang'an,  
Lives a man who divines.  
I give him a golden carp each day,  
He secretly teaches me by hand.  
Following his directions,  
I hit every mark.  
Today, he advised me to set a net east of the泾River Bend,  
And cast a line on the west bank,  
To ensure a bountiful return.  
Tomorrow, I'll sell in the city,  
Buy wine, and catch up with you."  

Thus, the two parted ways.

I put six rubles in the letter, sealed it, and asked Apollo to deliver it to Simonov. Learning that the letter contained money, Apollo became more polite and agreed to go. By evening, I went for a walk. My head still ached and spun from the previous day. But as evening fell and the twilight thickened, my impressions grew muddled, and with them, my thoughts. Something refused to die within me, deep in my heart and conscience, and showed itself as a burning sadness. I pushed my way through the busiest, industrial streets, along Meshchansky and Sadovaya, past Yusupov's garden. I especially loved walking through these streets at twilight, precisely when the crowds of various workers and craftsmen, their faces troubled to the point of anger, were dispersing to their homes after a day’s work. I found it pleasing that this ragtag bustle, this brazen ordinariness, suited me. This time, however, all this bustling on the streets irritated me even more. I could not calm myself down, could not find an end to it. Something kept rising, persistently, with pain, and would not be silenced. Disconcerted, I returned home. As if a crime lay on my conscience.

I enclosed six rubles in the letter, sealed it, and asked Apollo to deliver it to Simonov. Hearing that the letter contained money, Apollo became more respectful and agreed to go. By evening, I went out for a walk. My head still ached from the day before and spun. But as the evening advanced and twilight deepened, my impressions and thoughts grew more jumbled. Something inside me, in the depths of my heart and conscience, refused to die and expressed itself in a fiery longing. I pushed through the crowds more on the busiest, industrial streets, along Meshchansky, and along Sadova, by Yusupov’s garden. I always loved to stroll through these streets in twilight, especially when the crowd thickened with all sorts of passersby, workers, artisans, with their fretful faces, dispersing to their homes after their daily earnings. I liked precisely this petty hustle, this crude ordinariness. This time, the whole street jostle irritated me even more. I couldn’t calm myself or find an end to it. Something rose, continuously, with pain, and wouldn’t settle. Worn out, I returned home. As if a crime lay on my conscience.

Well, all right, my angel, all right! You think it's not a calamity that I haven't fetched the money. Well, all right, I'm calm, I'm happy for you! Even glad that you, my old man, won't be leaving and will stay on this apartment. Indeed, if we talk about everything, my heart was brimful of joy when I saw that you wrote about me so well in your little letter and gave my feelings due praise. I'm not saying this out of pride, but because I see how much you love me, when you worry about my heart. Well, all right; what else should we talk about my heart now! The heart is heart itself; but, my dear, you're scolding me so I'm not timid. Yes, my angel, perhaps I'll even say myself that timidity isn't needed; but, my dear, decide for yourself what boots I'll be wearing to work tomorrow! That's what it is, my dear; but such thoughts can destroy a person completely. The main thing, my dear, is that I don't worry for myself, I suffer not for myself; it makes no difference to me, whether I walk in a freezing cold without a coat or without boots, I'll endure it all, it means nothing to me. I'm a simple, little man, but what will people say? What will my enemies, these spiteful tongues, say when I go out without a coat? For people, you have to walk in a coat, and perhaps even in boots. My dear, my little darling, boots are needed for the sake of preserving honor and a good name; but in patched boots, both are lost, believe me, my dear, believe me with my years of experience; listen to me, my old man who knows the world and people, not to some chatterboxes or meddlers.

So a shout from the adjoining room startled him so much that he bit his teeth into the glass. "The overseer is calling you!" they said. It was only the shouting that scared him, this short, broken, military shouting, which he would not have expected from guard Franz. The command itself was very welcome. "Finally!" he cried back, blocked the wardrobe, and immediately rushed into the adjoining room. There the two guards were pushing him back, as if it were the obvious thing to do, back into his room. "What do you think you're doing?" they cried. "Do you want to go before the overseer in your shirt? He'll beat both you and us!" "Leave me to the devil!" K., who was already pushed back to his clothes closet, shouted. "If they attack me in bed, you can't expect to find me dressed up for a formal occasion." "It's no good," said the guards, who, whenever K. shouted, became quite calm, almost melancholy, and thereby confused or brought him to his senses. "Insulting ceremonies!" he muttered, but already held a coat from the chair in his hands, as if presenting it to the guards' judgment. They shook their heads. "It must be a black coat," they said. K. threw the coat to the ground and said – he himself did not know what he meant by it –: "It's not the main hearing, though." The guards smiled but stuck to their words: "It must be a black coat." "If by that I hasten things, that's fine with me," said K., opened his wardrobe himself, searched through the many clothes for a long time, picked out his finest black coat, a jacket that had almost caused a stir among acquaintances because of its waistline, and now also pulled out another shirt and began to dress himself carefully. Secretly, he believed that he had thereby brought about a speeding up of the whole affair by making the guards forget to force him to take a bath. He watched them to see if they might suddenly remember, but of course that did not occur to them. Against this, Willem did not forget to send Franz with the message that K. was dressing to the overseer.

Here, Ippolit Kirillovich elaborately painted the picture of the tragic passion of the accused for Grushenka. He began with the moment when the accused went to the "young woman" to "beat her," as he put it in his own words. Ippolit Kirillovich explained that instead of beating, he remained at her feet — that was the beginning of his love. At the same time, the old man, the accused's father, also cast a glance at the same young woman — a remarkable and fateful coincidence, for both hearts were suddenly kindled at the same moment, although both had met her before, and had known her. Both hearts were kindled by the most unrestrained, the most Karamazov-like passion. This is where the young woman herself admits: "I — I laughed at both of them," she said. Yes, she suddenly felt like laughing at both of them; before, it hadn’t occurred to her, but suddenly, the idea had entered her head, and ended with her being prostrated before both of them. The old man, who worshipped money as a god, immediately prepared three thousand rubles just for her to visit his dwelling, but soon he was so infatuated that he would consider it a blessing to lay his name and all his fortune at her feet just to gain her as his lawful wife. This is amply attested to. As for the accused, the tragedy of his situation was plain for all to see. But such was "the game" of the young woman. The unfortunate young man was not even given the slightest hope by the seductress; genuine hope was only given to him at the very last moment, when he, kneeling before his tormentor, stretched out hands drenched in the blood of his father and rival: it was in this position that he was arrested. "Send me to the mines with him, I made him so miserable, I am more to blame than anyone else!" the woman cried out herself in sincere repentance at the moment of his arrest. A gifted young man, taking it upon himself to describe the case — the same Mr. Rakitin, whom I mentioned earlier — succinctly characterizes the character of this heroine: "Early disappointment, early deception and fall, betrayal by the seducer-fiancé who abandoned her, then poverty, a curse on a honest family, and, finally, the patronage of one rich old man, whom she still considers her benefactor. Perhaps, in that young heart, there was still much good that was hidden too early. A calculating, capital-accumulating character was formed. A sneering and vengeful attitude to society was formed." After this characterization, it is clear that she could laugh at both of them solely for the sake of the game, a malicious game. And so, in the month of despairing love, moral falls, betrayal of her fiancée, and the appropriation of money entrusted to his honor — the accused almost reached the point of madness, even frenzy, from unceasing jealousy, and to whom else but his father! And the main point is that the mad old man lured and enticed the object of his son's passion with the same three thousand rubles, which the son considered his ancestral heritage, bequeathed by his mother, in which he reproached his father. Yes, I agree, it was hard to endure! Even delusions could have appeared. It was not about the money, but about the fact that with such revolting cynicism, her happiness was being shattered by these very same coins!

'Send me to the penal colony with him, I have driven him to this extent, I am more to blame than anyone else!' – exclaimed this woman herself, in genuine repentance, at the moment of his arrest. A talented young man who took upon himself to describe this case – the same Mr. Rakitin, whom I already mentioned – defines the character of this heroine in a few concise and telling phrases: 'Early disillusion, early deception and fall, betrayal by the seducer-fiancé who abandoned her, then poverty, a curse on a decent family, and finally, the protection of one rich old man, whom she still considers her benefactor today. In a young heart, perhaps containing much goodness, there still lurked resentment from an early age. The character formed was calculating, accumulating capital. A sense of mockery and revenge against society.' After this characterization, it is clear that she could laugh at them both solely for the sake of a game, a malicious game. And now, in this month of hopeless love, moral degradation, betrayal of her fiancée, appropriation of someone else's money entrusted to his honor, the accused, to add to all this, nearly reaches madness, frenzy, from incessant jealousy – and to whose father, indeed!
