The old man, who venerated money as his god, immediately prepared three thousand rubles just for her to visit him, but soon he was brought to the point where he would consider it a blessing to lay his name and all his possessions at her feet just to win her consent to become his lawful wife. This is corroborated by solid testimony. As for the defendant, the tragedy of his situation was obvious, it was right before our eyes. But this was ‘the game’ of the young woman. The unfortunate young man was not even given the slightest hope by the temptress; true hope was only given to him at the very last moment, when, kneeling before his tormentor, he was already stretching out his hands stained with the blood of his father and rival: it was in this very position that he was arrested. ‘Send me to the gulag with him, I led him to it, I am more to blame than anyone else! ’ this woman cried in genuine repentance at the moment of his arrest. The talented young man who took on the task of describing the real case – the same Rakitin whom I mentioned earlier – characterizes this heroine in a few telling phrases: ‘Early disillusionment, early deceit and fall, betrayal by her seducer-fiancé, who then abandoned her, followed by poverty, a curse on a respectable family, and, finally, the patronage of a wealthy old man, whom she still considers her benefactor. Perhaps there was still a good deal of goodness in that young heart, though it had been soured too early. A calculating, capital-accumulating character formed. A mocking and vindictive attitude toward society took root.’ After this characterization, it becomes clear that she could only laugh at both for the sake of the game, for a malicious game. And so, in this month of despairing love, moral degradation, betrayal of her fiancée, and embezzlement of entrusted money, the defendant almost reached the brink of madness, of frenzy, from unceasing jealousy, and to whom, to his father! And the main thing, the mad old man enticed and captivated the object of his son’s passion with those very three thousand rubles that the son considered his birthright, his mother’s inheritance, in which he reproached his father. Yes, I agree, it was hard to bear! Here madness could even set in. The issue was not about the money, but about the fact that this happiness was being destroyed with such revolting cynicism by those same three thousand rubles!

– Why "A I"? Why the "A"? It's so womanly. – I grabbed her violets irritably (I admit it). – There you have your violet. Smell it: nice, isn't it? So be logical for once. Violets do smell nice: that's true. But surely you can't say that smell, the concept of smell, is good or bad? You can't, right? There is the smell of a violet and the stench of a wild hyacinth: both are scents. There were spies in the ancient state, and there are spies among us… yes, there are. I don't fear words. But it's clear: there, a spy is a wild hyacinth, here, a spy is a violet. Yes, a violet, yes!

"Why 'I' – why the 'A'? That's distinctly womanly." – I snatched her violets crossly (admitting it now). "Well, there's your violet. Smell it: nice, isn't it? So have the decency to use some logic. Violets smell nice: that's true. But can you honestly say that a smell, the very concept of 'smell,' is good or bad? No, you can't, can you? There are violets and there are stinking wolfsbane; both are smells. Spies existed in the ancient state and we have spies too… yes, we do. I'm not afraid of words. But it's clear: a spy there is wolfsbane, a spy here is a violet. Yes, a violet, yes!"

Indeed, God blessed me with family and community! My little girl, you are so lovely! What are you talking about, those four undershirts I sent you? You needed them, I learned from Fyodor. But, my dear, it gives me a special kind of happiness to please you; that is my delight, leave me be, my dear; don't disturb me or contradict me. I've never experienced anything like this, my dear. The child laughed and said, "Master, to be frank, the upper character is proper to offer incense to, but the lower one cannot bear our offerings. It was our master who cajoled it out of flattery." Tang僧 asked, "What is cajoled?" The child replied, "The Three Pure Ones are my master’s friends, the Four Sovereigns are his old acquaintances, the Nine Stars are his juniors, and the Jade Emperor is his inferior guest." Upon hearing this, the Monkey King burst into laughter, falling down. Pig asked, "Brother, why are you laughing?" The Monkey King said, "Only saying I’m good at playing tricks, and lo and behold, this child is skilled at blowing smoke!" Tang僧 asked, "Where is your master?" The child replied, "My master, the Primordial Beginning Heavenly尊, has been summoned to the Palace of Incomparable Nirvana in the Upper Clear Sky to listen to the teachings of the Primordial Dao, and is not at home." At about that time, as Surikov had “frozen” the child, around mid-March, I suddenly felt much better for no particular reason, and this state lasted for about two weeks. I began going out more and more often in the twilight. I liked March twilight, when it started to get cold and the gas lamps began to light; sometimes I walked a long way. Once, in Six-lidded Alley, I was overtaken in the darkness by some “noble,” whom I did not see clearly. He was carrying something wrapped in paper and was wearing an ungainly and grotesque overcoat, too light for the season. When he passed a lamp, ten paces in front of me, I noticed that something had fallen out of his pocket. I hurried to pick it up, for there was still time, since a man in a long caftan had already jumped up, but he did not argue when he saw the object in my hands; he glanced in my direction and slipped past. The object was large, a saffron-colored leather wallet stuffed with papers, but for some reason, from the first glance, I knew that it contained nothing but money. The man who had lost it was already forty paces ahead of me and soon vanished from sight among the crowd. I ran after him and shouted at him, but since I could only shout “Hey!” there was no point in trying to call out anything else. Suddenly, he slipped to the left, into the gate of a house. When I rushed into the gate, where it was very dark, no one was there. The house was enormous, one of those monstrosities built by conmen for tiny apartments; in some such houses, there could be up to a hundred numbers. When I passed through the gate, it seemed to me that someone was moving in the right, rear corner of the vast courtyard, though in the darkness I could hardly make it out. When I reached the corner, I saw the entrance to a staircase; the staircase was narrow, extremely dirty, and completely unlit, but I could hear a man climbing the stairs above me, and I started up the stairs, hoping that he would be stopped somewhere and I would catch up with him. It worked out that way. The stairs were short and numerous; I was choking as I climbed. A door was opened and closed again on the fifth floor, and I guessed this was so even three flights below. This matter was then put to rest.

While they were feasting merrily, someone came to report, "Sire, there are two One-Horned Demon Kings outside the door who wish to see you." The Monkey King said, "Bid them come in." The Demon King straightened his clothes and ran into the cave, then prostrated himself and prostrated again before the beautiful Monkey King. The Monkey King asked, "What brings you here?" The Demon King replied, "I have long heard that Your Highness seeks talent, but I had no way to present myself. The Monkey King was overjoyed and exclaimed several times, "Good! Good! Good!" This matter was left for another time.

He walked the entire length of the long and narrow corridor, searching everywhere, and was about to shout out when he suddenly noticed a strange object in a dark corner, between an old wardrobe and the door. It seemed like some living thing. He bent down with a candle and saw a child – a little girl, about five years old, in a sodden dress like a mops, shivering and sobbing. She seemed not to be frightened by Svidrigailov, but stared at him with her large black eyes, dazed and wide with confusion, and occasionally hiccupped like children who had stopped crying after a long while, even finding some comfort, though every now and then a fresh hiccup would escape her. The girl’s face was pale and gaunt; she was stiff with cold, but “How did she get here? She must have hidden and slept outside all night.” He started to ask her questions. Suddenly, the girl came to life and chattered quickly in her childish language. There was something about her mother and that she would be “whacked,” and that she had broken “chashchik” (the cup), which she called “lyazbil’ya” (had broken). The girl kept on talking, and from all these stories, one could vaguely understand that this was a child whom the mother, likely some chronically drunk kitchen-maid from the same inn, had beaten and terrorized; that the girl had broken her mother’s cup and was so frightened she had run away that very evening; that she had spent the night somewhere outside, under the rain, and finally made her way here, hiding behind the wardrobe, where she had sat all night shivering and crying, cold, in the dark, and terrified that now she would be severely punished for it. He picked her up, went to his room, put her on the bed, and began undressing her. Her worn-out little shoes, on her bare feet, were soaked as if she had lain in a puddle all night. After undressing her, he put her to bed, covered her, and wrapped her completely in a blanket. She fell asleep immediately. After that, he brooded gloomily again.

An hour passed before she appeared. They had arrived and were not; they had no haste, yet were driven by impatience. The young Polonians, patriotically dressed and perhaps inspired by the military horn signals wafting from the vicinity of the public gardens over the water, had come on deck, and, enthused by the Asti, they cheered the Bersaglieri exercising over there. But it was repulsive to behold the state in which their false camaraderie with the youth had left the stiffened elders. Their aged minds could not keep pace with the wine as the young and ready troops had, they were despondently drunk. With a dazed look, a cigarette between trembling fingers, he swayed there, struggling to maintain his balance, pushed forward and backward by the wine. Had he taken a single step, he would have fallen, and so he did not move, yet he showed a miserable gaiety, grabbing anyone who approached him by the button, slurring, blinking, giggling, raising his bejeweled, wrinkled forefinger for a silly jest, and lolling about with his tongue tasting the corners of his mouth in a disgusting and ambiguous manner. Aschbach watched him with darkened brows, and again a feeling of drowsiness came over him, as though the world showed a slight, though not to be hindered, inclination to degenerate into the bizarre and grotesque; a feeling against which the circumstances held him, since the thudding activity of the machinery was beginning anew, and the ship resumed its nearly interrupted journey through the Canal of San Marco. So he saw again the most astonishing landing place, that brilliant composition of fantastical architecture, which the Republic presented to the awed eyes of approaching seafarers: the light splendor of the palace and the Sighing Bridge, the columns with lions and saints at the shore, the prancing flank of the Temple of Romance, the view to the Torso and the huge clock, and as he gazed, he reflected that, on land, arriving at the train station in Venice was like entering a palace through a back door, and that one could approach the most unlikely of cities, as now he was, only by sea, high over the water, the most improbable of towns.

The pain did not lessen; but Ivan Ilyich made an effort to convince himself that he was feeling better. And he could fool himself as long as nothing troubled him. But as soon as there was some unpleasantness with his wife, a setback at work, or a losing hand at cards, he now felt the full force of his illness. He would endure these setbacks, hoping that things would improve, that he would triumph, that he would win the big pot. Now, however, every misfortune undermined him and plunged him into despair. He told himself that he had just begun to recover, and that the medicine had already started to take effect, and then this cursed misfortune or inconvenience… And he lashed out at the misfortune or at people who gave him a hard time, and felt how this anger was killing him; but he could not help himself. It seemed to him that he should clearly understand that this anger at circumstances and people was worsening his illness and that he should therefore ignore unpleasant coincidences; but he did the opposite: he told himself that he needed calm and kept a watchful eye on anything that disturbed it, and at the slightest disturbance he would become irritable. His situation was further worsened by the fact that he read medical books and consulted doctors. The deterioration was so gradual that he could deceive himself by comparing one day to the next—there was little difference. But when he consulted doctors, it seemed to him that things were getting worse very quickly. And yet, despite this, he constantly consulted doctors.

I am a Buddhist monk sent by the Emperor of Great Tang on a mission to the Western Heavens to worship Buddha and seek scriptures. Just now, when I arrived here, I met with some fierce wolves, tigers, serpents, and insects surrounding me, preventing me from advancing further. Suddenly, I saw Governor Hou arrive, and all the beasts fled, saving my life. Thank you! Thank you! Governor Hou said, "I live here and rely on hunting wolves and tigers for a living, and trapping serpents and insects for sustenance. Therefore, all the beasts fear me and flee when I pass. You are from Great Tang, so we are fellow countrymen. This place still falls within the territory of Great Tang, and I am a commoner of Great Tang. We both drink from the same land and air, truly fellow countrymen. Do not fear, follow me, and stay at my dwelling to rest your horse. Tomorrow, I will send you on your way." Upon hearing this, Tripitaka was filled with joy and thanked Governor Hou, then led the horse and followed.

If, however, the wickedness of people angers and saddens you so uncontrollably that it even stirs a desire for revenge against the wicked, then fear that feeling most of all; immediately go seek sufferings as if you yourself were guilty of that wickedness. If you had shone, you would have illuminated the path for others, and the one who did the wickedness might not have committed it in your light. Do not fear the noble or the mighty, but be wise and always noble. Know the measure, know the times, learn this. Stay in solitude and pray. Love to fall to the earth and kiss it. Kiss the earth ceaselessly, insatiably, love all, love all, seek the exaltation and madness of this. Drench the earth with the tears of your joy and love these tears of yours. Be not ashamed of this madness, treasure it, for it is a divine gift, a great one, given not to many but to the chosen few.

If, however, the wickedness of people upsets you with outrage and an unquenchable grief, even to the point of wanting to take vengeance on the wicked, fear this feeling most of all; at once go and seek out punishments for yourself as if you were guilty of this wickedness committed by people. Accept these punishments and endure them, and your heart will be comforted, and you will understand that you too are guilty, for you could have been a sinless one shining upon them, yet you did not. If you had been shining, you would have illuminated for others the way, and the one who committed the wickedness might not have committed it in your light. Even if you had been shining, but saw that people were not saved even in your light, be firm and do not doubt the power of divine light; believe that if they were not saved now, they will be saved later. And if they are not saved later, their children will be saved, for your light will not perish even if you yourself have died. The righteous departs, but his light remains. And they are saved, and they are always saved after death. People do not accept their prophets and persecute them, but people love their martyrs and honor those whom they tortured. You, on the other hand, work for the whole, and do for the coming. Seek no rewards, for you already have great reward on this earth: the spiritual joy that only the righteous attain. Fear neither the noble nor the strong, but be wise and always magnanimous. Know the measure, know the times, and learn this. Stay in seclusion and pray. Love to prostrate yourself on the ground and kiss it. Kiss the earth constantly, unsatiably, love all, and love all unsatiably, seeking this ecstasy. Drench the earth with the tears of your joy, and love these tears of yours. Do not be ashamed of this ecstasy, treasure it, for it is a divine gift, great and granted to few, chosen ones.

Peter Ivanovich sighed even more deeply and sorrowfully, and Praskovya Fedorovna gratefully squeezed his hand. Entering her pink brocade-lacquered living room with its somber lamp, they sat at the table: she on the sofa, and Peter Ivanovich on the lopsided, sagging ottoman whose springs were pressing into his seat. Praskovya Fedorovna wanted to warn him to sit on another chair, but she decided this warning was inappropriate for her position and desisted. Sitting on this ottoman, Peter Ivanovich remembered how Ivan Ilich had arranged this living room and consulted with him about this very pink with green-leafed brocade. As she sat on the sofa and passed by the table (the entire living room was filled with trinkets and furniture), the widow snagged the black lace of her black mantilla on the table’s carving. Peter Ivanovich stood to untangle it, and the now liberated ottoman began to squirm and push against him. The widow started to untangle her lace herself, and Peter Ivanovich sat back down, pressing down on the rebellious ottoman. But the widow did not manage to untangle it all, and Peter Ivanovich stood up again, and the ottoman rebelled once more, even creaking. When this ended, she pulled out a clean muslin handkerchief and began to cry. The episode with the lace and the battle with the ottoman had cooled Peter Ivanovich’s ardor, and he sat frowning. The awkward situation was broken by Sokolov, Ivan Ilich’s butler, with a report that the plot of land on the cemetery, as Praskovya Fedorovna had designated, would cost two hundred rubles. She stopped crying and, with a martyr’s look at Peter Ivanovich, said in French that it was very difficult for her. Peter Ivanovich made a silent sign expressing his unquestionable conviction that it could not be any other way.

Three years had passed when the Patriarch again took his seat and spoke to the assembly. He spoke of public cases and parables, and argued over outer appearances. Then he asked, "Where is Sun Wukong?" Sun Wukong stepped forward and kneeled: "Master, here I am." The Patriarch said, "What spiritual practice have you been undertaking of late?" Wukong replied, "I have been steadily cultivating my wisdom and strengthening my foundations." The Patriarch said, "You have reached a good understanding of the wisdom and strengthened your foundations. But you must guard against the 'three disasters and calamities'." Upon hearing this, Wukong pondered for a long time and said, "Master, your words are incorrect. I have often heard of those with high virtue living long, water and fire being no threat, with no diseases at all, yet how can there be these three disasters and calamities?" The Patriarch said, "This is an extraordinary path: it seizes the secrets of heaven and earth, intrudes on the mysteries of the moon and sun; after the elixir is complete, even ghosts and gods cannot tolerate you. Although you will look youthful and live longer, in five hundred years, you will be struck by lightning. You must see your true nature and clear your heart, and seek to avoid it. If you can avoid it, you will live as long as heaven and earth; if not, you will die. In five hundred years, there will be a fire disaster that will burn you. This fire is not heavenly or mundane; it is called Yin Fire. It begins from your涌泉穴 (yǒngquán xué, the spot on the soles of the feet), and passes through the brain palace, turning your organs to ash and your limbs to dust, making all your austerities in vain. In another five hundred years, there will be a wind disaster that will blow you apart. This wind is not the east, west, south, or north winds, nor the warm or cold breeze; it is called the赑 (bì) wind. It enters through the top of your head, passes through your organs, and through your nine orifices, causing you to disintegrate. Therefore, you must avoid it." Hearing this, Wukong was terrified and knelt and bowed, saying, "If the Master has pity and teaches me how to avoid the three disasters and calamities, I will not forget your kindness." The Patriarch said, "This is not difficult, but you are different from others, so I cannot teach you." Wukong said, "I am as round as heaven and as solid as earth at my feet, with the same nine orifices, four limbs, and five organs and six腑 (fǔ, internal organs). Why am I different?" The Patriarch said, "Although you look like a human, you have fewer cheeks than humans." Indeed, the monkey had a flat and concave face, a pointed nose, and no cheeks. Wukong reached out to touch it and said, "Master, you are not clever! Although I have fewer cheeks, I have a white bag, which can be used to offset this." The Patriarch said, "Alright, what do you wish to learn? There is the Heavenly罡 (gāng) number, thirty-six transformations, and there is the Earthly煞 (shà) number, seventy-two transformations." Wukong said, "I am willing to try. Teach me the Earthly transformations." The Patriarch said, "Since this is so, come up here and I will teach you the technique." He whispered in Wukong's ear, unknown to him what wonderful methods were imparted. This monkey, once one hole was opened, all others opened as well, and learned the technique and began to practice, mastering the seventy-two transformations.

Yet three years had passed, and the Master ascended the throne once more to discourse with his disciples. He spoke of anecdotes and metaphors, and discussed external forms and coverings. Suddenly, he asked, "Where is Monkey?" Monkey stepped forward and knelt, saying, "Disciple is here." The Master said, "What practice have you been engaged in recently?" Monkey replied, "Disciple has recently attained a profound understanding of the Dharmic nature and a gradually firm foundation." The Master said, "Since you have mastered the Dharmic nature and achieved a solid foundation, you are imbued with divine essence. However, you must guard against the 'Three Disasters and their Malevolence'."

Hearing this, Monkey pondered for a long time and said, "Master, your words are mistaken. I have often heard that those of high Dao and noble virtue live as long as heaven, with both water and fire pacified, and no sickness. How then are there these three disasters and their malevolence?" The Master said, "This is an extraordinary path: it seizes the essence of heaven and earth, invades the secrets of the sun and moon; once the elixir is perfected, even gods and demons cannot bear it. Though you may retain your youth and gain longevity, after five hundred years, a thunderstorm will descend upon you. You must be alert to guard your true nature and clear heart in advance. If you can dodge it, your lifespan will be as long as heaven and earth; if not, you will die. After another five hundred years, a fire will descend. This fire is neither a heavenly nor a mundane fire, but a 'yin fire'. It starts from your涌泉穴 and burns up to your泥垣宫, reducing your five organs to ashes and your four limbs to dust. All the austerities of a thousand years will be in vain. After yet another five hundred years, a wind disaster will descend. This wind is neither the southeast, northwest, gentle, or fierce wind; it is not the wind of flowers, trees, or bamboo. It is called the '赑 wind'. It enters from your crown and passes through your six腑, through the dantian, and out through your nine orifices, dissolving your bones and flesh, causing your body to disintegrate. Therefore, you must avoid it." Monkey heard this and shuddered, then prostrated himself and said, "Sage Master, show mercy and impart the methods for avoiding the three disasters. I will never forget your kindness." The Master said, "This is not difficult, but you are different from others, hence I cannot teach you." Monkey said, "I, too, have a round head and face the sky with my feet planted on the ground, with nine orifices and four limbs, and five organs and six腑. How am I different from others?" The Master said, "Although you resemble a human, you lack a chin compared to others." Originally, that monkey had a lopsided face, an凹脸, and a sharp mouth. Monkey stretched his hand out and laughed, saying, "Master, you have failed to see! Although I lack a chin, I have this white pouch, which can compensate for it." The Master said, "Very well. What do you wish to learn? There is the Heaven's Righteous Path with thirty-six transformations, and the Earth's Malefic Path with seventy-two transformations." Monkey said, "I wish to learn the Earth's Malefic Path with seventy-two transformations." The Master said, "Since that is so, step forward, and I will teach you the秘诀." So he whispered in Monkey's ear, and it is unknown what he said. This monkey also mastered one when he understood one, and at that moment, after learning the秘诀, he practiced and refined himself, and mastered the seventy-two transformations.

Yet three years had passed before the Master reoccupied his throne to expound the Dharma to the assembly. He spoke of cases and similes, and argued about outer forms and coverings. Suddenly, he asked, "Where is Sun Wukong?" Wukong stepped forward and kneeled, "Student is here." The Master said, "What practice have you been engaged in of late?" Wukong replied, "Student has recently thoroughly understood the dharma and fortified the root." The Master said, "Since you understand the dharma, have mastered the root, and have infused your body with spirit, you must beware the three calamities." Upon hearing this, Wukong pondered for a long moment and said, "Master, your words are erroneous. I have often heard that one who is highly revered and possesses great virtue lives as long as heaven, that the body is tempered by fire and water, and that no illness arises, so how can there be three calamities?" The Master said, "This is an extraordinary path: it appropriates the creation of heaven and earth, invades the mysteries of the sun and moon; after the elixir is completed, ghosts and gods will find it intolerable. Although it preserves your youth and extends your life, in five hundred years, heaven will send a thunderstorm to strike you; you must purify your mind and preserve your essence to avoid it. If you avoid it, your lifespan will be as long as heaven’s; if you do not, your life will end here. In five hundred years, a fire from the heavens will descend; this is not heavenly fire, nor is it ordinary fire; it is called Yin Fire. It rises from the涌泉穴 and burns through the mud wall palace, reducing the five viscera to ashes and the four limbs to dust, nullifying a thousand years of ascetic practices. In another five hundred years, a wind calamity will descend. This wind is not from the east, west, south, or north; it is not warm spring or cold winter wind; nor is it the wind of flowers, trees, bamboo, or reeds; it is called Buifeng. It enters through the囱门, passes through the six bowels, and reaches the dantian, piercing through the nine orifices, causing the flesh and bones to disintegrate, and the body to dissolve. Therefore, you must avoid it. "Wukong heard this and was chilled to the bone, bowing and prostrating, saying, "Master, show pity and impart the method for avoiding the three calamities; I will not forget your kindness." The Master said, "There is no difficulty, but you are different from others, so the method cannot be imparted." Wukong said, "I have a round head and a sky above me; I have a flat foot and the earth below me, with the same nine openings and four limbs, and five viscera and six bowels; how can I be different?" The Master said, "You may resemble a human, but you lack cheeks compared to others." Originally, the monkey had a one-eyed face, an inwardly concave face, and a sharp mouth. Wukong reached out and touched it, smiling and saying, "Master, your calculations are flawed! Although I lack cheeks, I have this white pouch, which can be offset." The Master said, "Very well. What practice do you wish to learn? There is one of the Heavenly罡, which has 36 transformations, and one of the Earthly煞, which has 72 transformations." Wukong said, "Student is willing to learn the more difficult. Let me learn the 72 transformations of the Earthly煞." The Master said, "Since that is so, step forward, and I will impart the secret." Thus, the Master whispered into his ear, and Wukong, being quick of mind, mastered the secret at once. He then practiced and cultivated, and mastered all 72 transformations.

Yet three years had passed when the Master once again ascended the throne to discourse with his disciples. The topic was cases and comparisons, and he discussed external appearances and surface traits. He suddenly asked, "Where is Monkey?" Monkey advanced and knelt, saying, "Disciple is here." The Master said, "What have you been practicing of late?" Monkey replied, "Disciple has lately comprehended the Dharma and solidified the root." The Master said, "Since you have mastered the Dharma and secured the root, your spirit has been nourished; yet, you must guard against the 'Three Calamities of Disaster.'" Upon hearing this, Monkey pondered for a long while and said, "Master, your words are wrong. I often hear of those who are virtuous and of high conduct, living as long as the heavens, with water and fire quelled, free from illness. How can there be calamities and disasters?" The Master said, "This is an extraordinary path: it steals the essence of Heaven and Earth, invades the secrets of the sun and moon; once the elixir is formed, the spirits and gods cannot endure it. Although your youth and vitality have increased, after five hundred years, a heavenly thunderstorm will descend on you. You must attain a clear mind and prepare to avoid it. If you can avoid it, you will live as long as the heavens; if not, you will die. After five hundred years, a fiery calamity will descend upon you. This fire is neither celestial nor mundane; it is called 'yin fire.' It starts from your涌泉穴 (yǒngquán xué, the涌泉穴is a point on the sole of the foot in traditional Chinese medicine) and ascends to your mud wall palace (泥垣宫, the mind or heart), burning your five viscera to ash and rotting your four limbs, making a thousand years of arduous practice all in vain. After another five hundred years, a wind calamity will descend upon you. This wind is neither east, west, south, nor north; it is not the warm or cold wind, nor the wind of flowers and leaves or bamboo and trees; it is called 'gǔ wind.' It enters from your forehead and blows through your six organs, passes through your dantian (丹田, the center of energy in the body), and exits through your nine orifices, causing your flesh and bones to wither, disintegrating your body. Therefore, you must avoid it." Monkey heard this and was suddenly startled, bowing and kneeling, saying, "O Grandmaster, if you pity me, please impart the methods to avoid the three calamities; I will not forget your kindness." The Master said, "This is not difficult, but you are different from others, so I cannot teach you." Monkey said, "I too have a head that is round and touches the sky, feet that are square and rest on the earth, nine openings and four limbs like everyone else, and five viscera and six organs. How am I different?" The Master said, "Although you resemble a human, you lack cheeks." It turned out that the monkey had a crooked face and a sharp nose. Monkey touched himself and smiled, saying, "Master, you are without thought! I may lack cheeks, but I have this bag, which may be used as compensation." The Master said, "Very well, which skill do you wish to learn? There is a heavenly technique with 36 changes, and a earthly technique with 72 changes." Monkey said, "Disciple is willing to learn the earthly technique." The Master said, "Since that is so, come forward, and I will impart the incantation to you." Thus, he whispered in Monkey's ear, not disclosing the words. This monkey, with one hole open, all holes opened. At that moment, he learned the incantation and practiced and refined himself, mastering the seventy-two changes.

Three years had passed before the Master ascended the dais again to expound the Dharma to his disciples. He spoke of koans and parables, and then addressed the outer appearances and appearances within. Suddenly, he asked, "Where is Monkey?" Monkey approached and kneeled, replying, "Your disciple is here." The Master said, "What have you been practicing of late?" Monkey replied, "Lately, I have found my Dharmic nature well-versed, and my foundation gradually strengthened." The Master said, "Since you have mastered the Dharmic nature and established the foundation, you are imbued with divine essence, but you must guard against the 'Three Disasters and Their Hazards.'" Upon hearing this, Monkey pondered for a long while and said, "Master's words are mistaken. I have often heard of sages who are highly revered and long-lived, who are in harmony with heaven and earth, and whose diseases are quelled by the unification of water and fire. How can there be the Three Disasters and Their Hazards?" The Master said, "This is a way beyond the ordinary: it seizes the essence of heaven and earth, breaches the secrets of the sun and moon; when the elixir is formed, it becomes indiscernible to the gods. Although it can preserve your youth and prolong your life, after five hundred years, you will be struck by heavenly lightning, and you must cultivate your wisdom and clarity of mind to avoid it. If you can avoid it, your lifespan will be as long as that of heaven and earth; if you cannot, your life will end. Five hundred years later, a fire disaster will fall upon you. This fire is neither heavenly nor mundane; it is called Yin Fire. It begins from the涌泉穴, burns through the mud walls, consuming the five viscera to ash and rotting the four limbs, rendering all your thousand-year spiritual practices an illusion. Another five hundred years later, a wind disaster will strike. This wind is not the east, west, south, or north wind, nor is it a gentle or fierce wind, nor the wind of flowers, grass, pines, or bamboos; it is called the赑wind. It enters through the fontanelle, passing through the six bowels, the Dantian, and the nine apertures, causing the flesh and bones to disintegrate, and the body to disintegrate. Thus, you must avoid all three disasters. "Monkey heard this and felt a chill, prostrating and beseeching, "O Grandmaster, have mercy and teach me the method to avoid the three disasters, so that I do not forget your kindness." The Master said, "This is not difficult; you are different from others, so the method cannot be taught to you." Monkey replied, "I have a round head and a heaven above, and my feet are flat, touching the earth. I have the same nine orifices, four limbs, and five viscera and six bowels as others. How am I different?" The Master said, "Although you resemble a person, you lack a chin." Indeed, the monkey had a face that was lopsided and an angular, pointed mouth. Monkey reached out and touched himself, smiling, "Master is without foresight! Though I lack a chin, I have this additional pouch, which may compensate for it." The Master said, "Well, then, what would you like to learn? There is the Heaven's Heavenly Count, which has 36 transformations, and the Earth's Fiendish Count, which has 72 transformations." Monkey said, "I am willing to learn, so let me learn the 72 transformations of the Earth's Fiendish Count." The Master said, "Since that is the case, come forward and I will teach you the oral formula." He then whispered into Monkey's ear, not revealing the content of his teachings. This Monkey was quick to learn; upon receiving the oral formula, he practiced and cultivated on his own, mastering all 72 transformations.

And so, let the celebration cease. When I send envoys to fetch the Great Vehicle Sutra, come and make your offerings with sincerity and re-establish your merit. All the officials did as they were instructed. At that time, within the temple, the emperor asked, "Who is willing to carry out my旨意and journey to the Western Heavens to pay homage to the Buddha and seek the scriptures?" Before he could finish, a monk stepped forward and prostrated himself before the emperor. He said, "Your Majesty, though I am unworthy, I am willing to undertake this difficult task and seek the true scriptures for you, to pray for the stability of your kingdom." Emperor Taizong was overjoyed and took the monk’s hand, pulling him up. He said, "If you can be as loyal and virtuous as this, I am willing to be your brother and support you in your journey." Tripitaka humbly thanked him. Emperor Taizong was indeed very virtuous, and so he went to the Buddha before the temple and prostrated himself four times, calling Tripitaka his "Imperial younger brother, holy monk." Tripitaka could not thank him enough. He said, "Your Majesty, what virtue or talent of mine could warrant such kindness from heaven? On this journey, I will risk my life to reach the Western Heavens. If I do not reach the Western Heavens and cannot obtain the true scriptures, I will not return, no matter what." He then lit incense before the Buddha and made a vow. The emperor was very pleased and immediately ordered the royal return, awaiting a favorable date to issue a decree and depart. Thereafter, he returned to the palace.

And so the festival was put to rest, awaiting the envoy to retrieve the Great Vehicle Sutra. All the officials followed without exception. At that time, in the temple, the emperor asked: "Who is willing to convey my旨意to the Western Heavens to seek the sutras and pay homage to the Buddha?" Before the question was finished, a priest stepped forward and knelt before the emperor, saying: "Your humble servant is not talented, but is willing to serve like a dog or a horse to seek the true scriptures for Your Majesty, praying for the permanence of our kingdom." The Tang emperor was delighted and, advancing, helped the priest to his feet, saying: "If you are truly loyal and wise, fear no distant journey or perilous terrains. I am willing to be brothers with you." Tripitaka bowed gratefully. The Tang emperor was indeed most virtuous, and went to the Buddha before the temple, and with Tripitaka, he performed four bows, calling him "Imperial younger brother, Sage Monk." Tripitaka expressed boundless gratitude, saying: "Your Majesty, what virtue or merit of mine could I have that you would bestow such grace upon me? I shall give my life to this mission, reaching the Western Heavens. If I do not reach the West Heavens and bring back the true scriptures, I shall not return, risking eternal damnation." He then lit incense at the Buddha's altar, making this his vow. The Tang emperor was very pleased and immediately ordered the return, waiting for a propitious day to issue the edict for departure, after which the emperor returned, dismissing everyone.

And let this assembly end. I shall send men to fetch the Great Vehicle Sutras. Then we can offer our sincere hearts and redouble our good deeds. All the officials agreed without reservation. At that time, the emperor asked in the temple, "Who will undertake the mission to go to the Western Heavens to pay homage to the Buddha and obtain the scriptures?" Drinking and singing alone, dancing with the wild wind,  
Long songs and long sighs, in the midst of turmoil unconfined.  
Calling brothers, urging shipmates to join,  
Leading friends, gathering countrymen with joy.  
Playing drinking games, throwing cups,  
Unfolding tiles, writing characters, passing time at ease.  
Cooking crabs and boiling crabs every day,  
Frying ducks and roasting chickens every day.  
A foolish wife brewing tea with carefree delight,  
A mountain wife cooking rice with tranquil glee.  
In the morning, wielding a stick to stir light waves,  
At sunrise, carrying firewood over the great ford.  
After rain, wearing a raincoat to catch live carp,  
Before the wind, playing with an ax to fell withered pines.  
Hiding in seclusion, pretending to be foolish and simple,  
Hiding one's name, pretending to be deaf and mute.

"A Russian heart can even discern a great man in its very enemy, its own homeland!" That is, to be honest, I don’t remember if I actually said it that way... I was just a child... but the meaning was certainly that! Napoleon was moved. He pondered for a moment and said to his retinue, "I love the pride of this child! But if all the Russians think like this child...?"—he left the sentence unfinished as he entered the palace. I immediately intervened with the retinue and ran after him. By now, the retinue was parting for me and looking at me as a favorite. But all of that was fleeting... I only remember that, entering the first hall, the Emperor suddenly stopped before a portrait of Empress Catherine and stared at it in thought for a long time before finally saying, "This was a great woman!" and walked past it. Two days later, everyone in the palace and the Kremlin already knew me and called me "le petit boyard." I only went home at night. At home, they nearly went mad with excitement. Two days after that, the chamber page to Napoleon, Baron de Bazanкур, who could not endure the campaign, died. Napoleon remembered me; they took me, brought me in without explaining the reason, dressed me in the deceased page’s uniform—a twelve-year-old boy—and when they brought me to the Emperor in uniform and he nodded his head, they informed me that I had been honored and promoted to chamber page to his Majesty. I was delighted. I really felt a warm sympathy for him, and for a long time... well, admit it, the splendid uniform for a child meant a lot... I went around in a dark green frock coat with long and narrow tails; gold buttons, crimson cuffs with gold embroidery, a high standing collar embroidered in gold, embroidery on the tails; tight white tights, a silk waistcoat, silk stockings, gaiters with buckles... and during the Emperor’s horseback rides, and if I was part of his retinue, tall boots. Although the position was not glamorous and ominous misfortunes were already anticipated, the etiquette was observed as much as possible, and even more meticulously the more ominous the misfortunes seemed to be.

But they had not even climbed the stairs when the painter above had flung open the door and invited K. to enter with a deep bow. The girls, on the other hand, he refused entry to; he did not want any of them to come in, despite their pleading and their attempts to force their way in, whether with or against his will. Only the hunchback managed to slip through under his outstretched arm, but the painter chased after her, grabbed her by the skirts, spun her around, and then sent her back to the other girls at the door, whom he had not dared to cross even while he was away. K. did not know how to judge the whole affair, for everything seemed to be happening in friendly accord. The girls at the door stretched their necks one after another towards the ceiling, called out to the painter various jesting words that K. could not understand, and the painter laughed while the hunchback flew in his hands. Then he closed the door, bowed to K. again, held out his hand, and, introducing himself, said, "Kunstmaler Titorelli." K. gestured towards the door behind which the girls were whispering and said, "They seem to be very popular in the house." "Oh, those silly things!" said the painter and struggled in vain to button his nightshirt at the neck. He was, after all, barefoot and only clad in a broad, yellowish linen pantaloons tied with a belt whose long end swung freely back and forth. "These silly things are a real nuisance to me," he continued, while he let go of the last button of his nightshirt, which had just popped off, fetched a chair, and forced K. to sit down. "I once painted one of them—she is not here today— and ever since, they have been hounding me. If I am here, they only come in when I permit it, but if I leave, then at least one of them is always there. They have made themselves keys to my door and lend them to one another. One can hardly imagine how annoying this is. For example, I come home in the evening with a lady whom I am to paint, open the door with my key, and find the hunchback there at the little table, as she paints her lips red with the brush, while her small children, whom she has to look after, run around and dirty the room in all corners. Or, as happened to me yesterday evening, I come home late at night—excuse me for my state and the disorder in the room—I come home late at night and want to go to bed, when something bites me on the leg, I look under the bed, and pull out such a thing again. I do not know why they are crowding around me like this, or that I do not try to entice them to me, as you surely have noticed. Naturally, they also disturb my work. K. did not know how to assess the whole situation; it seemed to be taking place in friendly accord. The girls outside stretched their necks in turn, one after the other, and called out various jesting words to the painter that K. did not understand, and the painter laughed, while the hunchback nearly flew in his grasp. Then he closed the door, bowed again to K., held out his hand, and, introducing himself, said: "Kunstmaler Titorelli." K. pointed to the door behind which the girls were whispering and said: "It seems they are very popular in the house." "Ah, those silly faces!" said the painter and, in vain, tried to fasten his nightshirt at the neck. He was barefoot and wore only a broad, yellow linen trousers tied with a strap whose long end swung freely back and forth. "Those silly faces are a real burden to me," he continued, letting go of the nightshirt, whose last button had just popped off, as he fetched a chair and forced K. to sit down. "I once painted one of them—she’s not even there today—and ever since, they’ve all been bothering me. If I’m here, they only come in if I allow them, but if I’m gone, then at least one is always there. They have made a key to my door, which they circulate among themselves. It’s hard to imagine how annoying this is. For example, when I come home in the evening with a lady who I’m supposed to paint, and open the door with my key, I might find the hunchback at the little table, coloring her lips red with a brush, while her small children, whom she’s supposed to look after, are running around and dirtying the room in all corners. Or, as happened to me yesterday evening, I come home late at night—please excuse me and the condition of my room—, and want to go to bed, when something pricks me in the leg. I look under the bed and pull out some such thing. I don’t know why they’re all pushing themselves on me, and I don’t think I’m inviting them. Of course, I’m also distracted in my work. If this studio hadn’t been provided to me for free, I would have moved out long ago." Just then, a faint and timid voice behind the door called out: "Titorelli, may we come in already?" "No," the painter answered. "Not even me?" the voice asked again. "Not even me," said the painter, went to the door, and locked it.

"I once painted one of them—she’s not here today, either—and since then they have all been following me. When I am here, they only come in if I allow them, but as soon as I leave, then there is always at least one there. They have had a key to my door made, which they lend to one another. One can hardly imagine how bothersome this is. For example, I come home late at night with a lady I am to paint, open the door with my key, and find the Hunchback there at the little table, painting her lips red with a brush while her small children, whom she is supposed to supervise, are running about and soiling the room in all corners. Or, as happened to me yesterday evening, I come home late at night and want to go to bed, when something pricks my leg, I look under the bed, and pull out something like that. I do not know why they press themselves on me so; you have probably noticed that I do not seek to entice them. Naturally, I am also disturbed in my work by this. If this studio were not provided to me free of charge, I would have moved out long ago." Just then, a little voice behind the door called out in a soft, anxious tone: "Titorelli, can we come in now?" The next morning, they prepared the horses, packed their belongings, and set out. The monks saw them off before returning. The pilgrim led the way, and it was early spring. What was seen was: 
The grass soft under the horse's hooves, the willows swaying with golden threads of new dew. Peaches and apricots in full bloom vied for beauty, while creeper vines added vitality along the paths. On the warm sand dune, pairs of mandarin ducks slept, and in the mountain stream, butterflies flitted about, perfumed by the flowers. Thus, through half the season of spring, the travelers wondered how many years it would take to fulfill their journey and attain true scriptures. For five or seven days they walked on the wild roads, until one evening, they saw a village in the distance. Tripitaka said, "Wukong, see that farmhouse over there. Let's stay the night there and continue our journey tomorrow." Wukong said, "Let me check first to see if it's safe, then we'll decide." The monk pulled the reins, while Wukong squinted to see. The scene was truly: 
Thick bamboo fences and multiple straw-roofed houses. High wild trees welcomed the guests, while a meandering stream reflected the courtyard. Along the roadside, the willows were lush, and flowers bloomed sweetly. At dusk, the sun sank, and birds chirped in the mountains and valleys; smoke rose from the chimneys, and herds of cattle and sheep followed the winding paths. Then, plump chickens and pigs lay in corners, while drunk neighbors sang their songs. Wukong said, "Master, come on. It’s a fine village. We can stay here." The monk urged the horse, and they arrived at the village entrance. They saw a young man with a headscarf, blue coat, umbrella, and backpack, with rolled-up trousers and three-ear straw sandals, bustling on the street. Wukong grabbed him by the hand. "Where are you going? I need to know the place." The man struggled and shouted, "I can't even send a message, as no one’s at home!" Wukong said with a smile, "Don’t be angry, it will be beneficial to you and me. Just tell me the name of the place; it won’t hurt." The man struggled but couldn’t escape, and angrily said, "Misery! I can’t bear the oppression, and this bald man makes it worse!" Wukong said, "If you have the strength, break my hand and you can leave." The man tried to twist his hand free but couldn’t, and in frustration, he dropped his bag and umbrella, lunging at Wukong with his bare hands. Wukong held the baggage with one hand and the man with the other, deftly countering every move. Wukong tightened his grip, and the man grew increasingly agitated. Tripitaka said, "Wukong, someone’s coming. Ask him and let him go." Wukong said, "Master, I must talk to him first; it will be worth it." The man finally said, "This is the border of U-tsang, called Gao Lou Village. Almost half the people are named Gao, hence the name. Let me go." Wukong said, "Your luggage, you’re not a traveler. Tell me where you’re going and what you want. Then I’ll let you go." The man said, "I’m a servant of Old Gao, named Gao Cai. My master’s daughter is twenty, never married, and was abducted by a demon three years ago. The demon has been her husband for three years, and my master’s not happy. One, it discredits the family; two, no relatives visit. He’s been trying to get rid of the demon, but it won’t go, locking her in the back house for half a year now. I got some silver to find a holy man to defeat the demon. I’ve tried many, but they couldn’t. I was just beaten and given more silver to come back. This time I came across you and am mistreated. Please let me go." Wukong said, "This is a good opportunity for you. You don’t need to travel far, and no need for silver. We’re not the useless holy men or weak Taoists; we can fight demons. This is one to cure your ailments and another to improve your sight. Go and tell your master, we’re holy monks from the East, going to the West to seek scriptures, and we can defeat demons." Gao Cai said, "Don’t mislead me. I’m full of anger. If you can’t defeat the demon, I’ll still suffer." Wukong said, "I’ll make sure you’re not misled. Follow me to your doorstep." The man had no choice and led the monks to his house. He said, "Masters, wait on the horse platform. I’ll go in and inform the master." Wukong released his hand and led the monks to wait by the door.

The next morning, he had the horses groomed and packed his belongings before leaving. The monks saw him off, then returned. The pilgrim led the way, the spring thaw just setting in. The view was: the grass cushioned the jade hooves of the horses softly; willows swayed with golden threads of dew in the new blooms. Cherries and peaches bloomed, vying for beauty; creepers wrapped around the paths, vivacious. The sandy embankment warmed with sleeping mandarin ducks; the mountain stream was perfumed by flowers, with butterflies tamed. In this season, from the late autumn to the spring half over, who knew when his journey would be full and he would attain true scriptures? For five or seven days, the disciples walked along the desolate roads. As evening approached, they saw a village in the distance. Tripitaka said, "Wukong, see! There is a farmhouse not far off. Let us seek shelter for the night and continue our journey tomorrow." Wukong said, "Wait a moment while I investigate the place." The monk held back the reins while Wukong stared intently, seeing: dense bamboo fences, thick straw huts. Ancient trees stretched towards the entrance, a winding stream and bridge reflected by the houses. Along the roadside, willows swayed green; in the garden, flowers bloomed, fragrant. As the sun sank, the evening brought birds to the woods; smoke from chimneys rose from narrow lanes, sheep and cattle moved along the paths. They saw fat chickens and pigs sleeping in corners, and a neighbor with a full belly singing as he came from a tavern. Wukong said, "Master, let us go. It is a good family, we can seek shelter." The monk urged the horse, and they arrived at the village entrance. They saw a young man wrapped in a cloth headband, wearing a blue jacket, carrying an umbrella, and a packed bag, with rolled-up trousers and straw sandals on his feet, bustling out the street. Wukong smiled, "My friend, no offense, but you are welcome to my help, and I will help you. Tell me your location, what harm will that do? You might be relieved." The young man could not free himself, frustrated, "Wretched! Wretched! Tired of long hours and unfair treatment, and now this bald one! Sucks his air!" Wukong said, "If you can break my grip, you may go." The young man tried to wriggle but could not, as if bound, and let go the bag and umbrella, grabbing Wukong with his hands like raindrops. Wukong held the baggage with one hand and the young man with the other, no matter how he struggled, he could not seize him. Wukong tightened his grip, agitated like a thunderclap. Tripitaka said, "Wukong, someone is coming! You should ask the person again. Why keep holding him?" Wukong smiled, "Master, I know. If I ask others, I might feel foolish. But him, he is the one." The young man, unable to break free, said, "This place is in the border of the Utsang country, known as Gao Lou庄. Most people are called Gao. You can let me go now." Wukong said, "Your belongings are not of a traveler. Tell me where you want to go, and what you are truly seeking. I will let you go." The young man, with no other choice, told the truth, "I am Gao Cai, a servant of Gao the Elder. He has a daughter, age twenty, who was taken by a demon three years ago. The demon has been her husband all these years. The elder is unhappy, saying it ruins the family and there's no human to visit, wanting to remove the demon. The demon refuses, keeping his daughter in her quarters, not showing her to the family for half a year. My elder gave me silver to find a priest to subdue the demon. I am in a hurry and was misled by you. I am here to complain. You have some skill, I can't break free, so I told the truth. Let me go." Wukong said, "Good luck to you! I have work for you. This is perfect for our goals. You don't need to travel far, don't waste the silver. We are not weak monks or shrimpy priests; we are skilled at subduing demons. This is a chance to help the master. This orderly presentation initially stunned K. However, he spoke just as softly as the painter: "I believe you contradict yourself." "How so?" the painter asked patiently, leaning back with a smile. Yet, he did not back down and said, "Earlier, you mentioned that the court was inaccessible to evidence. Additionally, you previously stated that one could influence the judges personally, but you now deny that genuine acquittals, as you call them, can ever be achieved through personal influence. This is the second contradiction."

"These contradictions are easily resolved," the painter said. "We are talking about two different things: what is stated in the law, and what I personally experienced. You must not confuse them. In the law, as I did not read it, of course, it states that the innocent will be acquitted. However, it does not say that judges can be influenced. But I have experienced the opposite. I have not seen a single genuine acquittal; I know of many instances of influence. It is certainly possible that in all the cases I know, there was no real innocence. But isn't that unlikely? In so many cases, not a single instance of real innocence? When I was a child, I listened carefully to my father’s stories about trials, and even the judges who came to my studio talked about the court; in our circle, we talk about nothing else. As soon as I had the chance to sit in on trials myself, I always took it, and I have heard and followed countless trials at various stages—yet, I must admit, I have not witnessed a single genuine acquittal."

"Then there has never been a genuine acquittal," K. said to himself and his hopes. "This confirms the view I already had of the court. It is also useless from this perspective. A single executioner could replace the entire court." "You must not generalize," the painter said unsatisfied. "I was only speaking about my experiences." These legends do include genuine acquittals, but they cannot be verified. Nonetheless, one must not disregard them; they certainly contain a certain truth and are very beautiful. The painter laughed. "No, you cannot," he said. It was a very rainy and stormy morning when K., full of anger about the day ahead, arrived at the office at seven, just to finish some work before the visitor would take over everything. He was very tired, for he had spent half the night studying Italian grammar to prepare a bit; the window, where he had often sat of late, beckoned more than his desk, but he resisted and sat down to work. Unfortunately, the servant entered just then and reported that the director had sent him to see if the prokurist was already there; if so, he should go to the reception room, for the Italian was already there. "I'll come right away," said K., put a small dictionary in his pocket, took up an album of the city's sights, which he had prepared for the visitor, and went through the deputy director’s office into the director’s room. He was glad to have arrived so early and to be immediately available; it was not something that anyone had seriously expected. The deputy director’s office was still empty, as in the middle of the night; perhaps the servant had also called him to the reception room, but unsuccessfully. When K. entered the reception room, the two men stood up from their deep armchairs. The director smiled friendly, clearly very pleased with K’s arrival; he immediately introduced everyone, the Italian shook K’s hand warmly and called someone a morning lark, smiling. K did not fully understand who he meant; it was, besides, a peculiar word whose meaning K only figured out after a while. K answered with some smooth sentences, which the Italian took with a laugh and, while laughing, frequently ran his nervous hand over his grayish, bushy mustache. This mustache was obviously perfumed; one was almost tempted to approach and smell it. When everyone was seated and a preliminary conversation began, K noticed with great discomfort that he could only understand the Italian in fragments. If he spoke very slowly, he understood almost completely, but these were rare exceptions; mostly, the Italian’s words spilled out, and he shook his head as if in delight over it. In such moments, he regularly got tangled up in some dialect that no longer had anything Italian about it, a dialect that the director not only understood but also spoke, which K could have foreseen, for the Italian was from Southern Italy, where the director had also spent some years. Anyway, K recognized that the possibility of understanding the Italian was mostly taken away from him, for his French was also difficult to understand and the mustache concealed the movements of his lips, which might have helped in understanding. K began to foresee many inconveniences; for now, he gave up trying to understand the Italian – it would have been an unnecessary effort in the presence of the director, who understood him so easily – and instead, he confined himself to watching him with a sulky expression, how he sat deep in the armchair, with a light yet easy posture, how he frequently tugged at his short, sharply cut skirt, and how he once raised his arms and showed something with loose, arm movements, something K could not understand, even though he was leaning forward and did not take his eyes off his hands. Finally, K, who was otherwise unoccupied and only mechanically followed the to-and-fro of the conversation, began to succumb to his earlier fatigue. He caught himself once, to his shock, in the middle of his distraction, about to stand up, turn around, and leave. Finally, the Italian looked at his watch and jumped up. After bidding farewell to the director, he pressed himself close to K, so much so that K had to push his armchair back to be able to move. The director, who clearly recognized K’s distress regarding this Italian, intervened in the conversation with such intelligence and delicacy that it appeared as if he were only giving minor suggestions while, in reality, he summed up in brief all that the Italian, who was tirelessly interrupting himself, said to K. K learned that the Italian still had some business to attend to, that unfortunately he would not have much time, that he did not plan to rush through the city sights, but, rather, in case K agreed, had decided to visit only the cathedral, but thoroughly. He was extremely pleased to be able to conduct this tour with such a learned and pleasant man – meaning K, who was occupied solely with trying not to overhear the Italian and quickly grasping the director’s words – and asked K, if the time suited him, to meet him in the cathedral at ten o'clock, in two hours. He himself hoped to be there by that time. K answered some appropriate things, the Italian shook the director’s and then K’s hand again and left, followed by both, still only half facing them, still not ceasing to talk. K then remained for a while with the director, who looked especially distressed today. He seemed to be trying to atone for something and said, in a confiding manner, standing close to him, that at first he had intended to go with the Italian himself, but then, without giving any further reasons, had decided to send K instead. If he did not understand the Italian in the beginning, he should not be surprised; the understanding would come very quickly. Even if he did not understand much at all, it would not be so bad, for it was not so important for the Italian to be understood. Moreover, K’s Italian was surprisingly good, and he would certainly adapt well to the situation. With that, K was dismissed. The time that was still free for him was spent writing out rare vocabulary he would need for the cathedral tour from the dictionary. It was an extremely tiresome task; the servant brought the post, officials came with various inquiries and stood at the door, not moving until K heard them, the deputy director interrupted K several times, took his dictionary from him, and apparently pored over it aimlessly; when the door opened, groups appeared from the semi-darkness of the anteroom and bowed hesitantly – they wanted to be noticed, but were not sure whether they were seen –, all of this moved around K as if he were its center, while he himself put together the words he needed, then searched for them in the dictionary, then wrote them down, then practiced their pronunciation, and finally tried to memorize them. His once good memory seemed to have deserted him; sometimes he was so furious with the Italian, who caused him this effort, that he buried the dictionary under papers, with the firm intention of not preparing for it, but then he saw that he could not be silent and walk around the artworks in the cathedral with the Italian, and with even greater fury, he took the dictionary out again.

Should I take your last words as a bad omen?" "I know what you are thinking," said K. submissively, "you have probably heard about my trial." "So it is," answered the uncle, nodding slowly, "I have heard about your trial." "From whom?" asked K. "Erna wrote me," said the uncle, "she has no dealings with you, and yet you don't take much interest in her. Nevertheless, she found out. I received the letter today and came here immediately. For no other reason, but it seems a sufficient one. I can read you the part that concerns you from the letter." He took the letter from his wallet. "Here it is." She writes: "Josef, I haven't seen you for a long time. Last week, I went to the bank, but Josef was so busy that I was not admitted; I waited for almost an hour, but had to go home because I had a piano lesson. I would have liked to speak to him, perhaps there will be a chance next time. For my birthday, he sent me a large box of chocolate, it was very thoughtful and considerate. I had forgotten to tell you about it, only now, when you asked, do I remember. You see, chocolate disappears as soon as one realizes one has been given it. But as for Josef, I still want to tell you something. As I said, I was not admitted to him because he was discussing something with a gentleman. After a while of waiting quietly, I asked a servant if the discussion would last long. He said, that probably it would, for he thought that it was about a lawsuit against the gentleman Procurator. I asked whether that lawsuit was really about the Procurator, and he said, no, he was not mistaken, it was a lawsuit, and a serious one, but he knew nothing more. He would like to help the gentleman Procurator, for he is a good and just man, but he did not know how to begin, and he wished that influential gentlemen would take up the matter. This would certainly happen, and it would all end well, for the time being, however, one could conclude from the gentleman Procurator's mood that it was not going well. I did not attach much significance to these words, tried to calm the simple servant, forbade him to talk about it to others, and considered it all to be nonsense. Nevertheless, it would perhaps be a good idea if you, dear father, looked into the matter next time you visit. It will be easy for you to learn more details and, if necessary, to intervene through your influential acquaintances. But if it is not necessary, which is probably the case, then it will at least give your daughter the opportunity to embrace you, which she would be delighted to do." —A good child," said the uncle when he finished reading, and wiped some tears from his eyes. K. nodded; he had completely forgotten about Erna due to the various disruptions of recent times, even her birthday, and the story about the chocolate was obviously invented to shield him from his uncle and aunt. It was very touching, and the theater tickets he would now send her regularly would certainly not be enough to make up for it, but he felt unqualified for visits to the pension and conversations with a sixteen-year-old gymnasium student. "And what do you say now?" asked the uncle, who, having read the letter, had forgotten his eagerness and excitement and seemed to be reading it again. "Yes, Uncle," said K., "it is true." "True?" cried the uncle.

The family was completely absorbed by the violin playing; the guests, who had initially stood close behind their sister’s music stand with their hands in their pockets, so close that they could have seen all the notes, which surely disturbed their sister, soon withdrew to the window, where, under their father’s anxious watch, they remained. It was really clear that they were disappointed in their assumption of hearing beautiful or entertaining violin playing; they had grown tired of the whole performance and only bothered with their politeness to remain in their comfort. Especially the way they all blew smoke out of their nose and mouth suggested great nervousness. And yet, his sister played so beautifully. Her face was tilted to the side, her gaze, probing and sorrowful, followed the music sheets. Gregor crawled a little further forward and kept his head close to the floor, hoping to possibly catch her gaze. Was he a creature that music could affect in such a way? He felt as if the path to the longed-for unknown nourishment were revealed to him. He was determined to get to his sister, pull at her skirt, and thereby indicate that she should come to his room with her violin, because no one appreciated the playing here as much as he wanted to. The Dete had probably waited ten minutes and looked around in all directions to see if the children and the goats had not been anywhere to be seen; when this was not the case, she climbed a little higher, where she could overlook the entire alp down to the bottom, and now from here she looked now to one side and now to the other with signs of great impatience on her face and in her movements. In the meantime, the children approached by a wide detour, for Peter knew many places where there was plenty of good stuff for his goats to nibble on among the bushes and undergrowth; therefore, he made many turns with his herd on the way. At first, the child had struggled to climb, panting heavily and exerting all his strength, wearing his heavy armor. He said nothing, but he did not take his eyes off Peter, who jumped around with his bare feet and light shorts without any trouble, or the goats, which clambered up bushes and stones and steep slopes with their slender, delicate legs. Suddenly, the child sat down on the ground, quickly removed his shoes and stockings, stood up again, took off his red, thick scarf, opened his little dress, quickly took it off, and had another one to knit, for Dete had put his Sunday dress over his everyday clothes out of laziness, so he would not have to wear it. The everyday dress was gone in a flash, and now the child stood in its light underdress, stretching its bare arms up into the air with delight. Then it piled everything into a heap, and now it leaped and scrambled after the goats and beside Peter, as light as any one in the entire group. Peter had not paid attention to what the child was doing when it had fallen behind. As it now came bounding up in its new clothes, he grinned broadly, threw his face into a wide smile, and looked back. And as he saw the heap of clothes lying down there, his face spread even more, and his mouth came almost from one ear to the other; but he said nothing. As the child now felt so free and light, it started talking to Peter, and he also began to speak and had to answer a lot, for the child wanted to know how many goats he had, where he was taking them, and what he was doing wherever he went. Finally, the children, with the goats, reached the hut and met Dete. But as soon as she saw the climbing company approaching, she cried out loudly: "Heidi, what are you doing? How do you look? He dozed on a bench, but his alarm continued even in his dreams. Just before he slept, he remembered that Hippolyt would kill ten people, and he chuckled at the absurdity of the thought. Around him was a beautiful, clear silence, with only the rustling of leaves, which seemed to make the surroundings even quieter and more secluded. He dreamt a great many dreams, all of them troubling, which made him shudder every now and then. Finally, a woman came to him; he knew her, knew her to the point of suffering; he could always name her and point her out— but strangely, her face now seemed to be quite different from what he had always known, and it pained him terribly not to recognize her. In that face was so much repentance and horror that it seemed she was a terrible criminal who had just committed a terrible crime. A tear trembled on her pale cheek; she beckoned to him with her hand and pressed a finger to her lips, as if warning him to follow her silently. His heart stopped; he did not want to recognize her as a criminal for anything in the world; but he felt that something awful, that would taint the rest of his life, was about to happen. It seemed she wanted to show him something, right there in the park. He stood up to follow her, and suddenly a light, fresh laughter sounded beside him; a hand suddenly found its way into his. He grabbed it, clutched it tightly, and woke up. In front of him stood Aglaya, laughing loudly.
