Finally, a woman approached him; he knew her, known to him in pain; he could always name and point to her, but strangely, it seemed that her face was now quite different from the one he had always known, and it ached inside him not to recognize her. There was so much contrition and horror in her face that it seemed she was a terrible criminal who had just committed a terrible crime. A tear trembled on her pale cheek; she beckoned to him with her hand and pressed a finger to her lips, as if warning him to follow her silently. His heart stopped; he would not, under any circumstances, recognize her as a criminal; but he felt that something terrible was about to happen, something that would haunt him for the rest of his life. She, it seemed, wanted to show him something nearby, in the park. He stood to follow her, and then a light, fresh laugh sounded beside him; a hand suddenly appeared in his. He seized it and clung to it, and then he woke up. Aglaya stood before him and laughed loudly.

He dozed on a bench, but his unease continued even in his dreams. Just before falling asleep, he remembered that Hippolyt would kill ten people, and he laughed at the absurdity of the thought. Around him stood a beautiful, clear silence, with only the rustling of leaves, which seemed to make the silence even more profound and solitary. He dreamed many dreams, all of them filled with dread, causing him to startle at intervals. Finally, a woman came to him; he knew her, knew her to the point of suffering; he could always name her and point to her, but strangely, her face now seemed to be quite different from the one he had always known, and it pained him terribly to recognize her as that woman. There was so much repentance and fear in that face that it seemed she must be a terrible criminal who had just committed a terrible crime. A tear trembled on her pale cheek; she beckoned to him with her hand and touched her finger to her lips as if warning him to follow her quietly. His heart stopped; he would never, never want to recognize her as a criminal; but he felt that something horrific would happen, for the rest of his life. It seemed she wanted to show him something, right there, just nearby, in the park. He stood up to follow her, and then, suddenly, a bright, fresh laugh sounded beside him; a hand suddenly found its way into his; he grabbed it, squeezed it tightly, and woke up. In front of him stood and laughed loudly Aglaya.

He dozed on a bench, but his worry continued even in his dreams. Just before he fell asleep, he remembered that Hippolyt would kill ten people, and he laughed at the ridiculousness of the thought. Around him stood a beautiful, clear silence, with only the rustling of leaves, which seemed to make everything around him even quieter and more secluded. He had many dreams, all of them very troubling, and he was startled at intervals. Finally, a woman approached him; he knew her, knew her to the point of suffering; he could always name her and point her out— but strangely, her face now seemed quite different from what he had always known, and it ached within him not to recognize her as that woman. In that face was such sorrow and fear that it seemed she must be a terrible criminal who had just committed a terrible crime. A tear trembled on her pale cheek; she beckoned to him with her hand and pressed her finger to her lips as if warning him to follow her silently. His heart stopped; he did not want to recognize her as a criminal for anything in the world; but he felt that something terrible, for the rest of his life, would soon happen. It seemed to her that she wanted to show him something, right there, nearby, in the park. He rose to follow her, and suddenly there sounded near him a bright, fresh laughter; a hand suddenly found its way into his. He grabbed it tightly and woke up. In front of him stood Aglaya and laughed loudly.

Meanwhile, the Monkey King found the door closed and had to return to the觀音院. The monks from the temple had already buried the old monk and were attending to Tripitaka in the meditation hall. They had just finished their morning meal and were setting up for lunch when the Monkey King descended from the sky. The monks greeted him, led him to the meditation hall, and introduced him to Tripitaka. Tripitaka said, "Wukong, you're here. What about the robe?" Wukong replied, "I have a lead. Fortunately, I didn't wrong these monks; the robe was stolen by a monster from Black Wind Mountain. Old孙 went to track him down and saw the black monster, a white-robed scholar, and an old Taoist sitting on a meadow. The monster confessed that tomorrow was his mother's birthday, and he had invited all sorts of demons to celebrate. Last night, he acquired a brocade robe and planned a grand banquet to celebrate it. It's called the Festival of the Buddha Robe. I ambushed him and struck him with my staff, but the black man fled and the old Taoist disappeared. The white-robed scholar was killed, which turned out to be a white snake demon. I then raced to his cave and challenged him to battle. He admitted that he had taken the robe. We fought for half a day, and it was still even. The monster returned to his cave to eat and closed the stone door, refusing to come out. Old孙 came back to report this to you, and we now know where the robe is. I fear he won't return it." The monks rejoiced, clapping and bowing, and recited, "South-North Amitabha Buddha! Today, we have found its location; we are saved!" Wukong said, "Do not be too elated, for I haven't gotten it yet, and you haven't escorted me out. Wait until I get the robe and safely see off my master before you can truly feel at ease. If anything untoward happens, I will not be trifled with! Have you provided good food and feed for my master?" The monks all responded, "Yes, yes, yes! We have not neglected the master in the slightest."

Then, as the Monkey King could not break through the door, he had no choice but to return to the Purple-Haired Monkey Temple. The monks from the temple had already buried the old monk and were attending to Tang僧 in the main hall. Early morning meal was over, and they had set out for the midday meal. Just as they were adding hot water and changing tea sets, the Monkey King descended from the sky. The monks paid their respects, leading him into the main hall to meet Tang僧. Tang僧 said, "Wukong, you've returned. Where's the robe?" Wukong replied, "I've found out. Fortunately, I didn't wrong these monks. It was actually a monster from Black Wind Mountain who stole it. I went to track him down secretly, and found him sitting with a White Robed Scholar and an old Taoist on the meadow. This was a monster who confessed without being interrogated. He suddenly revealed that the next day was his mother's birthday, and he was inviting all evil spirits to celebrate. Last night, he had obtained a celestial robe and planned to use it as a birthday gift, hosting a grand feast called the Festival of the Celestial Robe. I rushed to him, and after a blow with my staff, the black creature vanished. The Taoist was nowhere to be seen, but the White Robed Scholar was killed—turns out he was a white water snake in disguise. I hurried to his lair, called him out to fight. He admitted that it was him who took the robe and returned with it. We fought for half a day, but there was no clear winner. The monster returned to his lair, closed the stone door, and did not come out to fight. I returned here to inform you, to tell you that the robe's whereabouts are known. There's no need to fear that he won't return it." The monks bowed and thanked him, saying, "Praise be to Amitabha! Now that we have found the robe, we can breathe easy." Wukong said, "Do not be so elated yet. I have not secured it yet, and my master has not left the temple. Wait until the robe is in my hands and I have sent my master out safely before you can truly rest easy. If anything untoward happens, I won't be so easily angered! Have you prepared any good food for my master? Have you provided good fodder for the horse?" The monks responded with one voice, "Of course! Of course! Not a bit has been neglected."

But the Monkey King found the gate closed and had no choice but to return to the Pilgrim Temple. By this time, the monks had buried the old monk and were now in the Zen Hall serving Master Tripitaka. The morning meal had ended, and they had just begun the midday meal when the Monkey King descended from the sky. The monks bowed and led him into the Zen Hall, where they introduced him to Master Tripitaka. Master Tripitaka said, "Wukong, you have returned. What about the robe?" The Monkey King replied, "I have the answer. It is fortunate that I did not wrong these monks. The culprit was the demon of Black Wind Mountain. I followed him to a meadow where he was seated with a white-robed scholar and an old Taoist, and he did not deny his guilt. He claimed it was his mother’s birthday, and he had invited various demons to celebrate. Last night, he obtained a robe and planned to use it as a birthday gift, holding a grand feast called the Robe Celebration. I intercepted him and struck him with my staff, and the demon escaped into the wind. The old Taoist was nowhere to be seen, but I killed the white-robed scholar, who turned out to be a white flower snake demon. I then hurried back to his lair to challenge him to a fight, but he admitted that he had taken the robe. We have been fighting for half a day without either of us gaining an upper hand. The demon retreated to his cave to eat, shutting the stone door and refusing to come out. I have come back to tell you this. We already know the whereabouts of the robe, so there is no need to fear that he will not return it." The monks clapped their hands and bowed, exclaiming, "南无阿弥陀佛！今日寻着下落，我等方有了性命矣！”Wukong said, "Do not be so joyful just yet. I have not secured the robe yet, and the master has not even left the temple. We must wait until I have the robe and can see to it that Master Tripitaka leaves safely before you can enjoy peace and safety. And have you prepared good tea and food for the master? Have you fed the horses well?" The monks all responded, "Yes! Yes! Yes! And there has not been the slightest neglect of your lord."

And so, the Monkey King found the door locked and could not enter, and so he returned to the Pilgrim’s Temple. The monks there had already buried the old monk and were attending to Tang僧 in the main hall. Early morning and noon meals had been served, and as they were adding water to the bowls and replacing them, the Monkey King descended from the sky, and the monks fell to their knees in reverence. He was led into the main hall and greeted Tang僧. Tang僧 said, "Wukong, you have returned. How is the robe?" Wukong replied, "I have the reason for it. I was lucky not to have wronged these monks; it was a black wind demon who stole it. Old孙 went to secretly track him down and found him with a White Robe Scholar and an old Taoist sitting by the grassy slope, discussing. The demon could not resist confessing. He said that the next day would be the day of his mother's enlightenment, when he would invite all demons to celebrate his birthday. Last night, he obtained a brocade robe and wanted to use it as a birthday gift, organizing a grand banquet called the Celebration of the Robe Banquet. Old孙 rushed up and struck him with a staff, and the black demon escaped in a puff of smoke. The old Taoist was nowhere to be seen, but the White Robe Scholar was killed; it was a white-flowered serpent demon. I quickly rushed to the entrance of his lair and challenged him to a battle. He acknowledged that he had taken the robe back. After fighting for half a day, neither side had gained the upper hand. The demon returned to his lair to eat and locked the stone door, fearing to come out and fight. Old孙 returned to report to the master. The robe’s whereabouts have been found, and I am not afraid he will not return it. But you must not be too pleased yet; I have not yet gotten the robe, and Master has not yet left the temple. Wait until I get the robe, send off Master safely, and then it will be your peaceful time; if anything untoward happens, you will not be able to complain to me. Have you prepared good food and drink for Master? Have you fed the horse with good fodder?" The monks replied, "Yes, yes, yes! We have not in the slightest neglected Master’s needs."

But as the Monkey King could not breach the gate, he could do nothing but return to the Woldperception Temple. The monks in the temple had already buried the old monk and were now attending to Tang僧 in the assembly hall. The early meal was over, and a midday meal had just begun, when the Monkey King descended from the air and landed. The monks knelt and welcomed him into the assembly hall, where they met with Tripitaka. Tripitaka said, "Wukong, you're here. How is the robe?" Wukong replied, "I have traced the matter. It was fortunate that these monks were not wronged. It turned out to be a black wind demon who stole it. I hurried back to his cave to demand a fight with him. He had admitted the theft and was now returning with the robe. After a half-day of combat, neither of us had an advantage. "Master, I have brought the saddle and bridle," said the old man. Tripitaka saw them and joyfully accepted them, instructing the Monkey to carry them and put them on the horse to see if they were a good fit. The Monkey climbed up and examined each item, finding them indeed to be excellent. There was a poem to attest to this:
Jade-hued saddle, silver stars gleam,
Golden threads flash on the jeweled seat.
Layered with velvet, cushioned and soft,
Three strands of purple silk secure.
Flower patterns on the reins, splendid and fine,
Fan-shaped trappings, beasts in motion, gilded divine.
Bit crafted from refined iron, polished and bright,
Two hanging tassels, wet with water’s light.

The Monkey was secretly delighted, placing the saddle and bridle on the horse, as if made specifically for it. Tripitaka thanked the old man, who hastily pulled him up, saying, "Pardon, pardon, there is no need for such gratitude." The old man did not linger and invited Tripitaka to mount the horse. The monk stepped out and mounted, the Monkey taking the luggage. The old man, from his sleeve, took out a whip, a stem made of finely braided fragrant vines, with tiger sinew braided into the lash. In a courteous gesture, he offered it, saying, "Holy monk, I have also a bridle, all in one set for you." Tripitaka, from his seat, accepted it, saying, "I am deeply grateful, I am deeply grateful!" Before he could finish his words, the old man was nowhere to be seen. And when Tripitaka looked back at the place of the shrine, it was just an open field. They heard someone speaking from above, "Holy monk, I apologize for the rudeness. I am the spirit of Mt. Pilaga, sent by the Bodhisattva to deliver these saddles and bridles to you. Go west with effort, and do not be careless." This alarmed Tripitaka, who dismounted and bowed to the sky, saying, "Disciple with eyes of flesh, ignorant and unseeing, I pray for forgiveness. Please convey my gratitude to the Bodhisattva." He continued to bow towards the heavens, uncounted, and nearby, the Monkey was laughing out loud, while the Monkey King was delighted. The Monkey came forward and pulled Tripitaka up, saying, "Master, get up, he is long gone. You cannot hear him or see him with your head down like that." The monk replied,

"Buddhist master, please receive the saddle and bridle." Seeing this, Tripitaka was pleased and accepted them, instructing the monk to hold them while he checked to see if they suited the horse. The monk stepped forward and examined each item, finding them indeed to be of fine quality. There is a poem to attest to this:

Embellished with silver stars, the brocaded saddle glows,
Golden threads shine on the precious bench.
Several layers of velvet cushions fold and stack,
Three purple threads make for the reins.
The bridle’s headpiece, embroidered in intricate patterns,
Heralds the dancing beasts in gilded fan.
Meticulously forged iron forms the bit,
While the tassels dangle, wet as if rinsed in water.

Inside, the monk’s heart rejoiced as he placed the saddle and bridle on the horse, finding them to fit perfectly. Tripitaka thanked the old man, who hurriedly replied, "Fear not! Fear not! Why the gratitude?" Without further ado, the old man bid them farewell and invited them to mount. 

Leaving the door, Tripitaka mounted his horse and started off, while the monk carried their luggage. The old man then withdrew a whip from his sleeve, a crafty stick of fragrant vine, and the end bound with tiger sinew, and presented it to the monk. "Buddhist master," he said, "I also have a whip. I shall offer this to you as well."

Tripitaka, mounting his horse, received the whip with gratitude: "Many thanks for your generous gift! Many thanks for your generous gift!" Just as he was about to thank, the old man had already vanished, and the shrine stood empty as though on barren land. From the air, a voice sounded: "Buddhist master, forgive our slight. I am the deity of Llagsha Mountain. At the Buddha’s behest, I have brought you saddle and bridle. Be strong on your journey westward, and do not grow slack." 

Hearing this, Tripitaka dismounted, bowed towards the sky, and repeatedly begged forgiveness from the unseen deity. The monk who was waiting on the side, the robust Sun Wukong, could barely contain his laughter at his master’s devotion, and his companion, the agile Sun Wukong, seized his master and said, "Master, you need not continue to bow. Tripitaka, from his horse, took them, saying: "I thank you greatly for your kindness! I thank you greatly!" Please convey my gratitude to the Bodhisattva, who has bestowed great benevolence." He continued to bow towards the heavens, not counting the number of times, until the Monkey King, laughing beside the road, pulled at the elder's sleeve, saying, "Master, get up, he's already gone. He won't hear your prayers or see your bows." The elder said:

Disciple, the saddles and bridles are here." Seeing this, Tripitaka was delighted and accepted them, instructing the monk to carry them and put them on the horse to see if they fit. The monk walked forward and examined each one carefully, indeed finding them to be fine. A poem attests to this: 

The carved saddle glitters with silver stars,  
The jeweled bench shines with golden threads.  
Several layers of velvet cloths are cushioned inside,  
Three strands of purple silk make the reins.  
The bridle's leather headstall is inlaid with floral patterns,  
The cloud fan is adorned with golden beasts.  
The bit is forged from tempered iron,  
Two tassels hang down, glistening with moisture.  
The monk secretly rejoiced, putting the saddles and bridles on the horse, feeling as if they were made just for it. Tripitaka thanked the old man, who hurriedly pulled him up and said, "Frightened! Frightened! No need for thanks." The old man did not stay, and Tripitaka mounted the horse. The elder came out, grabbed the saddle, and the monk carried the luggage. The old man then took out a whip from his sleeve, a fine piece of intertwined stingy vines and tiger sinew, and offered it to the monk saying, "Sage Monk, I also have a bridle, why don't you take them both?" Tripitaka got off the horse, bowed, and said, "Thank you for your generosity! Thank you for your generosity!" Just as he was bowing, the old man had already vanished, and looking back, the old temple was nothing but a patch of empty land. From above, someone spoke, "Sage Monk, I was rude to you. I am the Mountain God of L落伽Mountain, sent by the Bodhisattva to deliver saddles and bridles to you. You must continue your journey westward, and do not let your spirit grow slack." Tripitaka quickly got off the horse, bowed to the sky, and said, "Disciple I am but a coarse man, not recognizing your divine form, I beg for your forgiveness. Please convey my gratitude to the Bodhisattva, who has shown such kindness." You see him continuing to bow to the sky, counting no more. Beside him, the Monkey King laughed himself silly, while his master Sun Wukong was overjoyed, grabbing Tripitaka and saying, "Master, get up, he has gone far, we can no longer hear your prayers or see your bows. Why continue to bow?" The elder said:

"Ashrama, the saddle and bridle are now in your hands." Seeing this, Tripitaka was delighted and gratefully accepted them, instructing the pilgrim to mount the horse and see if they fitted. The pilgrim ascended and, taking each item in turn to inspect, found them to be of excellent quality. The poem attests to this:

Gaily the colored saddles glisten with silver stars,
The ornate saddles sparkle with golden thread.
Several layers of soft furs line the cushioned seat,
And the reins are triple-stranded purple silk.
The harnesses are carved with intricate designs,
The cloud-shaped fans are adorned with golden beasts,
The bit is made of tempered iron, polished and smooth,
And the hanging whips have tassels of flowing silk.

The pilgrim was secretly pleased, and placed the saddle and bridle on the horse's back, finding them to fit perfectly. Tripitaka thanked the old man, who hastily replied, "Please forgive me, please forgive me, why be so grateful?" The old man did not stay to offer more, but invited Tripitaka to mount his horse. The elder stepped out, mounted his horse, and the pilgrim took up the luggage. The old man, once again, withdrew from his sleeve a whip, a piece of supple rattan bound with tiger sinew. He presented it to the pilgrim, saying, "Saint, I have also a whip for your saddle, may I give it to you now?" 

Tripitaka, alighting the horse, thanked the old man again: "Much gratitude, much gratitude!" While paying his respects, he could not see the old man, who had already vanished. Looking back, he could see no sign of the small shrine. The old man's voice seemed to come from the air above, "Pilgrim, I apologize for my rudeness. I am the deity of the Wulasha Mountain, sent by the Bodhisattva to provide your equipment. I hope you will continue on your journey with diligence, and do not be negligent."

Tripitaka dismounted and bowed towards the heavens, "Disciple, I am but a simple person, unable to recognize you. Please forgive me. Please convey my gratitude to the Bodhisattva." Seeing this, the Monkey King laughed while the Guardian of the Path simply smiled, saying, "Master, don't keep bowing; he's gone far now. No one can hear your prayers or see your bowing." The elder, still kneeling, did not cease his prostrations.

As K. passed one of the following evenings through the corridor separating his office from the main staircase — he went home almost last that time, only two servants were still at work in the small light of a bulb — he heard, behind a door where he had always only imagined a dusty storeroom, a sigh. He paused in astonishment and listened again to verify that he had not imagined it — for a moment there was silence, then the sighs resumed. — At first, he wanted to summon one of the servants; perhaps a witness would be needed. Then, however, an uncontrollable curiosity seized him, and he flung the door wide open. It was, as he had correctly surmised, a dusty storeroom. Insignificant, old printing type and overturned empty earthenware ink bottles lay beyond the threshold. But in the room itself, three men were hunched in the low space. A candle fastened to a shelf gave them light. "What are you up to here?" K. demanded, his excitement spilling over, but not loudly. The man who apparently dominated the others and was the first to turn his gaze toward him, clad in a kind of dark leather garb that exposed his throat to the collar and his entire arms, remained silent. But the other two cried out: "Sir! We are to be flogged because you complained to the examining judge about us." And only then did K. realize that they were indeed Franz and Willem, and that the third one held a rod to flog them. "Well," said K., staring at them, "I did not complain, I merely said what had happened in my room. And you have behaved impeccably, as far as I can see." "Sir," said Willem, while Franz, behind him, evidently tried to shield himself from the one who held the rod, "if you knew how little we are paid, you would judge us better. I have a family to feed, and Franz wanted to get married; one must enrich oneself in every way possible, for sheer hard work does not suffice, no matter how strenuous. Your fine linen clothes tempted me, it is naturally forbidden to the keepers, but it is a tradition that the clothes belong to the keepers, it has always been so, believe me; it is understandable what such things mean for one who is so unfortunate as to be arrested, is it not? But as soon as one speaks of it publicly, punishment is called for." "What you are saying now, I did not know, I did not demand your punishment, I was concerned about a principle." "Franz," said Willem to the other keeper, "didn't I tell you that the master did not demand your punishment? Now you hear that he did not even know that you would be punished." "Don't let such words move you," said the one with the rod to K., "the punishment is both just and inevitable." "Listen to him not," said Willem and, interrupting to quickly bring his hand to his mouth, added, "We are only being punished because you reported us. Nothing would have happened to us if anyone had discovered what we did. Can that be called justice? We two, especially me, have proven our worth as keepers for a long time — you must admit that we have, from the point of view of the authorities, kept well — we had prospects for advancement, and we would certainly have become floggers like the one who just had the luck to be reported by no one, for such a report is quite rare. Now, sir, everything is lost, our careers are over, we must perform much more subordinate tasks than the keeper's, and besides, we are now receiving these terribly painful floggings." "Can the rod cause such pain?" K. asked and examined the one the flogger held out to him. "We will have to take off all our clothes," said Willem. "Ah, so," said K. and looked closely at the flogger, who was tanned like a sailor and had a wild, fresh face. "Is there no way to spare the two of them the flogging?" he asked. "No," said the flogger and shook his head with a smile. "Strip!" he ordered the keepers. And to K., he said, "You need not believe everything they say; they are a little mad from fear of the flogging. What this one," he pointed to Willem — "said about our future prospects is just plain ridiculous. Look at how fat he is — the first lashing will probably go right through the fat. — Do you know how he got so fat? He has the habit of eating everyone's breakfast. Did he not also eat your breakfast? As I said. But a man with such a paunch can never become a flogger, that is out of the question." "There are floggers like that too," asserted Willem, who was now unfastening his belt. "No," said the flogger, and, striking Willem's neck with the rod, made him flinch, "listen to him, not to me. Strip!" "I would reward you well if you let them go," said K. and, without once looking at the flogger — such deals are best conducted with lowered eyes on both sides — he took out his wallet. "Do you want to accuse me as well and have me flogged too?" said the flogger. "No, no!" "Be reasonable," said K., "if I had wanted to have them punished, I would not now be paying to set them free. I could just close the door here, see and hear nothing more, and go home. But I am not doing that, rather I am earnestly trying to set them free; if I had known that they were to be punished, or even that they could be punished, I would never have mentioned their names. I do not even think they are guilty, the organization is guilty, the high officials are guilty." "So it is!" the keepers cried and received an immediate blow over their already undressed backs. "If you had a judge under your rod here," said K. and, while speaking, pressed down on the rod that was rising again, "I would certainly not prevent you from lashing, on the contrary, I would give you even more money to help you with the good cause." "What you say sounds quite credible," said the flogger, "but I cannot be bribed. I am hired to flog, so I flog." Franz, who until now, in expectation of K.'s intervention, had been rather reserved, now, in his underwear, knelt before the door and whispered to K., "If you cannot procure mercy for both of us, at least try to set me free. "Can a rod cause such pain?" asked K. and inspected the one held by the flogger. "We will have to take off all our clothes," said Willem. "Ah, so," said K., and looked closely at the flogger. He was as tanned as a sailor and had a wild, fresh face. "Is there no way to spare them their beating?" he asked the flogger. "No," said the flogger and shook his head with a smile. "Get undressed!" he ordered the guards. And to K. he said, "You need not believe everything they say; they are already a little demented from fear of the beatings. What this one, for example," he pointed to Willem, "told you about his prospects is laughable. Look, how fat he is—his first blows will be wasted in his fat. Do you know why he is so fat? He eats all the prisoners’ breakfasts. Did he not also eat your breakfast? I told you so. But a man with such a belly can never become a flogger, that is entirely out of the question." "There are floggers like that," Willem said as he untied his belt. "No," said the flogger and struck Willem’s neck with the rod so hard that he shrank, "listen to me and take off your clothes." "I would reward you well if you let them go," said K. and drew his wallet out without looking at the flogger again—such deals are best conducted with lowered eyes on both sides. "Do you want to have me accused too, and to receive a beating as well?" the flogger said, "and be compensated for it? No, no!" "Be reasonable," said K., "if I had wanted these two to be punished, I would have simply closed the door and left. I would not have even wanted to see or hear what was happening. But I am not doing that, for I am earnestly concerned with freeing them; had I known they were to be punished or even that they might be punished, I would never have mentioned their names. I don’t consider them guilty, the organization is guilty, the high officials are guilty." "So it is!" the guards shouted and received a blow on their already undressed backs. "If you had a high judge here under your rod," said K., pressing the rod that was already raised down, "I would not stop you from striking; on the contrary, I would give you money to strike for the good cause." "What you say sounds plausible," the flogger said, "but I am not bribed. I am hired to flog, and so I flog." Now Franz, who until now had been rather reserved in hope that K. might be successful, in his only clothes knelt by the door and, in a low voice, whispered, "If you cannot obtain leniency for both of us, at least try to free me. Willem is older than me, less sensitive in every respect, and he once received a light beating a few years ago, whereas I have yet to be disgraced, and was brought to this only through Willem, my teacher in both good and bad. My poor bride is waiting for news in front of the building; I feel so ashamed." He wiped his face, which was now drenched with tears, with K.’s coat. "I am not waiting any longer," the flogger said, grasped the rod firmly, and struck Franz, while Willem crouched in a corner, looking on furtively, without daring to turn his head. Then a cry rose from Franz, unbroken and unchanging, as though it came not from a human being but from a tortured instrument. The whole corridor resounded with it, and the whole house must have heard. "Don’t scream," K. shouted, unable to hold back, and while he anxiously watched the direction from which the servants were bound to come, he pushed against Franz, not hard enough to knock him down but hard enough to send the unconscious man to the floor in convulsions, his hands rummaging the ground. But he still did not escape the blows; the rod found him even on the ground. As he writhed beneath it, its tip swayed up and down regularly. Then in the distance a servant appeared, and another followed a few steps behind. K. had quickly shut the door, rushed to one of the windows, and opened it. The screaming had stopped completely. To prevent the servants from coming near, he shouted, "It’s me!" "Good evening, Master Procurator!" they replied. "Has something happened?" "No, no," K. answered, "only a dog is howling on the yard." When the servants did not move, he added, "You can continue your work." To avoid having to converse with the servants, he leaned out the window. After a while, when he looked again into the corridor, they had already gone. K. stayed at the window, not daring to enter the storeroom and not wanting to go home. It was a small square yard below, to which he looked down, surrounded by offices, whose windows were all dark, with only the upper ones catching a glimmer of moonlight. K. strained his eyes to penetrate the darkness of a corner of the yard where several handcarts were piled up. It distressed him that he had not been able to prevent the beating, but it was not his fault that he had not been able to; surely, if Franz had not screamed—indeed, it must have hurt very much, but at a decisive moment one must master oneself—then K. would have found a way, at least very likely, to persuade the flogger. If the entire lower echelon of the administration was made up of scoundrels, why should the flogger, who had the most inhumane office, be an exception? K. had observed well that his eyes had lit up at the sight of the note, and he had apparently only acted so seriously in the beating because he wanted to increase the bribe sum a little. And K. would not have spared a penny; it was really his goal to free the guards; now that he had started fighting the corruption of this judicial system, it was only logical that he would also do so from this angle.

One cannot, however, say that the hero's nature was so harsh and barren that his feelings were dulled to the point where he could neither pity nor sympathize. He felt both, and he would even wish to help, but only if it did not involve a large sum, if it did not touch on the money that was meant to be left untouched; in short, the father's advice to save and hoard pennies was well heeded. But there was no real attachment to money for its own sake; he was not driven by miserliness and meanness. No, not these emotions moved him: he imagined a life ahead of him filled with all kinds of luxuries and comforts; carriages, a splendid home, sumptuous dinners—these were the things that constantly filled his thoughts. To finally be able to taste all of this at some point, that was why he was so careful with his savings, giving them sparingly to himself and others at the appropriate time. When a wealthy man would pass by in his elegant sleighs, riding fine horses with rich harnesses, he would stop in his tracks, like a statue, and then, after waking from a long sleep, he would say, "He used to be a clerk, and he used to wear his hair in a round! " And whatever brought to mind wealth and comfort produced an effect on him that he could not explain to himself. After leaving the school, he did not even want to rest; he had such a strong desire to plunge immediately into work and service. Nevertheless, despite praiseworthy testimonials, he found it very difficult to be appointed to a place in the state chancery. And even in remote outposts, one needed connections! The place that was given to him was insignificant, with an annual salary of thirty or forty rubles. But he resolved to ardently take to his duties and to conquer and overcome everything. Indeed, he showed an extraordinary self-sacrifice, patience, and self-restraint. From early morning until late at night, without ceasing, either mentally or physically, he wrote, getting mired in bureaucratic papers, did not go home, slept on desks in the offices, sometimes ate with the watchmen, and yet managed to maintain his neat appearance, put on clothes properly, and give his face a pleasant expression, even something noble in his movements. It must be said that the clerks of the chancery especially stood out for their unprepossessing and ill-mannered appearance. On some, faces were misshapen like a poorly baked loaf of bread: one cheek was swollen in one direction, the chin skewed in another, the upper lip swollen and cracked; in short, they were completely unattractive. They spoke in a gruff manner, as though ready to attack someone; they often made sacrifices to Bacchus, thereby showing that there were still many vestiges of paganism in Slavic nature; they even sometimes came into the presence intoxicated, making the air unpleasant and the atmosphere completely unaromatic. Among such officials, Chichikov could not fail to stand out, presenting a complete contrast in appearance, his voice, and the absolute abstention from strong drinks. But his path was still difficult; he fell under the command of an elderly governor, who was a kind of stone of insensibility and inviolability: always the same, unapproachable, never showing a smile, never greeting anyone even with a query about their health. No one had ever seen him change in any way, whether on the street or at home; no one had ever seen him show any interest in anything, become drunk, or laugh in his drunkenness; not even a hint of such things was found in him. There was nothing in him at all: neither wicked nor good, and something terrible was revealed in that absence of everything. His marble-like face, without any harsh or irregular features, gave no hint of any resemblance; his features were in a stern proportion. Only the frequent wrinkles and potholes, which punctuated his face, would cause him to be considered one of those faces on which the devil came at night to thresh peas. It seemed that no human effort could bring him around and win his favor, but Chichikov tried. At first, he tried to please him in insignificant ways: he carefully examined the quill pens he used and, preparing several according to their model, put them in his hand every time; he blew and swept the sand and tobacco from his desk; he bought a new rag for his inkwell; he found his hat, a shabby hat that had never existed in the world, and placed it beside him just before the end of the session; he cleaned his back if he had dirtied it with chalk by the wall—all this was met with no reaction, as if it had not been done. Finally, he found out about his personal life, that he had a grown daughter, whose face, too, resembled someone being threshed for peas at night. From this side, he planned his assault. He found out which church his daughter went to on Sundays and, every time, would stand opposite her, neatly dressed, ironing his soutane— and this had its effect: the stern governor staggered and invited him for tea! And before the chancery could even look around, Chichikov was settled in the governor's house, a useful and necessary person, buying flour and sugar, treating his daughter like a bride, calling the governor "Dad" and kissing his hand; everyone in the chancery had put it about that there would be a wedding at the end of February, before the Great Lent. The stern governor even began to intercede for him with his superiors, and shortly after, Chichikov himself was appointed governor for the vacancy. It seemed that the main purpose of his connections with the old governor was fulfilled here, because he sent his trunk secretly home and the next day found himself in a different apartment. He no longer called the governor "Dad" and no longer kissed his hand; and the matter of the wedding was hushed up as though nothing had happened. However, when meeting him, he would always warmly shake his hand and invite him for tea, so that the old governor, despite his constant immobility and his cold indifference, would shake his head and mutter to himself: "What a swindler, what a swindler, that son of a b*tch!"

It is true, however, that the hero's nature was not so hard and callous, and his feelings were not so dulled that he did not know pity or compassion. He felt both and even wanted to help, but only if it did not involve a significant sum, if it did not touch on the funds that were supposed to be untouched; in short, the fatherly advice to save and hoard a penny had served him well. But he did not have any genuine attachment to money for its own sake; he was neither a miser nor a tightwad. No, it was not his motivation: he envisioned a life of every conceivable comfort, with all necessities, carriages, a well-appointed house, sumptuous dinners. To taste all this eventually, gradually, was why he saved his pennies, sparing them to himself and others for the right time. When a wealthy man drove by in a beautifully-painted barouche, in a steed with rich harness, he would stop in his tracks, as if rooted to the spot, and when he finally recovered, as from a long sleep, he would say, “He used to be a clerk, and he used to wear his hair in a queue!” Everything that signified wealth and comfort made an incomprehensible impression on him. After graduating from the academy, he did not even want to rest: his desire to start working and serving was so intense. Despite commendable testimonials, he struggled to be assigned to the public chancery. And in remote provinces, one needed patronage! He secured an insignificant post, with a salary of thirty or forty rubles a year. But he was determined to take his service seriously, overcome all obstacles. Indeed, he showed a remarkable degree of self-sacrifice, patience, and restriction. From early morning until late at night, without tiring his mental or physical faculties, he wrote, mired in official papers, he did not go home, slept in the chancery offices on tables, sometimes ate with the guards, and yet managed to maintain neatness, dress properly, and give his face a pleasant expression, even something noble in his movements. It must be said that the chancery officials were notably unattractive and undignified. Some had faces like a poorly baked loaf: one cheek puffed out in one direction, the chin crooked in another, the upper lip swollen and cracked; in short, quite unattractive. They spoke in a stern manner, as if preparing to assault someone; they drank often to honor the god Bacchus, thereby demonstrating that there were still many remnants of paganism in the Slavic nature; they would even sometimes come to the office in a state of inebriation, making the atmosphere unpleasant and the air unaromatic. Among such officials, Chichikov was noticed and stood out, representing the complete opposite in demeanor, voice, and abstention from strong drinks. But his path was still difficult; he fell under the jurisdiction of an elderly collector, who was a model of stone-like insensitivity and invincibility: forever the same, impervious, never showing a smile, never asking about anyone's health even in passing. No one had ever seen him in a different state, whether on the street or at home; he never showed any concern, never got drunk and laughed, never even indulged in drunken revelry like a bandit might. Not a trace of any of that was visible in him. Nothing was quite balanced in him: neither evil nor good; something terrifying was evident in his lack of anything. His marble face, with no sharp or irregular features, did not hint at any likeness; its severe symmetry was flawless. Only the frequent ripples and potholes, which marked his face, might have been likened to a field where the devil came at night to thresh beans. It seemed that no human effort could bend such a person to one's will and win his favor, but Chichikov tried. At first, he started to please in all insignificant ways: he carefully examined the pen feathers he used to write with and prepared several similar ones to place by his side; he blew away the sand and tobacco from his desk; he introduced a new rag for his inkwell; he found the old collector’s hat, a most abominable hat, and placed it beside him at the end of the session; he cleaned the back of his neck if he had smudged it with chalk against the wall — but all this was entirely unnoticed, as if it had not happened. Finally, he learned about his domestic life and discovered that he had an adult daughter with a face that also resembled a field where beans were threshed at night. He decided to try an approach from this side. He learned which church she attended on Sundays and would stand opposite her, neatly dressed, starching his undershirt — and the plan worked: the stern collector wavered and invited him for tea! Before long, in the chancery, it was arranged that Chichikov moved in with him, became a necessary man, bought flour and sugar, addressed the daughter like a fiancée, called the collector “father,” kissed his hand; everyone in the chancery decided that a wedding would take place in February before the Great Lent. The stern collector even began to intercede for him with his superiors, and before long Chichikov himself was appointed collector to the vacant post. It seemed that this was the main goal of his connections with the old collector, for he secretly sent his trunk home and the next day was already living in a different apartment. He stopped calling the collector “father” and no longer kissed his hand, and the wedding was never mentioned, as if nothing had happened. Nonetheless, whenever they met, Chichikov would warmly shake the collector’s hand and invite him for tea, and the old collector, despite his perpetual immobility and insensibility, would shake his head and mutter to himself, “Trickster, he tricked me!”

And before the officials could react, the matter was settled: Chichikov moved into his house, became indispensable, bought flour and sugar, treated his daughter like a bride, called the inspector father, kissed his hand; everyone in the chamber said that there would be a wedding at the end of February before Great Lent. The stern inspector even began to fuss over him at the office, and soon Chichikov himself was appointed inspector on a vacant post. It seemed that this was the main aim of his connections with the old inspector, for he then sent his trunk secretly to his home, and on the next day he found himself already in a different flat. He stopped calling him father and no longer kissed his hand; and the matter of the wedding was forgotten, as if nothing had happened. However, every time they met, he affectionately shook his hand and invited him for tea, so that the old inspector, despite his constant immobility and hard, indifferent demeanor, would always shake his head and mutter to himself, “He cheated, he cheated, the son of a devil!”

Meanwhile, Emperor Taizong was playing chess with Wei Zheng in the secondary hall, each move carefully considered and the positions laid out. As The Annals of Go state: In the art of chess, precision is of utmost importance. The superior stones are in the center, the inferior ones on the sides, and the medium ones at the corners; this is the common practice in playing chess. The principle is: rather lose a single stone than lose a move. Attack the left and look to the right, strike the back and gaze ahead. There is a prior move and a subsequent move, a move in advance and a move behind. Do not sever two living stones, do not link two stones that are already alive. Do not make spaces too wide, nor arrangements too tight. Rather abandon a stone to ensure its survival than hold onto it and risk defeat; rather stick to one's own business without purpose than fortify and provide for oneself. When one is outnumbered, first secure one's own position; when one is in the majority, assert one's influence. The adept does not contest, the skillful does not engage; the victor does not succumb, the loser does not panic. Chess begins with straightforward positioning and ends with ingenious victory. If an opponent makes a move without apparent threat, it is likely a ploy to invade or isolate; if they forsake a minor gain without protection, it indicates an ambition for a greater prize. To play impulsively is to lack strategy; to respond without thought is a path to defeat. The Book of Poetry says: “Be careful and cautious, as if you stand by a deep valley.” This is the essence of the matter.

"And now?" Gregor wondered and looked around in the darkness. He soon realized that he could no longer move at all. He did not wonder about this; instead, it seemed unnatural to him that he had actually managed to move with these slender legs until now. Otherwise, he felt relatively comfortable. Although he felt pain all over his body, it seemed to be growing weaker and weaker, and would probably disappear entirely. He could hardly feel the rotting apple in his back and the inflamed area, which was completely covered in soft dust. With tenderness and love, he recalled his family. Perhaps his opinion that he should disappear was even stronger than his sister's. In this state of empty and peaceful reflection, he remained until the tower clock struck the third hour of the morning. He still witnessed the gradual brightening outside the window. Then his head sank completely of its own accord, and his last breath issued weakly from his nostrils.

The small room, in which the young man entered, had yellow wallpaper, geraniums, and silk curtains at the windows. At this moment, it was brightly illuminated by the setting sun. "And then, it seems, the sun will shine just the same!" it flashed in Raskolnikov's mind as he quickly surveyed the room to study and remember the arrangement. But there was nothing remarkable about the room. All the furniture, which was very old and made of yellow wood, consisted of a sofa with a greatly arched wooden back, an oval table in front of the sofa, a dressing table with a mirror in a recess, chairs along the walls, and a couple of cheap paintings in yellow frames depicting German girls with birds in their hands—all that there was. In a corner before a small image, a lamp was burning. Everything was extremely clean: the furniture and floors gleamed as if polished; everything sparkled. "Lizaveta's work," the young man thought. Not a single speck of dust could be found throughout the apartment. "This kind of cleanliness is characteristic of bitter and old spinsters," Raskolnikov continued to himself, casting a curious glance at the muslin curtain before the door to the second tiny room, where the old woman's bed and dressing table stood, and which he had never before entered. The entire apartment consisted of these two rooms.

Here, Ippolit Kirillovich deemed it fitting to briefly outline the character of the deceased Smerdyakov, who “ended his life in a paroxysm of painful mental derangement and frenzy.” He depicted him as a mentally feeble man, with a trace of some vague education, confused by philosophical ideas beyond his mental capacity, and frightened by the modern teachings about duty and obligation, which had been practically imparted to him through the reckless lifestyle of his master, who may have been his father, Fyodor Pavlovich, and theoretically through various strange philosophical conversations with his master’s older son, Ivan Fyodorovich, who enjoyed these discussions – most likely out of boredom or a need for mockery, which had found no better outlet. He himself had told me about his mental state in the final days of his stay at his master’s house, – explained Ippolit Kirillovich – but the same conclusion can be drawn from other sources: the accused himself, his brother, and even Grigory the servant, who knew him intimately. Moreover, afflicted by a sudden illness, Smerdyakov was “cowardly as a chicken.” “He fell at my feet and kissed my feet,” the accused reported to us at the moment when he was still unaware of the harm such a revelation might bring him, – he expressed it in his characteristic language, referring to Smerdyakov as a chicken in a fit of illness. And it was his very own accused (as he himself testifies) that he chose as his confidant and terrified him to the point where he finally agreed to act as an informer and messenger for him. In this capacity, as a household spy, he reported to the accused about the existence of a money packet and about the signs by which one could enter the house – how could he not? “They will kill me, I saw it clearly, they will kill me,” he said during the investigation, shuddering even before us, despite the fact that the one who had frightened him was already in custody and could no longer punish him. “They suspect me every minute, I tremble in fear, just to appease their anger, I hasten to tell them every secret, so that my innocence could be seen by them and I might be allowed to live for repentance.” These were his own words, which I noted and remembered: “When he would shout at me, I would fall on my knees before them.” Being naturally a person of high honor and trust from his youth, and gaining the trust of his master by distinguishing himself with this honesty when his master returned the money he had lost, the unfortunate Smerdyakov, it is likely, suffered terribly from remorse for his betrayal of his master, whom he loved as his benefactor. Suffering greatly from a sudden illness, according to the testimony of leading psychiatrists, such individuals are always inclined to continuous, certainly painful self-accusation. They are tortured by their “guilt” toward something and someone, plagued by conscience, often exaggerating and even inventing their own crimes and offenses without any basis. And such a person really becomes guilty and criminal out of fear and intimidation. Additionally, he greatly anticipated that something unfavorable might happen from the circumstances unfolding before his eyes. When Ivan Fyodorovich, the older son of Fyodor Pavlovich, was leaving for Moscow just before the catastrophe, Smerdyakov implored him to stay, though he did not dare, for his cowardly habit, to express his fears openly. He was satisfied with hints, which were not understood. It must be noted that in Ivan Fyodorovich, he saw some kind of protection, some kind of guarantee that as long as he was at home, no disaster would occur. Recall the expression in Dmirty Karamazov’s drunken letter: “I’ll kill the old man if only Ivan leaves” – so the presence of Ivan Fyodorovich was considered by all as a guarantee of peace and order in the house. And so he leaves, and Smerdyakov falls ill immediately, almost an hour after the young master’s departure. This is completely understandable. One must mention that, troubled by fears and a kind of despair, Smerdyakov in the last days especially felt the possibility of impending epileptic seizures, which had always occurred with him during moments of moral tension and upheaval. The time and day of these seizures cannot be foreseen, but every epileptic can sense them beforehand. So says medicine. And just as Ivan Fyodorovich was leaving the courtyard, Smerdyakov, struck by his sense of abandonment and helplessness, went to the cellar to do household chores, descended the stairs, and thought: “Will there be a seizure or not, but what if it comes now?” And it was just this mood, this suspicion, these questions that brought on his laryngeal spasm, which always precedes the fit, and he flew headlong, unconscious, to the bottom of the cellar. And in this very natural coincidence, they seek to see some suspicion, some hint, some suggestion that he faked his illness on purpose! But if on purpose, then the question arises: for what purpose? With what calculations, with what aim? Let alone medicine; the science lies, the science is mistaken, the doctors could not distinguish truth from pretense – let it be, let it be, but answer me, however, the question: why did he pretend? Was it not to attract attention to himself in advance and more quickly through a seizure, after he had planned the murder? See, gentlemen of the jury, on the night of the crime, there were five people in Fyodor Pavlovich’s house: first, Fyodor Pavlovich himself, but he did not kill himself, that is clear; second, his servant Grigory, but he was almost killed; third, Grigory’s wife, the servant Marfa Ignatyevna, but to think of her as the murderer of her master is simply shameful. Therefore, two people remain: the accused and Smerdyakov. But since the accused maintains that he did not commit the murder, it must have been Smerdyakov who committed it, as there is no other person to blame. Just so, the “clever” and colossal accusation against the unfortunate, who ended his life yesterday as a lunatic, comes from this very fact: that there was no one else to blame! If there was even the slightest suspicion of a sixth person, I am convinced that even the accused would have been ashamed to point to Smerdyakov and would have pointed to this sixth person instead, for it is an absurdity to accuse Smerdyakov of this murder.

Here, Ippolit Kirillovich deemed it necessary to briefly delineate the character of the deceased Smerdyakov, "who had ended his life in an attack of ill-considered mental derangement and obsession." He depicted Smerdyakov as a man of feeble intellect with a faint trace of education, confused by philosophical ideas beyond his mental capacity, frightened by various modern teachings on duty and obligation, which were imparted to him practically—through the wild, reckless lifestyle of his master, perhaps his father, Fyodor Pavlovich, and theoretically—through strange philosophical conversations with the eldest son of his master, Ivan Fyodorovich, who willingly indulged in such entertainments—possibly out of boredom or a need for mockery, with no better outlet. Moreover, Smerdyakov was dreadfully afraid when struck by his paralytic illness, "as timid as a hen," as the accused put it, "he would fall at my feet and kiss my feet, just like a hen stricken by paralysis," in his characteristic language. And so it was that the accused himself chose Smerdyakov as his confidant and coerced him to such an extent that eventually Smerdyakov agreed to serve as a spy and messenger. In this capacity, Smerdyakov betrayed his master and informed the accused of the existence of a package of money and the signs by which one could gain access to the master—how could he not do so! "They will kill me, I can see it plainly," he said during his interrogation, shaking and trembling even in front of us, despite the fact that the torturer who had intimidated him was already under arrest and could not come to punish him. "They suspected me at every moment, I was in constant fear and trembling, just to appease their anger, I would hasten to inform them of any secret, so that my innocence might be visible to them and I might be set free in the flesh for repentance." These were his own words, which I wrote down and remembered. "When he would shout at me, I would fall to my knees before them." Being an inherently upright young man and thus trusted by his master, Smerdyakov, it seems, suffered immensely from guilt over his betrayal of his master, whom he loved as his benefactor. Strongly affected by his paralytic illness, according to the testimony of the most eminent psychiatrists, such patients are prone to incessant and painful self-accusation. They torment themselves over some perceived guilt and are seized by pangs of conscience, often exaggerating and even fabricating imagined crimes without any basis. Thus, such a subject truly becomes guilty and criminal from fear and intimidation. Furthermore, he had a strong premonition that something unpleasant might arise from the circumstances he was witnessing. Recall the expression in the "drunken" letter of Dmitry Karamazov: "I will kill the old man if Ivan only leaves"; thus, Ivan Fyodorovich's presence seemed to everyone as a guarantee of peace and order in the house. And so Ivan Fyodorovich departs, and Smerdyakov falls into a paralytic attack almost immediately, barely an hour after the young master left. This is perfectly understandable. One must note that, distressed by his fears and despair, Smerdyakov felt in his last days a heightened sense of the possibility of imminent paroxysms, which had always occurred in him during moments of moral tension. While it is impossible to predict the exact time and hour of these attacks, an epileptic can feel the premonition of an attack in advance. Medicine says so. And just as Ivan Fyodorovich was leaving the courtyard, Smerdyakov, overwhelmed by a sense of orphanhood and vulnerability, went down to the cellar to do household work and thought: "Will there be an attack or not, but what if it comes now?" And it is precisely from this state of mind, from this anxiety, from these questions, that he was seized by the premonitory spasm that always precedes a paralytic attack, and he plunged unconscious to the bottom of the cellar. In this very natural event, some suspicion or hint is sought to imply that he had feigned illness deliberately! But if feigned, then the question arises: for what reason? With what purpose? I am not speaking of medicine; the science lies, the science is mistaken, the doctors could not distinguish truth from feigned illness—let it be, let it be, but answer me this: what reason could he have for feigning it? Perhaps to attract attention in the household beforehand and more quickly by means of a sudden attack, if he had conceived the idea of murder? You see, gentlemen of the jury, in the house of Fyodor Pavlovich on the night of the crime there were and were present five people: first, Fyodor Pavlovich himself, but he did not kill himself, that is clear; second, his servant Grigory, but he was almost killed; third, Grigory's wife, the serving-maid Marfa Ignatievna, but it would be sheer absurdity to imagine her as the murderer of her master. That leaves two people in sight: the accused and Smerdyakov. But since the accused maintains that he did not commit the murder, then it must have been Smerdyakov, for there is no one else to be found and no other murderer to be discovered. Yes, yes, it is from this that arises this "ingenious" and colossal accusation against the unfortunate man who committed suicide yesterday! Simply because no one else can be found! If there had been even a shred, a hint of suspicion on some other person, or a sixth person, then I am convinced that even the accused would not have dared to point to Smerdyakov but would have pointed to this sixth person, for it is sheer absurdity to accuse Smerdyakov of this murder.

Additionally, Smerdyakov was overcome with fear due to his rapidly worsening illness, which made him “as timid as a hen.” “He would fall at my feet and kiss my shoes, just like a hen in a paroxysm of illness,” he expressed himself in his characteristic language. It was this defendant who chose Smerdyakov as his confidant and spy, who served him as a domestic spy and informed him about the existence of the money packet and the signs to gain access to his master. How could he not have informed? “They will kill me, I know it,” he said during his interrogation, trembling even in our presence, despite the fact that his tormentor, who had intimidated him, was already under arrest and could no longer punish him. “They suspect me at every moment, I was in fear and trepidation, only to appease their anger, I would hasten to share any secret with them, to make them see my innocence and let me live to repent.” These were his own words, which I wrote down and remembered: “Whenever he would yell at me, I would fall to my knees before them.” Young and inherently upright, Smerdyakov had gained his master’s trust, who had rewarded him for his honesty by returning the money he had lost. The unfortunate Smerdyakov, undoubtedly, suffered greatly from remorse for his betrayal of his master, whom he loved as a benefactor. People suffering from paroxysmal illness, according to the deepest psychiatrists, are always prone to continuous and, naturally, painful self-accusations. They are tormented by their supposed guilt and by pangs of conscience, often exaggerating or even inventing various sins and crimes without any basis. Thus, such a subject truly becomes guilty and criminal out of fear and intimidation. Moreover, he strongly sensed that something undesirable might emerge from the circumstances unfolding before his eyes. When Ivan Fyodorovich, the eldest son of Fyodor Pavlovich, left for Moscow just before the catastrophe, Smerdyakov implored him to stay, though he was too cowardly to express his fears openly. He was content with hints, which were not understood. It should be noted that in Ivan Fyodorovich, Smerdyakov saw his protector and a guarantee that as long as he remained at home, nothing bad would happen. Remember the expression in the drunk letter of Dmitry Karamazov: “I will kill the old man if Ivan leaves.” Therefore, Ivan Fyodorovich’s presence was seen as a guarantee of peace and order in the house. And so, he left, and Smerdyakov fell into a paroxysm of illness almost immediately after the young master’s departure. This was perfectly understandable. It must be mentioned that, overwhelmed by fears and a kind of despair, Smerdyakov especially felt the approaching possibility of paroxysms in the last days. The timing of these paroxysms could not be predicted, but every epileptic could feel in advance the approach of an episode. So says medicine. Just after Ivan Fyodorovich left the yard, Smerdyakov, feeling the orphaned state and his helplessness, went to the cellar for household duties, descended the stairs, and thought, “Will there be an episode or not, but what if it comes now?” And it was precisely from this mood, this suspicion, these questions, that his laryngeal spasm, always preceding a paroxysm, struck him, and he fell, half-conscious, to the cellar floor. And in this very natural event, people tried to see some suspicion, some hint, some implication that he had feigned illness on purpose! But if he feigned illness, the question arises: why? For what calculation and what purpose? I do not speak of medicine; it says that science lies, that science is mistaken, and that doctors could not distinguish between truth and pretense—let them, let them. But answer me, gentlemen of the jury, why would he pretend to be ill? Was it not to draw attention to himself in advance and more quickly, when planning the murder, by the resulting paroxysm? You see, gentlemen of the jury, in the house of Fyodor Pavlovich on the night of the crime, there were five people: first, Fyodor Pavlovich himself, but he did not kill himself, that is clear; second, his servant Grigory, but he was almost killed, third, Grigory’s wife, the maid Marfa Ignatievna, but it is simply disgraceful to imagine her as the murderer of her master. Thus, only two people remain: the defendant and Smerdyakov. Since the defendant claims he did not kill, then it must have been Smerdyakov who did, as there is no other option, and no other murderer can be found. This is how the “clever” and colossal accusation against the unfortunate man, who ended his life yesterday, arises! Only because no one else could be found! If there was even a hint or a suspicion of someone else, I am convinced that even the defendant would not have had the courage to point to Smerdyakov and would have pointed to this sixth person instead, for accusing Smerdyakov of this murder is sheer absurdity.

These ideas were reinforced theoretically through strange philosophical discussions with the elder son of his master, Ivan Fyodorovich, whom he took as an indulgent interlocutor—probably out of boredom or a need for mockery, which he found no better outlet for. He himself told me about his mental state in the last days of his stay with his master's household, explained Illicit Kirillovich. But his acquaintances and even Gregory the servant, the only ones who knew him well, also testified to the same. In addition, weighed down by an impending illness, Smirnov was "as cowardly as a hen." Being naturally a man of high integrity, he had won his master's confidence by his honesty when the master returned the money he had lost, and the unhappy Smirnov, who had surely suffered terrible remorse for his betrayal of his benefactor, must have been in terrible pain. Strongly affected by falling sickness, according to the testimony of the most profound psychiatrists, are prone to continuous and, naturally, painful self-reproach. And just as Ivan Fyodorovich left the courtyard, Smirnov, struck by a sense of loneliness and helplessness, went down to the cellar for household chores and thought: "Will there be an attack or not, but what if it comes now?" This was a terrible despot; even in the most ancient friendships, she could not tolerate equality, and she looked at Lizaveta Prokofievna precisely as a protégée, as she had thirty-five years ago, and could not reconcile herself with the sharpness and independence of her character. She remarked, for instance, that "it seems they all went too far in their usual way, and made a elephant out of a fly; that no matter how she listened, she did not convince herself that anything serious had actually happened; that it would be better to wait for something else to happen; that the count, in her opinion, was a decent young man, although sick, strange, and too insignificant. The worst part, that he openly supports a mistress." Lizaveta Prokofievna understood very well that Belokonskaya was somewhat vexed at the failure of Eugeny Panteleevich, whom she had recommended. What has happened? No matter how hard I look, I can’t conclude that anything has actually happened! Wait until something else happens! What could have fooled Ivan Fedorovich? "Your Excellency, what is this about?" said the dragon king. "I humbly request a divination of the weather in the heavens."

The Scholar promptly produced a text and pronounced, "Clouds will obscure the mountain peaks, and mist will surround the treetops. If this concerns rainfall, expect it tomorrow."

The dragon king inquired, "At what time will it rain tomorrow? How many inches will it amount to?"

The Scholar replied, "Clouds will form at辰时 (third hour), thunder will begin at已时 (fourth hour), rain will start at 午时 (fifth hour), and it will have ceased by 未时 (sixth hour), accumulating a total of 三尺三寸零四十八点 (three feet, three inches, and forty-eight points)."

The dragon king laughed and said, "This cannot be treated as a jest. If it rains as predicted tomorrow, I shall donate fifty taels of silver as thanks for your divination. If there is no rain, or if it does not occur at the specified times and amounts, I must warn you that I will smash your shop front and tear down your signboard. I will immediately have you expelled from Chang'an and banish you henceforth."

The Scholar replied with a smile, "I agree to this. Please, please, we shall see you tomorrow after the rain."

"Who comes to ask about matters?" the Dragon King said. "Please divinate the weather in the sky." The Scholar immediately reached into his sleeve and transmitted one course, predicting, "Clouds cover the mountain peak, fog shrouds the tree-tops. If you are asking about rain, it will certainly fall tomorrow."

The Dragon King said, "At what time will it rain tomorrow? How much rain will there be?" The Scholar replied, "Tomorrow, at the third watch, clouds will form; at the fourth watch, thunder will sound; at the fifth watch, it will begin to rain; and at the sixth watch, the rain will be sufficient. In total, it will be three feet three inches and forty-eight points."

The Dragon King laughed and said, "This cannot be a jest. If there is rain tomorrow as you have predicted, and if the times and amounts are as you have said, I will send fifty taels of silver as a thank-you gift. If there is no rain, or if the times and amounts do not match, I must truthfully inform you that I will destroy your storefront, tear down your signboard, and immediately expel you from Chang'an, not allowing you to continue deceiving the public!"

The Scholar responded with a smile, "This is certain. Please, please, we will meet again tomorrow after the rain."

"Shall the gentleman inquire about the matter?" the Dragon King said, "I beg to consult about the weather in the sky." The scholar immediately took out a fortune and predicted, "Clouds will cover the summit, fog will shroud the tree-tops. If this is an inquiry about rainfall, it will occur tomorrow."

The Dragon King said, "At what hour will it rain tomorrow? How much rain will there be in inches?" The scholar replied, "Tomorrow at the辰 hour, clouds will form; at 巳 hour, thunder will sound; at 午 hour, the rain will begin; by 戌 hour, the rain will cease. The total will amount to three feet, three inches, and forty-eight points." The Dragon King said, "This cannot be taken lightly. If there is rain tomorrow, and the time and amount conform to your prediction, I will present fifty taels of silver as gratitude. If there is no rain, or if the timing or amount does not match, I will honestly inform you, and you must immediately leave Chang'an; I will not allow you to continue misleading the public!" The scholar responded cheerfully, "This is entirely up to you. Goodbye, goodbye, we will meet again later tomorrow after the rain."

"Who comes to ask about something?" the Dragon King said. "I beg you to divine the weather in the heavens."

The scholar immediately took out a card and said, "The clouds are shrouding the mountain peaks, the fog is hanging over the treetops. If you ask about the rain, it will be in the morning."

The Dragon King said, "At what time will it rain tomorrow? How much rain will there be?"

The scholar said, "Tomorrow at the辰 hour the clouds will form, at the巳 hour the thunder will roll, at the午 hour the rain will start, and at the未 hour the rain will stop. A total of three feet three inches and forty-eight points of water will fall."

The Dragon King said, "This cannot be treated as a jest. If there is rain tomorrow and it follows the times and amounts you have predicted, I will send fifty taels of silver as thanks. If there is no rain, or if it does not follow the times and amounts you have predicted, I must honestly say that I will smash your door and tear down your signboard, and immediately expel you from Chang'an and not allow you to deceive the masses here!"

The scholar replied with delight, "This is certain as you wish. Please, please, we will see you later when the rain follows your prediction."

"Who comes to ask?" the Dragon King said. "I seek an astrological forecast of the weather." The scholar immediately withdrew a divination, and said, "Clouds shroud the mountain peaks, mists obscure the tree-tops. If you ask about rain, expect it tomorrow."

"What time will it rain tomorrow? How much rain will there be?" the Dragon King asked. The scholar replied, "Tomorrow at the辰 hour [9 AM-11 AM] the clouds will gather, at the已 hour [11 AM-1 PM] the thunder will sound, at the 午 hour [1 PM-3 PM] the rain will fall, and at the 未 hour [3 PM-5 PM] the rain will be heavy. The total will be three feet three inches and forty-eight points."

The Dragon King laughed and said, "This cannot be a joke. If there is rain tomorrow as you predicted, I will give you fifty taels of silver as a reward. If not, or if the rain does not fall at the time you predicted, I must tell you frankly, I will break your shop window and tear down your sign, and immediately drive you out of Chang'an for misleading the public!" The scholar answered with pleasure, "This I leave entirely to you. Goodbye, goodbye, we will meet again tomorrow if the rain does not come."

How adept the Deputy Director was at appropriating everything K. was now compelled to give up! Did K. not retain more than was strictly necessary? As he rushed off to an unknown painter with vague and, as he admitted to himself, very slim hopes, his reputation suffered an irreparable injury here. It would probably have been much better for K. to take off his overcoat again and at least try to win back the two gentlemen who still had to wait next door. K. might have done so too if he had not seen the Deputy Director in his room, searching through the bookshelf as if it were his own, looking for something. As K. hurried toward the door, he called out, "Oh, you haven’t left yet!"
