I was so struck by his offer that I do not even know why I started to cry. He took my tears for gratitude and said that he had always been sure I was a kind, sensitive, and learned young woman, but that he had not ventured on this measure until he had learned all the details of my current behavior. He then began to ask about you, saying that he had heard all about you and that you were a man of noble principles. He also said that he did not want to be in your debt and that five hundred rubles would be enough to compensate you for everything you had done for me. When I explained to him what you had done for me that no amount of money could repay, he said that it was all nonsense, that it was just stories, and that I was still young and read poetry, that novels corrupted young women, that books only ruined morality, and that he could not stand any books. He advised me to live his life and then to talk about people, adding, "then, you will know people." He also said that I should give his proposals a great deal of thought, that it would greatly upset him if I took such an important step without thinking it through, and that thoughtlessness and infatuation ruined inexperienced youth. But he was extremely eager for a favorable answer from me and, in any case, he was forced to marry a shopkeeper's widow in Moscow because, he said, he had sworn to deprive his criminal nephew of his inheritance. He left five hundred rubles on my knitting frame, as he said, for confections. He told me that in the village I would fatten up like a pancake, that I would roll around with him like cheese in oil, that he now had too many cares, that he had been dragging himself through his business all day, and that he had merely popped in on me in the middle of his busy schedule. With that, he left. I thought long and overthought, I was tormented, my dear friend, and finally I made up my mind. My dear friend, I will marry him. I must agree to his proposal. If anyone can save me from my disgrace, restore my good name, and protect me from poverty, deprivation, and misfortune in the future, it is only he. What else can I expect from the future? What more can I ask of fate? Fedya says that one should not lose one's happiness; she says, then, what is happiness? I do not see any other way out for myself, my dear invaluable friend. What can I do? I have already ruined my health through work; I cannot work constantly. To go out among people?—I will wither from boredom, and besides, I will not please anyone. I am naturally ill, and therefore I will always be a burden to others. Of course, I am not going to heaven now, but what can I do, my dear, what can I do? What do I have to choose from?

I was so taken aback by his proposal that I do not know why I began to cry. He took my tears as gratitude and said he had always been convinced that I was a kind, sensitive, and learned young lady, but that he had never dared to take such a step until he had learned all the details of my current behavior. He then asked about you, saying he had heard that you were a noble-minded person, and that on his part, he did not want to be in your debt. He also asked if five hundred rubles would be enough for all that you had done for me? When I explained to him what you had done for me that no money could repay, he said that it was all nonsense and the stuff of romances, that I was still young and read poetry, that romances ruined young girls, that books only corrupted morals, and that he could not stand any books. He advised me to live out his years and then talk about people, adding, “Then, and only then, will you truly understand people.” He also said that I should think carefully about his proposal and that it would be unpleasant for him if I took such an important step without thinking it through, and that thoughtlessness and infatuation ruined inexperienced youth, but that he would be extremely pleased with a favorable answer from me. Otherwise, he would be compelled to marry a shopkeeper’s widow in Moscow, because, he said, he had sworn to deprive his wicked nephew of his inheritance. He left five hundred rubles on my embroidery frame, as he said, for sweets. He told me that in the country I would fatten up like a pancake, that I would be rolling in the mud at his feet, that he had so many concerns now and that he had dashed about all day on business, but that he had dropped in on me as a favor. He then left. I thought long and overthought it, I was tortured, and at last I decided. My dear friend, I will marry him. I must agree to his proposal. If anyone can save me from my shame, restore my good name, and protect me from poverty, privation, and future misfortunes, it is only he. What can I hope for from the future, what else can I expect from fate? Fyodor says that one should not squander one’s happiness; but if that is the case, what, then, is happiness? Yet there were still moments of pause and half-bred reflection. Which paths! he then thought with dismay. Which paths! Like every man for whom natural achievements evoke aristocratic interest in his ancestry, he was accustomed to reflect on the accomplishments and successes of his life in relation to those of his forebears, to assure himself of their approval, satisfaction, and inevitable respect in his mind. He reflected on them even now, enmeshed in such an inappropriate experience, involved in such exotic excursions of feeling; and he thought of their dignified severity, their decent masculinity, and he smiled grimly. What would they have said? But, of course, what would they have said about his entire life, which so deviated from theirs as to verge on degeneration, about this life under the spell of art, about which he once, with the bourgeois mentality of his ancestors, had expressed such mocking juvenile insights and which in essence was so similar to theirs! He too had served, he too had undergone rigorous training; he too had been a soldier and a warrior, like many of them—since art was a war, an exhausting struggle, for which one could no longer be fit today. A life of self-overcoming and defiance, a harsh, steadfast, and abstemious life, which he had fashioned as a symbol of a delicate and contemporary heroism—indeed, he could call it manly and brave, and it seemed to him that the Eros who had mastered him was somehow particularly suited and inclined to such a life. Had he not enjoyed great prestige among the bravest peoples, and was it not said that he had flourished through bravery in their cities? Many ancient warriors had willingly borne his yoke, for no humiliation was inflicted by the gods, and acts that would have been branded as signs of cowardice if committed for other purposes—footsteps, oaths, importunate entreaties, and slave-like behavior—brought no shame to the lover, but rather he reaped praise for it.

Sages led the crowd into the inner chamber and greeted the Jade Emperor, then met with Laozi and Queen Mother of the West, and each took their seats. The Sages asked, "How was the Peach Banquet?" The Jade Emperor replied, "Every year, it was a grand affair. This year, however, was disrupted by that demon monkey, which was quite hollow." The Sages asked, "Where is this demon monkey from?" The Jade Emperor answered, "This demon monkey hails from the Flower and Fruit Mountain in the East Victory Continent of the nation of傲来国. At birth, he emitted golden light that shot up to the heavens. Initially, I paid no mind, but he eventually turned into a spirit and subdued the dragons and tamed the tigers, erasing his name from the register of the dead. It was then that the Dragon Kings and the King of Hell reported to me. I intended to capture him, but it was Long Star who reported that all creatures with nine orifices can become immortal. I then educated him and summoned him to heaven, where he was appointed as the attendant of the imperial stables, the Keeper of Horses. He was dissatisfied with the lowly position and rebelled against heaven. I then sent Heavenly King Li and Prince Nezha to subdue him, and later issued an imperial decree to appease him, summoned him to heaven, and bestowed upon him the title of ‘Great Sage Equal to Heaven,’ though he had no salary. Since then, he has roamed about idly. I feared he would cause trouble, so I appointed him as the manager of the Peach Garden. He, however, disregarded the laws and consumed all the old, large peaches. When the banquet was held, he, being an unremunerated individual, was not invited, so he plotted and tricked the Immortal Sandalwood, changed his appearance to enter the banquet, stole all the celestial dishes and drinks, stole Laozi’s immortal pills, and took several bottles of imperial wine to enjoy with his monkey compatriots. My heart is troubled by this, so I have dispatched a hundred thousand heavenly soldiers to ensnare and subdue him. I have not heard back from them today, so I wonder if they have prevailed."

The Bodhisattva led them into the inner chambers, paid respects to the Jade Emperor, then greeted Laozi and the Queen Mother, and they each took their seats. The Bodhisattva then asked, "How is the Peach Blossom Banquet?" The Jade Emperor replied, "We hold the banquet annually with great joy, but this year it was disrupted by the monkey demon, making it a mere pretense." The Bodhisattva asked, "What is the monkey demon's origin?" The Jade Emperor said, "The monkey demon originated from a stone egg on Flower and Fruit Mountain in the Eastern Victory States. When it first appeared, it radiated golden light that pierced the heavens. At first, we did not pay it any mind, but it later developed into a spirit capable of subduing dragons and tigers, and it struck its name from the records of the dead. It was then reported to me by the Dragon King and the Judge of the Soul. I intended to capture it, but Longxing Star announced that in the Three Realms, any creature with nine orifices can become immortal. So, I educated and promoted him, bringing him to the celestial court and appointing him as Director of the Imperial Stables. That fiend was dissatisfied with the position and rebelled against the Heavenly Palace. I then dispatched Heavenly General Li and Prince Nezha to subdue him, and after much effort, I appointed him as 'Great Sage Equal to Heaven' without providing him with a salary. In his spare time, he wandered about. Worried that he might cause trouble, I appointed him to oversee the Peach Blossom Garden. However, he disobeyed the laws and ate all the old trees and large peaches. When the banquet was set, as a non-paid individual, he was not invited. He then deceived and lured the Sandalwood Sandalwood Immortal to the banquet and, changing his appearance, stole all the celestial dishes and drinks, took the Immortal’s elixirs, and drank a great deal of imperial wine, which he shared with the other monkeys on the mountain. This caused me much distress, so I mobilized ten thousand heavenly troops to capture him. I have yet to hear of the outcome."

Bodhisattva led the crowd into the interior and, after paying respects to the Jade Emperor, greeted the Venerable Laojun and the Queen Mother of the West, then each took their seats. Bodhisattva then asked, "How was the Peach Blossom Banquet?" The Jade Emperor replied, "We hold this banquet annually, filled with joy, but this year it was disrupted by a monkey demon, making it a hollow affair." Bodhisattva inquired, "Where does this monkey demon come from?" The Jade Emperor answered, "This monkey demon hails from the Eastern Victory Region State of Huaguo Mountain. When it was born, it emitted golden light that pierced the celestial mansion of the Supreme Ruler of the Northern Dipper. At first, we did not take it seriously, but later it became a spirit, subduing dragons and taming tigers, removing its name from the register of the dead. The Dragon Kings and the King of Hell submitted reports to me. I wished to capture and punish it, but the Evening Star advised, ‘In the three realms, any creature with nine apertures can become immortal.’ So I educated and appointed him as a bureaucratic official, granting him the position of Stable Master of the Imperial Stables. He was dissatisfied with the small position and rebelled against the heavenly palace. I then sent Heavenly King Li and Prince Nezha to subdue him, but issued a decree to pacify the situation and had him brought to the heavenly palace, whereupon I bestowed upon him the title of ‘Great Sage Equal to Heaven,’ a position with title but no salary. Due to nothing to do, he roamed about the eastern and western regions. I feared that he might cause trouble elsewhere, so I assigned him to guard the Peach Blossom Orchard. But he disobeyed the laws and regulations, eating all the old and large peaches. When the banquet was set, he, as an untitled individual, was not invited, so he devised a trick to trick and deceive the Red-haired Immortal into the banquet, assuming his appearance to enter and steal all the immortal feasts and drinks. He also stole Laojun’s elixirs and several barrels of imperial wine, which he took to his fellow monkeys on his mountain to enjoy. This has caused me great distress, so I have deployed ten thousand heavenly soldiers, setting a trap to capture him. I have not heard back today; I do not know the outcome."

The Bodhisattva led the assembly inside and, after paying respects to the Jade Emperor, greeted the Elder Immortal and Queen Mother, each taking their seat. The Bodhisattva then asked, "How was the Peach Blossom Banquet?" The Jade Emperor replied, "Every year we have a feast filled with joy, but this year it was ruined by the havoc wrought by that monkey demon, leaving it mere pretense." The Bodhisattva inquired, "Where is this monkey from?" The Jade Emperor answered, "The monkey demon hails from the Flower and Fruit Mountain in the Eastern Shu Province of the country of Waigu. At birth, it was formed from a stone egg. Immediately after birth, it emitted golden light that shot up to the heavens. At first, we did not pay it heed, but soon it attained its own form and subdued dragons and tigers, striking its name from the register of the dead. Dragon Kings and the Jade Emperor then reported to me. I sought to capture the monkey, but it was Longju Star who advised that any being with nine orifices could become an immortal. I then educated and promoted him, summoned him to the celestial realm, and appointed him as the Assistant Stablemaster at the Imperial Stables. This wretch was dissatisfied with the position and rebelled against the celestial palace. I then sent Heavenly General Li and Prince Nezha to subdue him, but I later issued an imperial decree to appease him, summoned him to the celestial realm once again, and appointed him as the ‘Great Sage Equal to Heaven.’ However, he was only given a position without a salary. Unhappy with this, he spent his time idling around. Concerned that he might cause trouble, I appointed him as the custodian of the Peach Blossom Orchard. But he defied the laws, eating the old and large peaches from the orchard. When the banquet was held, as an unsalaried individual, he was not invited. He tricked the Barefoot Immortal into attending and disguised himself to enter the banquet, consuming all the celestial delicacies and drinks. He also stole the Elder Immortal’s immortal pills and many bottles of imperial wine, bringing them back to the mountain to share with his fellow monkeys. This caused me much distress, so I deployed ten thousand heavenly soldiers to capture him. I have not heard from them today, and I am uncertain of the outcome."

The Bodhisattva led them into the inner chambers and paid their respects to the Jade Emperor. After that, they met Laojun and the Queen Mother, each taking their seats. Then he inquired, "How is the Peach Blossom Banquet proceeding?" The Jade Emperor replied, "Every year, we hold the banquet with joy and merriment. This year, however, a mischievous monkey has caused chaos, leaving it far from a success." The Bodhisattva asked, "Where is this monkey from?" The Jade Emperor answered, "The monkey originated from the Flower Fruit Mountain in the Eastern Victory State in the land of Haoli. When it was born, it emitted golden light that pierced through the stars. Initially, we did not pay much attention, but it soon developed into a spirit capable of subduing dragons and taming tigers, removing its name from the list of the dead. The Dragon Kings and King Yama informed me of this. I intended to capture it, but Longjing Star advised, saying, 'In the three realms, anyone with nine orifices can become a仙.' So, I educated and appointed him as a governor in the heavenly court, bestowing upon him the title of弼马温, Supervisor of the Imperial Stables. However, he was displeased with the position's insignificance and rebelled against the heavenly court. I then sent Lao Tian Wang and Prince Nezha to subdue him, issued a proclamation to pacify the situation, and had him brought to the heavenly court where he was bestowed the title of ‘Great Sage Equal to Heaven,’ though without any salary. Bored with his duties, he went traveling, roving east and west. Worried that he might cause trouble, I made him the caretaker of the Peach Garden. My heart was troubled by this, and thus I mobilized ten thousand celestial troops, set up a net of heaven, and subdued him. Bronze serpents and iron dogs feast at will, forever plunged into the River of Unending Suffering with no way out. The poem says: "Hear the wails of ghosts and the cries of gods, blood turbid waves surge a hundred feet high. Countless heads of oxen and faces of horses, grimly guarding the Bridge of the River of Woe." As they spoke, the bridgekeepers had already returned. The Emperor Taizong's heart was once again filled with alarm, nodding and sighing in silent sorrow, following the official and marshal, swiftly crossing the evil waters of the River of Woe, and entering the bitter realm. They proceeded to the City of the Perished, where commotion was heard, clearly shouting, "Li Shimin has come! Li Shimin has come!" Taizong heard his name and was terror-stricken. He saw a horde of ghostly creatures with broken limbs and missing heads, blocking the path and shouting, "Return my life! Return my life!" Taizong, fearing for his life, hid and dodged, shouting, "Master Chu! Save me! Master Chu! Save me!" The official said, "Your Majesty, these people are the souls of the 64 places of smoke and dust, the 72 bandit groups, the spirits of princes and leaders; all are the unrightfully deceased, unrespected, and unable to cross over. Without money for passage, they are all hungry ghosts. Your Majesty can offer some money to release them." Taizong said, "I have arrived empty-handed, where could I find money?" The official said, "In the mortal world, there is a man with a certain amount of gold and silver in the netherworld, entrusted to me. If Your Majesty can provide your name and enter into an agreement, and I can vouch, I can borrow a treasury for you to distribute to these hungry ghosts, allowing them to cross." My friend, I only wanted to make you laugh, but by God, it was Jesuitical casuistry, and by God, everything happened letter for letter as I told you. This incident is recent and caused me much trouble. The unfortunate young man returned home that very night and shot himself; I was with him until the very last moment… As for these Jesuit confession huts, they are truly the sweetest amusement of my gloomy life. Here is another case, right from the other day. A blonde girl, a Norman, about twenty years old, comes to the old priest. She is a beauty, with a body and a nature that make one salivate. She leans over and whispers her sin to the priest’s ear. "My daughter, surely you have fallen again?..." the priest exclaims. "O Holy Mary," he cries, "what do I hear: not with the same person. But how long will this continue, and how shameful this must be for you!" – "Ah Father," the sinner replies, all in repentant tears. "It gives him so much pleasure, but to me it causes so little pain!" – Well, imagine such an answer! I couldn’t hold back any longer: this was the cry of nature itself, this, if you will, truer than innocence itself! I absolved her of her sin and was about to leave, but was immediately forced to turn back: I heard the priest make an appointment with her for a later evening, but the old man is as stubborn as a mule, and there he fell in an instant! Nature, truth, took its due! Are you turning up your nose at me again, are you getting angry once more? I don’t know what to do to please you any longer.

The monk delivered the sutras and stepped onto the cloud, heading for the blackbird's nest. But Tripitaka once more held him back, insisting on knowing the exact route to the West. The monk smiled and said, "The journey is not hard. Listen to what I say: across a thousand mountains and rivers, deep and perilous. Watch out for the Pinnacle Cliff, where you may be confident and not fear. When you reach the Towering Rock, take care when stepping. Be cautious in the Dark Pine Grove, where foxes often lurk. Evil spirits fill the cities, demons inhabit the mountains. Tigers and wolves sit in their thrones, lions and leopards reign as kings. Wild boars carry burdens, and water monsters wait ahead. The old stone monkey has been waiting for years, and will not bear any grudge. Ask the locals, they know the way to the West." Upon hearing this, the monkey smirked, saying, "We will not ask him; we will know it ourselves." But Tripitaka still did not understand. The monk turned into a golden beam and ascended to the blackbird's nest. The master bowed to thank him, and the monkey, enraged, raised his iron rod and pummeled the sky, but saw lotuses bloom a thousandfold and auspicious clouds encircle the nest. No matter how he tried, he could not reach even a single strand of the nest. Tripitaka held the monkey back and said, "Monkey, why are you destroying the nest of this holy man?" The monkey replied, "He cursed our two brothers." Tripitaka said, "He merely spoke of the route to the West; how could he curse you?" The monkey said, "You do not understand. 'Wild boars carrying burdens' refers to Sanzang's brother, and 'the old stone monkey' refers to me. How could you not understand?" Piggy said, "Brother, calm down. This monk knows past and future. Let us see if his prediction about water monsters holds true. Let him go." Seeing the lotuses and auspicious clouds, the monkey hesitated and asked the master to mount the horse and head west. As they went, it was foretold that they would have less peace on earth and more disasters in the mountains. They continued on, unsure of the road ahead, to be revealed in the next chapter.

The Zen master recited the scriptures and stepped on the cloud light, about to depart for the Black Nest, when Tripitaka held him back and insisted on asking about the exact route to the West. The Zen master smiled and said, "The journey is not difficult. Listen to my instructions: Through a thousand mountains and a thousand waters, deep and dangerous, there are many miasmas and demons. When you encounter the Sky-reaching Cliff, relax and do not be fearful. As you pass by the Finger-pointing Rock, take care to place your steps. Beware the dark pine forest, for bandits and fox spirits often lie in wait there. Demons and spirits fill the cities, and demons dwell in the mountains. Tigers and wolves sit in the hall as masters, lions and leopards are kings, and wild boars carry burdens. You will meet a long-lived stone monkey there, who will not bear any grudge. Ask any you meet, and they will know the road to the West." Upon hearing this, the Monkey King laughed coldly and said, "We need not ask him; we will ask ourselves." Tripitaka did not yet understand the meaning, so the Zen master transformed into a golden light and went straight to the Black Nest. The monk bowed in gratitude, but the Monkey King was furious and raised his iron rod, striking wildly at the sky. Only then did lotus flowers bloom in myriad blossoms and a layer of auspicious clouds protect everything. Even with the power to stir the sea and overturn the river, the Monkey King could not grasp a single strand of the nest. Tripitaka pulled him back and said, "Monkey, why are you destroying the abode of such a Buddha?" The Monkey King replied, "He verbally abused my two brothers just now." Tripitaka said, "What he said about the path to the West, how could he have abused you?" The Monkey King said, "You don't understand. He said the wild boar carrying a burden is a rebuke to Xuanzang, and the long-lived stone monkey is a rebuke to me. How can you understand this?" Xuanzang said, "Silence, Brother. Let him go." Seeing the lotus flowers and auspicious clouds, the Monkey King only then asked the monk to mount his horse and go down the mountain to head west. On this journey, the clear blessings of the world are few, but calamities and demons in the mountains are many. The exact outcome of their journey remains to be seen; tune in for the next chapter.

"Nothing of the kind!" Razumikhin interrupted with heat, "I'm not lying!... I'll show you their books: everything is there because 'society has got in the way,' – and nothing else! That's their favorite phrase! From that it follows directly that if society is organized properly, all crimes will disappear at once, since there will be nothing to protest against, and all will become righteous in one fell swoop. Nature is not taken into account, nature is driven out, there is no place for nature! They do not believe that humanity, having developed historically and organically to the end, will of its own accord turn into a normal society. On the contrary, a social system, emerging from some mathematical head, will instantly set everything right and make all of humanity righteous and sinless, before any living process can take place, before any historical and organic path can be followed! How it came about, however, that all the Epanchins suddenly all at once took to one and the same thought about what had befallen Aglaya and about how her fate was at stake—this is very difficult to set out in order. But as soon as the thought flashed, all of them at once got on to the idea that they had long since perceived everything and foreseen everything quite clearly; that everything had been clear even from the "poor knight," even before that, only they did not want to believe in such nonsense. This is what the sisters maintained. Of course, Lizaveta Prokofievna had seen and known everything in advance and for a long time her heart had ached; but whether long ago or not, now the thought of the prince all of a sudden became too much of a bother for her, precisely because it confused her. A question was now at hand that had to be resolved immediately; but not only could it not be resolved, but poor Lizaveta Prokofievna could not even put the question before herself in full clarity, however much she tried. The matter was difficult: "Is the prince good or not? Is everything all right or not? If not (and that is unquestionable), then why exactly not? And if, perhaps, he is good (which is also possible), then why exactly so?" Of course, the head of the family, Ivan Fedorovich, was first of all astonished, but then all of a sudden made a confession that for all these years, "by God, it had been all the same to him, now and then it seemed and all of a sudden it would seem as if it did!" "And from another angle, if we look at the matter straightforwardly, then the prince, by God, is a wonderful fellow, and... and... and..." (A long pause and a firm faltering). Lizaveta Prokofievna listened to her husband and then went out of herself.

— This is all true, — Rogozhin confirmed grimly and glumly, frowning, — and Zalezhiev was telling me the same thing. I was crossing Nevsky in my father's beshmet and shoe polish that day, when she came out of the shop and got into a carriage. That's when it really hit me. I ran into Zalezhiev; he was much more dressed up than I was, strolling about like a barber's clerk with a monocle in his eye, while we were standing out in the rain in our greasy boots and on our fasting bread. "You're no match for her," he said, "that's Mrs. Natassia Filippovna, they call her. She's Baryshnikov by her last name, and she's living with Totsky, who's now at a loss as to how to get rid of her, since she's reached the ripe old age of fifty-five and wants to marry the most beautiful woman in all of St. Petersburg." Zalezhiev then impressed upon me that I could see Natassia Filippovna tonight at the Great Theatre, in the ballet, in her own box, seated in the bays. He said it would be impossible to go to the ballet at our place — sheer damnation! But I managed to sneak out for an hour and saw Natassia Filippovna again; I didn't sleep all night. The next morning the deadbeat gave me two five-percent tickets, each worth five thousand, saying, "Sell these and take seven thousand five hundred to Andreiev's office, pay up, and bring the rest of the change from ten thousand, without stopping anywhere, I'll be waiting for you." I sold the tickets and got the money, but didn't go to Andreiev's office; instead, I walked around aimlessly, went to an English shop, and chose a pair of earrings, one diamond in each, each costing almost four hundred rubles. I gave my name and they believed me. With the earrings in hand, I went to Zalezhiev: "So, what do we do now, brother, shall we go see Natassia Filippovna?" We went. What was under my feet, in front of me, on either side — I have no idea, I don't remember. We went straight into the auditorium, and she herself came out to meet us. I didn't say that I was the one who sent him; Zalezhiev said, "This is from Parfen Rogozhin, to commemorate our meeting from yesterday; accept it, if you will." She opened the envelope, looked inside, and smiled, saying, "Thank you for Mr. Rogozhin's kind gesture," and left. Well, why didn't I just die then and there! But even if I did, I would have thought, "It doesn't matter, I won't come back alive anyway!" But the worst part was that this scoundrel Zalezhiev took all the credit for himself. I was short, dressed like a lackey, standing there, eyes fixed on her, embarrassed, while he was all the rage, painted, with curly red cheeks, wearing a checked necktie, and showering her with compliments, and she probably thought he was me! "So, how are you going to explain to Semen Parfenovich when we leave?" I wanted to go straight home, but thought, "Well, it doesn't matter anyway," and went home with the Devil.

I told the name, and they believed me. I came to Zalezhnev with the pendants: “Well, let’s go, brother, to Nastasya Filippovna.” We set off. I have no idea, no recollection of what was under my feet, what was before me, or what was on either side of me. We walked straight into her box, and she came to meet us herself. I did not reveal myself to be the one who had sent the pendants; instead, Zalezhnev said, “These are from Parfen Rogozhin, as a memento of yesterday’s meeting; please accept them.” She opened the box, looked at it, smiled, and said, “Thank you for the kind gift from Mr. Rogozhin,” and went away. Well, I wish I had died then! If I had, it would have been because I thought, “I won’t be coming back alive anyway!” The most hurtful thing to me was that Zalezhnev had taken all the credit for himself. I am short, I am dressed like a livery man, I stand there, I remain silent, and I fix my eyes on her because I am ashamed, while he is dressed according to the latest fashion, with a red lipstick, curly, rosy, and in a checked cravat, and he breaks into a run, bowing and scraping, and it is quite clear that she took him for me! “Well, what are you going to tell Semen Parfenich about it now?” I wanted to jump into the river and go straight home, but I thought, “It doesn’t matter anyway,” and went home like a sinner.

—"This is all true," Rogozhin confirmed gloomily and scowling, "and Zarozhev even told me that. At the time, your highness, I was crossing Nevsky Prospect in my father's beshmet, while she came out of a store and got into a carriage. That's when I felt the sting of it. I ran into Zarozhev; he was a cut above me, strutting like a store clerk from a barber, with a monocle in his eye, while we were distinguished in our greasy boots and hunger-stained shirts. 'You are not like him,' he said, 'this is Knyaginya Nastasya Filippovna, Barashkova by surname, and she lives with Toporkov, and now Toporkov doesn't know how to break away from her since she is now fifty-five and wants to marry the first belle of St. Petersburg. He convinced me then that I could see Nastasya Filippovna tonight in the Mariinsky Theatre, in the ballet, in her own box, she will be sitting there. You can't try to go to the ballet at home, your highness, it will be a catastrophe, it will kill you!' However, I snuck out for an hour and saw Nastasya Filippovna again; I didn't sleep the whole night. The next morning, the dead man gave me two five percent shares, each for five thousand, 'Go and sell them,' he said, 'and bring seven thousand five hundred to Andreiev's office, pay up, and the remaining change from ten thousand, without going anywhere else, give it to me.' I sold the shares and got the money, but I didn't go to Andreiev's office, instead, I walked to an English store and picked a pair of pendants, one diamond in each, it will be worth four hundred roubles, and I said the name, and they believed me. With the pendants, I went to Zarozhev: 'Well, so, brother, let's go and see Nastasya Filippovna.' We set off. I don't remember what was under my feet, what was in front of me, or what was by my sides at that moment. We went straight to her box, she came to greet us. I didn't say that I was the one; Zarozhev said, 'These are from Parfen Rogozhin, to remember our meeting from yesterday.' She opened the box, looked inside, smiled: 'Thank your friend, Mr. Rogozhin, for his kind thought,' and left. Well, why didn't I die right then! If I did, it would have been because I thought, 'I won't come back alive anyway!' But the most infuriating thing was that this bastard Zarozhev took everything for himself. I was short and dressed like a servant, standing there, saying nothing, staring at her, for shame, while he was all in vogue, painted, with curled hair, rosy, in a checked cravat, he was bowing and scraping, and she must have taken him for me! 'Well, what do you think, we're out, you're not going to even think of coming back here!' He laughed: 'And what do you think, you'll have to give an account to Semen Parfenovich?' I was thinking of drowning then, not going home, but then I thought, 'Well, it's the same either way,' and returned home like a damned man.

— This is all true, — Rogozhin confirmed gloomily, his brows drawn down, — and Zalézhëv told me the same thing. Back then, my lord, I was crossing Nevsky in my father’s brocade housecoat, while she was coming out of a shop, getting into a carriage. That’s when I was really burnt. I met Zalézhëv, who was the opposite of me, walking like a shop assistant from a barber’s, with a monocle in his eye, while we were distinguished in our greasy boots and fasting coats. He said, “You’re no match for this, this countess, named Natalya Filippovna Barashkova, who lives with Zotykin. Zotykin doesn’t know how to get rid of her because she’s reached a real age of fifty-five and wants to marry the most beautiful woman in all of St. Petersburg. He told me today that I could see Natalya Filippovna in the Bolshoi Theatre tonight, in the ballet, in her own box, sitting in the benoîre. You won’t be able to get into the ballet at our place, my lord, it’s all organized! — He said. I went there, however, and saw Natalya Filippovna again; I didn’t sleep the whole night. In the morning, the deceased gave me two five percent tickets, each for five thousand, and said, “Go, sell them, bring seven thousand five hundred to Andreiev’s office for payment, and leave the rest of the change from ten thousand at my place without going anywhere else; I’ll be waiting for you.” I sold the tickets and got the money, but didn’t go to Andreiev’s office. Instead, I went aimlessly to an English store and picked out a pair of earrings, one diamond in each, so that they would be about the size of walnuts, and said my name, which they accepted. With the earrings, I went to Zalézhëv: So, let’s go, brother, to Natalya Filippovna. We set off. I don’t know what was under my feet, in front of me, or to the sides at that moment. We walked directly into her box, where she came out to us. I didn’t say I was Rogozhin, but Zalézhëv said, “From Parfen Rogozhin, this is in memory of our meeting yesterday; please accept it.” She opened the box, looked at it, smiled, and said, “Thank you for your friend, Mr. Rogozhin, for his kind gesture,” and left. Well, why didn’t I die right there! If I did go, it’s because I thought, “It doesn’t matter, I won’t be coming back alive anyway!” But what hurt me the most was that Zalézhëv took all the credit for it. I was short, dressed like a valet, and stood there, looking at her in silence, because I was embarrassed, while he was dressed according to the latest fashion, in lipstick and curls, rosy, with a checked necktie, so he was the one who fell apart, the one who kept bowing, and it was likely she thought he was me! “So, when we came out, you’re not to think about it at all,” I said. He laughed and said, “So, are you going to give an account to Semen Parfenovich now?” I really wanted to go home, but then I thought, “Well, it doesn’t matter,” and I came back home like a damned man.

— This is all true, — Rogozhin confirmed gloomily, frowning. "It was even Zalezhov who told me that. I was crossing Nevsky Prospect in my father’s beshmertsk, in my oilskin shoes, while she came out of the shop, got into a carriage. That’s when I was burnt. I ran into Zalezhov; he was more like a shopkeeper than I was, sauntering about with a monocle in his eye, while we in our greasy boots and fasting shirts stood out. ‘This is not for you,’ he said, ‘this is Countess Natalya Filipovna Barashkova, and she lives with Tsokolov. But now Tsokolov doesn’t know how to get rid of her, as she’s reached the ripe age of fifty-five, and he wants to marry the foremost beauty in all of St. Petersburg. Here he told me that tonight you can see Natalya Filipovna at the Bolshoi Theatre, in the ballet, in her box, in the benzare. Try to go to the ballet at home — it’s nothing but a disaster, it’ll kill you! I snuck out for an hour and saw Natalya Filipovna again; I didn’t sleep all that night. The next morning, the corpse gave me two five-percent tickets, each for five thousand, and said, ‘Sell them and bring me seven thousand five hundred to Andreiev’s office for payment. Take the rest of the change from ten thousand; I’ll be waiting for you without going anywhere.’ I sold the tickets, took the money, but didn’t go to Andreiev’s office. I went straight to the English shop and picked out a pair of earrings, one diamond in each, they’ll cost me about four hundred. I gave my name, they believed me. With the earrings, I went to Zalezhov: ‘Well, brother, let’s go see Natalya Filipovna.’ We went in. I didn’t know what was under my feet, in front of me, or on either side. We walked straight into her box, and she came out to us. I didn’t reveal that I was the one; Zalezhov said, ‘These are from Parfen Rogozhin as a token of our meeting yesterday. Please accept.’ She opened the tickets, looked at them, and smiled: ‘Thank you for the kind gesture of Mr. Rogozhin, your friend, for his friendly attention,’ — she said, turned around, and left. Well, if only I had died there! But even if I had gone, I would have thought: ‘It makes no difference; I won’t come back alive!’ But what hurt me the most was that that beast Zalezhov took everything for himself. I am short and dressed like a servant, standing there, not speaking, just staring at her out of shame, while he, in all the latest fashion, with his lip gloss and curled hair, rosy, with a checked cravat, was effusively bowing and flunkeying, and she probably took him for me! ‘Well, when we left,’ I said, ‘don’t you dare think about me anymore!’ He laughed: ‘And will you now give an account to Semen Parfenich? ’ I really wanted to drown myself then and there, without going home, but I thought, ‘It makes no difference anyway,’ and I returned home in a state of utter debauchery.

– You won’t believe it, Polenka, you can’t even imagine, – she said, pacing the room, – how happily and magnificently we lived in Papa’s house, and how this drunkard destroyed me, and will destroy all of you! Papa was a civil military captain and was already nearly a governor; all it took was one more step, so everyone went to see him and said, “We already count on you, Ivan Mikhailovich, as our governor.” When I… cough! When I… cough-cough-cough… oh, accursed life! – she exclaimed, bringing up phlegm and clutching her breast, – when I… oh, at the last ball… at the governor’s… Countess Bezobrazova saw me, who later blessed me when I was marrying your father, Polya – she immediately asked, “Is this not the lovely girl who danced with a shawl at the graduation ball?…” (The hole needs to be sewn up; take the needle and mend it right now, just as I taught you, before it’s too late tomorrow… cough!… tomorrow… cough-cough-cough!… it will tear even more!)… The Count Scheglovsky, who had just arrived from Petersburg, had also danced a mazurka with me and was planning to visit the next day with an offer of marriage; but I thanked him warmly and said that my heart was already pledged to someone else. This someone else was your father, Polya; Papa was furious. Is the water ready? Well, bring me a shirt; and socks?… Lida, – she addressed her little daughter, – you will sleep without a shirt tonight; just… lay out the socks nearby… So we can wash everything at once… What a ragamuffin, this drunk! He brought a shirt, as though to wipe something with, and tore it to shreds… If only everything could be done at once, so we wouldn’t have to suffer through two nights! Oh Lord! Cough-cough-cough-cough! Again! What is it? – she cried, looking at the crowd in the hall and at the people cramming in with some burden. – What is it? What are they bringing in? Oh Lord!

"You won't believe it, you can't even imagine it, Polenka," she said, pacing the room, "how happily and magnificently we lived in Papa's house, and how this drunkard has ruined me, and how he'll ruin all of you! Papa was a state colonel and was almost a governor; there was just one more step for him, so everyone came to him and said, 'We already count on you, Ivan Mikhailovich, as our governor.' When I... cough! When I... cough-cough-cough... oh, cursed life! – she cried, coughing up phlegm and clutching her chest – when I... ah, when at the last ball... at the governor's... Princess Bezhdezhnaya saw me, who blessed me later when I married your Papa, Polina – she immediately asked, "Isn't that the sweet young lady who danced with a shawl at the graduation?" (This gap needs to be stitched; I could take the needle and stitch it right now, as I taught you, but it'll be worse tomorrow... cough!... tomorrow... cough-cough-cough!...)... Just then, the Camerer-cadet, Prince Shchedolsky, had just arrived from Petersburg... he danced with me a mazurka, and the next day he wanted to come with an offer; but I thanked him in flattering words and said that my heart belonged to someone else. That someone else was your father, Polina; Papa was terribly angry... Is the water ready? Well, get a nightgown; and the stockings?... Lida, – she addressed her little daughter – you'll sleep this night without a nightgown; you can manage... but put the stockings out next to... to wash them at the same time... What a ragamuffin, what a drunkard! He brought the nightgown, like some sort of wiping cloth, and tore it all to shreds... It would all be better if we could wash everything at once, to avoid suffering for two nights in a row! Oh Lord! Cough-cough-cough-cough! Again! What is this? – she exclaimed, looking at the crowd in the hallway and the people shoving in with some load. – What is it? What are they bringing? Oh Lord!

"你不会相信的，你简直无法想象，波琳卡，"她边说边在房间里走来走去，"我们父母家过得多么快活、多么铺张，而这个酒鬼却把我毁了，也会毁了你们所有人！爸爸是个文职上校，几乎就要成为知事了；对他来说，只是剩下最后一小步了，因此所有人都说他：‘伊万·米哈伊洛维奇，我们可把你当成知事看待了。’当我……咳！当我……咳-咳-咳……啊，可咒的命！——她咯了几下痰，双手捂住胸口尖叫道——当我……啊，就是在那个舞会上……在领头人的……贝兹杰姆诺娃公爵夫人看见了我，她后来在你爸爸迎娶我的时候还为我祝福过，——她立刻问道：‘难道你就是那位舞会上拿着披肩跳舞的可爱小姐吗……’（缝个口子吧；就拿针来，现在就缝上，像我教你的一样，明天……咳！……明天……咳-咳-咳！……会更坏！——她颤抖着喊道……）……还未来得及从彼得堡来的枢密官斯捷戈廖夫斯基公爵，在前一天晚上就跳了玛祖卡舞，并想第二天来求婚；但我用友好的言辞拒绝了他，并告诉他我早已把心许给了别人。这个别人就是你的父亲，波琳卡；爸爸为此大发雷霆……那水烧好了吗？好，拿套内衣来；袜子呢？……丽达，——她对着小女儿说道——今晚你就不用内衣了，睡吧；不一会儿……别忘了放些袜子……顺便洗洗……这流浪汉可不行，这个酒鬼！把内衣藏得像什么擦布似的，全给撕破了……要一起洗，好让两晚都免受折磨！主啊！咳-咳-咳-咳！又来了！这是什么？——她看了一眼门厅里的人群，还有那些把什么东西挤进她房间的人，尖叫道——这是什么？他们拿的是什么？

" she exclaimed, looking at the crowd in the hallway and the people pressing in with something in their hands. "What is this? What are they bringing?"

Soon after, the sound of bells and drums echoed, and sure enough, the three sea kings were startled awake. They arrived shortly and gathered outside. Ao Qin said, "Big Brother, what urgent matter is there that you’ve set the drums and bells a-ringing?" The old king said, "Brother! It’s not to be spoken of! There’s this Sage of Huaguo Mountain who came to recognize me as a neighbor in the morning. Then he requested a weapon, rejecting both the spear and the lance. He produced a piece of Divine Treasure Iron from the Heavens himself, performed some tricks with it, and now is seated in the palace, demanding some armor. I have nothing to offer him, so I’ve had the drums and bells rung, inviting you here. Do any of you have any armor to give him, so we can send him away?"

Hearing this, Ao Qin became very angry, saying, "I’ll call up my troops and capture him!" The old king said, "Not to mention capturing him! That piece of iron, even touching it slightly would result in death, and striking it even slightly would result in injury. One’s skin would be broken, and one’s tendons hurt!" Ao Ren, the king of the West Sea, said, "Brother, you shouldn’t fight him; just assemble some armor for him, send him on his way, and report to Heaven, and Heaven will deal with him." Ao Shun, the king of the North Sea, said, "That’s right. I have a pair of lotus-threaded cloud shoes here." Ao Ren, the king of the West Sea, said, "I have a suit of linked golden armor with me." Ao Qin, the king of the South Sea, said, "I have a phoenix-winged purple gold crown." The old king was overjoyed, and introduced Sun Wukong to the Crystal Palace, where the armor and shoes were presented. Sun Wukong dressed himself in the gold crown, the gold armor, and the cloud shoes, then wielded his如意棍, and went out to face the sea kings, saying, "Noisy! Noisy!" Not long after, as the chimes and gongs sounded, the three sea kings were indeed startled. They arrived shortly and gathered outside. After noon, he left the beach, returned to the hotel, and was driven up to his room. He lingered there in front of the mirror, examining his grey hair, his worn and sharp features. At that moment, he thought of his fame and of the many who knew him on the streets and looked at him reverently, for the precision and grace of his sure words—his countless external successes as a talent, all that came to mind—and even considered his knighthood. Then he went down to lunch in the dining room and ate at his little table. When he boarded the elevator after finishing his meal, a crowd of young people who had just come from breakfast pressed in after him into the moving alcove, and Tadzio entered as well. The boy stood very close to Aschenbach, closer than ever before, so close that he was no longer seen as a figure in an imagined distance, but exactly, as a person, in his humanity, which Aschenbach perceived and recognized. Someone addressed the boy, who replied with an indescribably charming smile and then went out again, on the first floor, with his head down and eyes cast back. Beauty makes one ashamed, thought Aschenbach, and he pondered deeply why. Yet he had noticed that Tadzio’s teeth were not altogether pleasing: sharp and pale, without the luster of health and with an unusual dry transparency like sometimes in the case of those with anorexia. He is very delicate, thought Aschenbach. He will probably not live long. And he refrained from giving any thought to a feeling of satisfaction or relief that accompanied these thoughts.

Again, the bamboo beat signaled the waning moon and the roosters crowed as dawn's clouds rose. The monks arose, tidied the tea and early breakfast. Tang Sanzang then put on his robe and ascended the main hall, kneeling before the Buddha and saying, "Disciple Chen Tang Sanzang travels westward to fetch the scriptures, but with my limited vision, I cannot discern the true form of the living Buddha. I hereby vow: upon encountering a temple, I shall offer incense; before every Buddha, I shall bow; and before every pagoda, I shall sweep. May the Buddha show compassion and appear in his full measure, granting me the true scriptures to disseminate to the Eastern lands."

With that, he returned to the dormitory for breakfast. After the meal, the two attendants prepared their saddles and spurred him to hasten. The trio emerged through the monastery gate, bidding farewell to the monks. The monks, unwilling to part, walked a full ten miles, weeping as they turned back. Tang Sanzang continued westward. The autumn was well advanced, and all around he saw: several hamlets with fallen trees and fragmented reeds, a few trees shedding crimson leaves. The travelers, few and far between in the misty and rainy roads, found only yellow chrysanthemums, fine hill veins, cold waters, withered lotuses, and despondent travelers. On the frosty sky, white water lilies and red aromatic rushes shivered; red and yellow sunsets, solitary cranes, and descending geese fell from the sky. Dark, somber wild clouds drifted by, as the swallows departed and geese arrived, their mournful cries filling the night sky.

Again it was the dawn with bamboo tapping against the waning moon, and roosters crowing as morning clouds rose. The monks arose, tidying the tea and breakfast. Then Tang went up to the main hall, before the Buddha, and said, "Disciple Chen Xuanzang, going to the Western Heavens to seek scriptures, but with dim eyesight, I cannot recognize the true form of the living Buddha. The monks were unwilling to part and followed him for ten miles, weeping as they turned back. Tang continued westward. It was late autumn. And there was: scattered villages with fallen trees and shattered rushes, a few poplars and firs shedding red leaves. On the road, mist and rain made people scarce, yellow chrysanthemums blooming, mountain bones fine, water cold, lotuses withered, and people haggard. White tules and red sedges in frosty skies, falling sunset cranes and lone wild geese plummeting into the vast sky. Dusk bringing clouds in shades of grey, swallows departing, wild geese arriving, their cries piercing the night.

Swallows departed, wild geese arrived, and their piercing cries echoed through the night.
